#### Collaboration Cursors

When supported by the provider, ART may display other users' current
editing locations.

For example:

    Alex — Editing: Finding 4, Description
    Jordan — Editing: Finding 4, Severity

Real-time cursor indicators shall be optional where practical.

They shall not interfere with keyboard navigation or screen-reader
operation.

#### Screen Reader Treatment of Collaboration Cursors

Visual collaboration cursors shall not automatically generate continuous
screen-reader announcements.

Screen-reader users shall have an accessible way to determine
collaborator locations when desired.

For example:

- 

Collaborator information command.

- 

Accessible collaborator list.

- 

Resource activity interface.

#### Selection Sharing

Where supported, ART may expose another user's current selection.

Selection information shall remain supplemental.

It shall not change the current user's keyboard focus or text selection.

#### User Presence Integration

Real-time editing shall integrate with the presence architecture
established in Part 6.

Presence shall indicate collaboration participation without implying
that a user is currently editing unless the provider can reliably
determine that state.

#### Editing Indicators

Where supported, ART may identify:

- 

Viewing.

- 

Editing.

- 

Typing.

- 

Selecting.

- 

Reviewing.

These states shall be provider-dependent.

Do not infer that a user is typing simply because they have a Report
open.

#### Resource Locking

Resource locking may be supported where the Collaboration Provider
requires it.

If locking is used:

- 

The locked resource shall be clearly identified.

- 

The reason for the lock should be available.

- 

The user who holds the lock should be identified where appropriate.

- 

The user shall know when the resource becomes available.

- 

Locking shall not prevent users from performing actions that do not
require the lock.

Avoid broad locking when granular synchronization is possible.

#### Field-Level Locking

If a provider requires locking, prefer the smallest reasonable scope.

For example:

- 

Lock a field rather than the entire Report.

- 

Lock a section rather than the entire Workspace.

Do not lock unrelated content unnecessarily.

#### Lock Expiration

Locks shall not remain permanently active because of:

- 

Browser crashes.

- 

Network failures.

- 

Application closure.

- 

Unexpected session termination.

The Collaboration Provider shall determine appropriate lock-expiration
behavior.

#### Conflict Detection

Conflicts shall be detected using the centralized Collaboration
Framework.

Do not implement separate conflict-detection logic for each report
component unless the component requires specialized behavior.

#### Conflict Resolution Interface

When automatic merging is not possible, ART shall provide an accessible
conflict-resolution interface.

The interface shall clearly identify:

- 

Local version.

- 

Remote version.

- 

Current shared version.

- 

User who made each change.

- 

Date/time of each change.

- 

Available resolution actions.

Possible actions include:

- 

Keep local change.

- 

Keep remote change.

- 

Merge changes.

- 

Review differences.

- 

Retry synchronization.

- 

Save a copy.

- 

Cancel.

Available actions shall depend on the resource type and provider
capabilities.

#### Conflict Resolution Safety

ART shall not silently discard data during conflict resolution.

Before destructive conflict resolution:

- 

Clearly identify what will be replaced.

- 

Provide an opportunity to review the change.

- 

Preserve recoverable version information where supported.

#### Conflict Resolution Accessibility

The conflict-resolution interface shall support:

- 

Keyboard navigation.

- 

Screen readers.

- 

Braille.

- 

Voice control.

- 

Switch access.

Users shall be able to understand the differences without relying solely
on color or side-by-side visual presentation.

If visual diff information is provided, equivalent semantic information
shall be available to assistive technologies.

#### Focus During Conflict Resolution

Opening a conflict-resolution interface shall move focus to the
appropriate control.

Closing it shall restore focus to the invoking control or logical
previous location.

Conflict resolution shall never unexpectedly move focus to the top of
the page.

#### Undo and Redo

Collaborative editing shall preserve appropriate Undo and Redo behavior.

Undo should apply to the current user's changes rather than
indiscriminately reversing another user's changes.

The implementation shall clearly define how Undo behaves when remote
changes occur between local operations.

#### Collaboration History

Users with appropriate permissions may be able to review collaborative
revisions.

History should identify:

- 

User.

- 

Change.

- 

Date/time.

- 

Resource.

- 

Revision.

History shall integrate with the existing Audit Log and version-history
architecture.

#### Restore Previous Version

Where supported, authorized users may restore a previous resource
version.

Restoration shall be treated as a new change rather than silently
deleting the intervening history.

For example:

    Version 1
    Version 2
    Version 3
    Restore Version 1
    Version 4 — restored from Version 1

#### Autosave

Collaborative editing shall continue to support appropriate autosave
behavior.

Autosave shall not:

- 

Steal focus.

- 

Interrupt typing.

- 

Cause unnecessary screen-reader announcements.

- 

Overwrite remote changes without applying synchronization rules.

#### Network Interruption

If the network connection is lost while editing:

- 

The user shall be able to continue working locally where possible.

- 

Local changes shall be preserved.

- 

ART shall indicate that synchronization is pending.

- 

ART shall attempt reconnection.

- 

Changes shall synchronize when connectivity returns.

#### Reconnection

After reconnection, ART shall:

1.  

Determine the latest shared resource state.

2.  

Determine pending local changes.

3.  

Merge changes when possible.

4.  

Identify conflicts when necessary.

5.  

Preserve local work.

6.  

Update synchronization status.

The user shall not be required to manually reload the entire application
merely because the connection was temporarily interrupted.

#### Provider Failure

If the Collaboration Provider becomes unavailable:

- 

Local editing shall continue where possible.

- 

ART shall clearly communicate the provider problem.

- 

Pending changes shall remain recoverable.

- 

ART shall not falsely indicate that changes have synchronized.

#### Server-Side Failure Recovery

The architecture shall support recovery from provider-side failures.

ART shall not assume that a failed request means that a change was never
received.

Where necessary, synchronization operations shall be idempotent or
otherwise safely retryable.

#### Duplicate Operations

Retrying a synchronization operation shall not create duplicate:

- 

Findings.

- 

Comments.

- 

Reports.

- 

Fields.

- 

Working Views.

- 

Plugins.

- 

Accessibility Standard packages.

Operations shall have identifiers or equivalent mechanisms that allow
duplicate processing to be detected.

#### Transaction Boundaries

Where supported by the provider, related changes may be synchronized as
a transaction.

For example:

    Add Finding
    + Add associated evidence
    + Add associated comment

The exact transaction model shall depend on the resource architecture
and provider capabilities.

ART shall not assume that every provider supports distributed
transactions.

#### Collaboration Performance

Real-time collaboration shall be designed to minimize:

- 

UI latency.

- 

Excessive network traffic.

- 

Unnecessary rendering.

- 

Duplicate synchronization.

- 

Screen-reader interruptions.

Remote changes should not cause the entire Report interface to re-render
unnecessarily.

#### Large Reports

The Collaboration Framework shall be designed to support large reports
without requiring the entire report to be synchronized after every
change.

Prefer granular changes where the architecture supports them.

For example:

    Change:
    Finding 42 → Severity = High

is preferable to synchronizing the entire report document when
technically appropriate.

#### Working Views

Working Views shall remain primarily personal.

Real-time changes to a Report shall not automatically modify another
user's personal Working View configuration.

If a user edits their personal Working View:

- 

The change remains personal.

- 

Other users do not automatically receive the change.

Shared Working Views shall participate in collaboration when explicitly
shared.

#### Shared Working Views

When multiple users use a shared Working View:

- 

Changes shall follow the shared resource's collaboration rules.

- 

Authorized users may edit the shared Working View.

- 

Viewers may use the shared Working View without editing it.

- 

Users may create personal copies.

A user shall never have their personal Working View unexpectedly
converted into a shared Working View.

#### Permissions During Collaboration

Real-time editing shall continuously respect the effective permission
model.

If a user's permissions change while they are actively editing:

- 

ART shall update the user's available actions.

- 

Unauthorized future changes shall be prevented.

- 

Pending changes shall be handled safely.

- 

The user shall receive an accessible explanation when appropriate.

A user whose Edit permission is revoked shall not retain indefinite
editing authority simply because the Report was already open.

#### Permission Changes During Synchronization

If a user loses access while they have pending local changes, ART shall
not automatically publish those changes without authorization.

The framework shall preserve the local work according to applicable
recovery rules and provide appropriate options.

#### Collaboration With Multiple Tabs

Multiple browser tabs or application instances belonging to the same
user shall not create conflicting identities.

ART shall distinguish:

- 

User identity.

- 

Application instance.

- 

Collaboration session.

- 

Resource session.

Changes from multiple sessions belonging to the same user shall be
handled consistently.

#### Validation

Verify that:

1.  

ART supports local, asynchronous, synchronous, and offline collaboration
modes as provider capabilities permit.

2.  

The Collaboration Provider exposes real-time and synchronization
capabilities.

3.  

Collaboration remains provider-independent.

4.  

Local-first editing remains functional.

5.  

Local changes are preserved during network interruption.

6.  

Independent concurrent changes are merged without unnecessary conflicts.

7.  

Same-field concurrent changes do not silently overwrite user work.

8.  

Concurrent additions are preserved.

9.  

Concurrent deletions are handled deterministically.

10. 

Delete/edit conflicts are detected and presented accessibly.

11. 

Reordering conflicts are handled deterministically.

12. 

Synchronization status is programmatically available.

13. 

Synchronization updates do not continuously interrupt screen-reader
users.

14. 

Remote changes do not unexpectedly steal focus.

15. 

Remote changes do not unexpectedly move the insertion point.

16. 

Remote changes do not unexpectedly scroll or reload the interface.

17. 

Collaboration cursors and selection indicators do not interfere with
keyboard or screen-reader use.

18. 

Resource and field locking, when required, use the smallest practical
scope.

19. 

Locks recover appropriately after unexpected session termination.

20. 

Conflicts are detected centrally.

21. 

Conflict-resolution interfaces clearly identify local and remote
changes.

22. 

Conflict resolution never silently discards user data.

23. 

Conflict-resolution interfaces are fully accessible.

24. 

Undo and Redo do not inadvertently undo another user's changes.

25. 

Version restoration creates a new revision rather than destroying
history.

26. 

Autosave does not interfere with typing or assistive technology.

27. 

Reconnection preserves local work.

28. 

Provider failures do not falsely report synchronization success.

29. 

Retried synchronization operations do not create duplicate resources.

30. 

Large reports can synchronize efficiently without unnecessary
whole-report updates.

31. 

Personal Working Views remain personal during collaborative Report
editing.

32. 

Shared Working Views follow shared-resource permissions.

33. 

Permission changes are enforced during active collaboration.

34. 

Revoked Edit permissions do not allow unauthorized continued editing.

35. 

Pending unauthorized changes are handled safely.

36. 

Multiple tabs or application sessions belonging to one user are handled
correctly.

37. 

Collaboration functionality remains fully accessible using keyboard and
assistive technologies.

38. 

Existing local-only ART functionality remains fully operational when
Collaboration is disabled.

39. 

The architecture supports future Google Docs/Sheets-style simultaneous
editing without requiring a fundamental redesign.

### Part 11: Collaboration Security, Data Protection, Provider Integration, and Deployment Readiness

#### Overview

Implement the security, data-protection, provider-integration, and
deployment-readiness requirements necessary to make the ART
Collaboration Framework suitable for production use.

The Collaboration Framework shall be designed so that ART can operate
with different Collaboration Providers without coupling the application
to a specific server language, database, hosting platform,
authentication provider, or real-time synchronization technology.

The implementation shall preserve ART's existing local-only
functionality when Collaboration is disabled.

#### Provider-Neutral Architecture

The Collaboration Framework shall use provider-neutral interfaces
between ART and external collaboration services.

ART shall not assume that the Collaboration Provider uses:

- Node.js.
- Python.
- Java.
- .NET.
- A specific database.
- A specific cloud provider.
- A specific hosting provider.
- WebSockets.
- Server-Sent Events.
- WebRTC.
- REST.
- GraphQL.
- Operational Transform.
- CRDTs.

These technologies may be used by a specific provider, but the ART
application shall communicate through defined Collaboration Provider
interfaces.

#### Collaboration Provider Interface

Define a clear interface between ART and the Collaboration Provider.

The interface should provide capabilities for operations such as:

- Authentication.
- User identity.
- Workspace access.
- Resource synchronization.
- Report synchronization.
- Comment synchronization.
- Sharing.
- Permissions.
- Invitations.
- Presence.
- Version history.
- Conflict detection.
- Conflict resolution.
- Notifications.
- Activity history.
- Audit events.
- Plugin/package sharing.
- Offline synchronization.

Provider capabilities shall be discoverable by ART.

#### Capability Detection

The Collaboration Framework shall determine which capabilities are
supported by the active provider.

For example:

``` text
Collaboration Provider Capabilities

Real-time editing: Supported
Presence: Supported
Offline synchronization: Supported
Comments: Supported
Resource sharing: Supported
Organization groups: Not supported
Version restoration: Supported
```

### Part 12: Collaboration Testing, Quality Assurance, Accessibility Validation, and Acceptance Criteria

#### Overview

Complete the Collaboration Framework with a comprehensive testing and
validation strategy covering the full collaborative experience.

The goal is to verify that Collaboration works reliably for users who:

- Work independently.
- Collaborate asynchronously.
- Collaborate synchronously.
- Work offline and synchronize later.
- Use different permission levels.
- Use personal or shared Working Views.
- Use personal or shared plugins.
- Use personal or shared Accessibility Standard packages.
- Use assistive technologies.
- Use keyboard-only interaction.
- Use mouse, touch, speech, or switch access.

Testing shall verify that Collaboration does not regress ART's existing
local-first functionality or accessibility.

#### Testing Architecture

Create a test strategy that separates:

- Unit tests.
- Component tests.
- Integration tests.
- End-to-end tests.
- Multi-user collaboration tests.
- Accessibility tests.
- Security tests.
- Synchronization tests.
- Conflict-resolution tests.
- Offline/online tests.
- Performance tests.
- Regression tests.

Tests shall be organized so that failures can be traced to the affected
Collaboration Framework component.

#### Provider Testing

The Collaboration Framework shall be testable independently of a
production Collaboration Provider.

Provide an appropriate development/test provider or mock implementation
where necessary.

The test provider shall support enough functionality to verify:

- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Resource access.
- Synchronization.
- Concurrent editing.
- Comments.
- Sharing.
- Permissions.
- Presence.
- Version history.
- Conflicts.
- Offline synchronization.

The test provider shall not be represented as a production-ready
Collaboration backend.

#### Multi-User Test Environment

Provide a way to simulate multiple users simultaneously.

At minimum, tests shall support users with different permission levels,
including:

- Owner.
- Administrator.
- Contributor.
- Reviewer/commenter where supported.
- Viewer.

The exact permission names shall match the final ART permission model.

#### Modular Permission Testing

Verify that permissions can be assigned independently where supported.

For example:

``` text
User A:
Workspace = Viewer
Report 1 = Editor
Report 2 = Viewer
```

### Part 13: Production Readiness, Migration, Administration, Monitoring, and Long-Term Extensibility

#### Overview

Prepare the Collaboration Framework for production deployment and
long-term maintenance.

This part shall establish the operational architecture, administration
capabilities, migration strategy, monitoring, observability, feature
rollout, and extensibility requirements necessary for ART to evolve from
a local-first application into an application that can optionally
support secure individual and collaborative workflows.

The Collaboration Framework shall remain optional.

Users who do not use Collaboration shall continue to be able to use ART
as a local-first application without requiring a Collaboration account,
server connection, or external service.

#### Production Readiness Principles

The Collaboration Framework shall be designed around the following
principles:

- Local-first functionality remains available.
- Collaboration is optional.
- Collaboration Providers are replaceable.
- Provider-specific implementation details remain isolated.
- Security is enforced independently of the client UI.
- Accessibility is a core architectural requirement.
- User data shall not be silently lost.
- Collaboration features shall degrade gracefully.
- New collaboration functionality shall not unnecessarily clutter the
  ART interface.
- The architecture shall support future providers and infrastructure
  without requiring major frontend rewrites.

#### Production Environment Separation

The Collaboration architecture shall distinguish between:

- Development.
- Testing.
- Staging.
- Production.

Each environment shall have independently configurable:

- Collaboration Provider.
- Authentication configuration.
- API endpoints.
- Database/storage.
- Real-time services.
- Notification services.
- Secrets.
- Logging.
- Monitoring.
- Feature flags.

Production credentials shall never be reused in development or testing
environments.

#### Deployment Configuration

Provider and deployment configuration shall be externalized from the ART
frontend.

Do not hard-code production:

- API URLs.
- Authentication endpoints.
- Database credentials.
- API keys.
- Signing keys.
- Encryption keys.
- Service credentials.

Configuration shall be supplied through the appropriate deployment
mechanism.

#### Environment Validation

At startup or deployment, the Collaboration services should validate
required configuration.

If required configuration is missing:

- The service shall fail safely.
- The error shall identify the missing configuration without exposing
  secrets.
- ART shall not falsely report Collaboration as operational.

#### Health Checks

The Collaboration Provider should expose appropriate health information
for administrators and deployment infrastructure.

Health checks may include:

- API availability.
- Database connectivity.
- Real-time service availability.
- Authentication service availability.
- Storage availability.
- Background job availability.

Health checks shall not expose sensitive data.

#### Readiness Checks

Distinguish between:

- Service is running.
- Service is ready to accept requests.

A service shall not be reported as ready if critical dependencies
required for its operation are unavailable.

#### Graceful Startup

The Collaboration Provider shall initialize dependencies in a controlled
manner.

ART shall not assume that every collaboration service is immediately
available after deployment.

#### Graceful Shutdown

The Collaboration Provider shall support graceful shutdown.

Where applicable:

- Complete safe pending operations.
- Stop accepting new operations.
- Close real-time connections.
- Release resources.
- Preserve queued work.
- Shut down background processing safely.

#### Deployment Failure Safety

A failed deployment shall not result in silent data corruption or loss.

Deployment processes should support:

- Health validation.
- Rollback.
- Version identification.
- Database migration validation.
- Configuration validation.

#### Database and Storage Migrations

If the Collaboration Provider uses persistent storage, schema/data
migrations shall be versioned.

Migrations shall:

- Be repeatable where appropriate.
- Be tested before production deployment.
- Preserve existing data.
- Provide rollback or recovery procedures where feasible.
- Clearly identify incompatible migrations.

Do not modify production data structures manually without documenting
the change.

#### Migration Strategy

The Collaboration Framework shall define how new versions of the
Collaboration data model are introduced.

The strategy shall account for:

- Existing users.
- Existing Workspaces.
- Existing Reports.
- Existing permissions.
- Existing comments.
- Existing Working Views.
- Existing plugins.
- Existing packages.
- Existing Audit Log entries.
- Existing synchronization state.

#### ART Version Compatibility

The Collaboration Provider should be able to determine which ART client
versions are compatible with the provider API.

Where practical, provider APIs should support backward-compatible
changes.

Breaking API changes shall be versioned and documented.

#### API Versioning

If the Collaboration Provider exposes APIs, establish a versioning
strategy.

For example:

``` text
/api/v1/
```

### Part 14: Final Integration, User Experience Consistency, Documentation, and Epic Closure

#### Overview

Complete the Collaboration Framework by integrating all Collaboration
capabilities into ART's existing architecture and user experience.

This part focuses on ensuring that Collaboration feels like a natural
extension of ART rather than a separate application layered on top of
it.

The final implementation shall preserve ART's:

- Accessibility-first design.
- Local-first functionality.
- Existing navigation patterns.
- Existing command architecture.
- Existing menu-bar behavior.
- Existing settings architecture.
- Existing Analytics architecture.
- Existing Audit Log architecture.
- Existing Working View architecture.
- Existing Report and Workspace concepts.

Do not introduce unnecessary new UI patterns when existing ART patterns
can be reused.

#### Collaboration Feature Integration

Integrate Collaboration into the existing ART application rather than
creating a separate Collaboration application or duplicate interface.

Collaboration shall operate consistently across:

- Standalone Reports.
- Project Workspaces.
- Reports within Project Workspaces.
- Working Views.
- Shared Working Views.
- Personal plugins.
- Shared plugins.
- Personal Accessibility Standard packages.
- Shared Accessibility Standard packages.

The implementation shall clearly distinguish between features that apply
to standalone Reports and features that apply only to Project
Workspaces.

#### Standalone Report Collaboration

Standalone Reports shall be capable of participating in Collaboration
independently of a Project Workspace when the user's permissions and
Collaboration configuration allow it.

Users shall be able to:

- Share a standalone Report.
- Assign permissions to a standalone Report.
- Collaborate on a standalone Report.
- Comment on a standalone Report where supported.
- View appropriate activity/history.
- Synchronize changes.
- Work asynchronously.
- Work synchronously where supported.

A standalone Report shall not need to be placed into a Workspace solely
to enable collaboration.

#### Project Workspace Collaboration

Project Workspaces shall provide the broader collaboration container.

Where appropriate, Workspace collaboration may include:

- Reports.
- Workspace members.
- Workspace permissions.
- Shared Working Views.
- Shared plugins.
- Shared Accessibility Standard packages.
- Workspace activity.
- Workspace Analytics.
- Workspace-level sharing.

Workspace-level permissions shall not automatically eliminate more
granular Report-level permissions.

#### Resource Scope

Every collaborative resource shall have a clearly defined scope.

The implementation shall distinguish among:

- Personal resources.
- Report-level resources.
- Workspace resources.
- Organization-level resources.
- Public resources, if supported.

Do not assume that because two resources exist inside the same Workspace
they must have identical sharing or permissions.

#### Personal Resources

Personal resources shall remain private unless explicitly shared.

Examples include:

- Personal Working Views.
- Personal plugins.
- Personal Accessibility Standard packages.
- Personal preferences.
- Personal saved configurations.

Creating or modifying a personal resource shall not automatically make
it available to other collaborators.

#### Shared Resources

When a user explicitly shares a resource, ART shall clearly communicate:

- What is being shared.
- With whom.
- What permissions are granted.
- Whether the resource is personal, Workspace, or organization-level.
- Whether the recipient can further share it.

#### Permission Consistency

Use the same underlying permission model throughout Collaboration.

Do not create separate incompatible permission systems for:

- Reports.
- Workspaces.
- Working Views.
- Plugins.
- Packages.

The permission system shall remain modular and resource-aware.

#### Permission Inheritance

Where permissions are inherited, clearly define the inheritance
relationship.

For example:

``` text
Workspace
    └── Report
        └── Report-specific permissions
A Report may inherit Workspace access while also having additional or more restrictive resource-level permissions where the architecture permits.

Do not silently override explicitly configured resource-level permissions.
```

#### Permission Presentation

The user interface shall present effective permissions clearly.

Where a permission is inherited, identify it as inherited.

Where a permission is explicitly assigned, identify it as explicit.

For example:

Jordan — Editor\
Source: Workspace membership

or:

Jordan — Viewer\
Source: Report-specific permission

The exact wording may vary, but the distinction shall be understandable.

#### Collaboration Status

ART should provide an accessible indication of Collaboration status when
Collaboration is enabled.

Possible states include:

- Collaboration disabled.

- Offline.

- Connecting.

- Connected.

- Synchronizing.

- Changes pending.

- Synchronization failed.

- Conflict requires attention.

The status shall not require a visually rendered indicator alone.

#### Collaboration Status Accessibility

Collaboration status shall be programmatically available to assistive
technologies.

Routine status changes shall not repeatedly interrupt users.

Critical status changes may be announced appropriately.

#### Collaboration Presence

If presence is implemented, users may be able to determine that other
collaborators are currently active.

Presence information shall:

- Be optional where appropriate.

- Respect privacy settings.

- Respect permissions.

- Be accessible.

- Avoid excessive screen-reader announcements.

- Avoid moving focus.

- Avoid disrupting active editing.

Do not announce every cursor movement or keystroke made by another user.

#### Presence Privacy

If presence information is displayed, clearly define what is exposed.

For example:

- Online/offline state.

- Active in Report.

- Active in Working View.

- Last active time.

Do not expose unnecessary activity information.

#### Collaboration Notifications

Notifications shall be designed to avoid clutter.

Do not create persistent notification controls for every collaboration
event.

Users should be able to access relevant notifications through existing
ART patterns.

#### Notification Preferences

Application Settings should provide appropriate notification preferences
where notifications are implemented.

Users may be able to control:

- Comments.

- Mentions.

- Sharing.

- Permission changes.

- Invitations.

- Conflict notifications.

- Collaboration activity.

The exact settings shall depend on implemented functionality.

#### Comments

Comments shall integrate with ART's existing content and accessibility
patterns.

Users with appropriate permissions should be able to:

- Add comments.

- Reply to comments.

- Edit their comments where permitted.

- Resolve comments where permitted.

- Reopen comments where permitted.

- Delete comments where permitted.

#### Comment Accessibility

Comments shall:

- Have meaningful accessible names.

- Be keyboard accessible.

- Preserve logical focus.

- Provide clear author information.

- Provide clear timestamps where appropriate.

- Identify resolved/unresolved state.

- Avoid excessive live-region announcements.

#### Comment Focus Management

When a user:

- Adds a comment.

- Opens a comment.

- Resolves a comment.

- Closes a comment.

focus shall remain logical.

Closing a comment interface should return focus to the control that
invoked it whenever practical.

#### Mentions

If mentions are supported, autocomplete suggestions shall be accessible.

Suggestions shall:

- Have meaningful accessible names.

- Be keyboard navigable.

- Be announced when programmatic focus moves to a suggestion.

- Not interrupt active typing with repeated announcements.

#### Activity History

Collaboration activity shall integrate with the existing Audit Log and
activity architecture where possible.

Do not create redundant activity systems unless technically necessary.

Activity may include:

- Report changes.

- Workspace changes.

- Sharing.

- Permission changes.

- Comments.

- Working View sharing.

- Plugin sharing.

- Package sharing.

- Ownership changes.

#### Activity Accessibility

Activity history shall be accessible through:

- Keyboard.

- Screen readers.

- Appropriate semantic structures.

- Accessible tables or lists where appropriate.

Do not rely solely on visual timelines.

#### Analytics Integration

Use the existing Analytics tab rather than creating unnecessary new
analytics interfaces.

Collaboration analytics shall be integrated into the existing Analytics
architecture.

Analytics sections shall remain:

- Collapsed by default.

- Expandable.

- Configurable through Application Settings.

- Permission-aware.

- Accessible.

#### Collaboration Analytics

Where data is available, collaboration analytics may include:

- Collaboration Overview.

- Workspace Activity.

- Report Activity.

- User Activity.

- Sharing and Permissions.

- Comments and Reviews.

- Synchronization.

- Conflicts.

- Version History.

- Working View usage.

- Plugin usage.

- Accessibility Standard package usage.

Do not include resource statistics that are unrelated to the requested
Collaboration analytics.

#### Analytics Privacy

Analytics shall not expose information to users who do not have
permission to see it.

For example, a Workspace contributor should not automatically receive
organization-wide analytics.

#### Analytics Empty States

If an Analytics section has no data:

- Explain that no data is currently available.

- Do not display misleading zero values when the data is simply
  unavailable.

- Provide an accessible explanation where appropriate.

#### Analytics Configuration

Application Settings shall allow users to control which applicable
Analytics sections are displayed.

Settings shall not grant access to Analytics that the user is otherwise
unauthorized to view.

#### Menu Integration

When Collaboration is enabled, add a **Collaboration** menu to the ART
menu bar.

The menu shall contain appropriate Collaboration commands.

Do not add Collaboration controls directly to the primary application
interface unless already established by the existing ART design.

#### Collaboration Menu Organization

Organize Collaboration commands logically.

Possible categories include:

- Collaboration status.

- Share.

- Permissions.

- Comments.

- Activity.

- Working Views.

- Plugins.

- Packages.

- Synchronization.

- Settings.

The final grouping should follow ART's established menu conventions.

#### Collaboration Toolbar

The Collaboration Toolbar shall remain optional.

It shall:

- Be disabled by default.

- Be enabled through Application Settings.

- Be fully keyboard accessible.

- Be screen-reader accessible.

- Provide accessible names.

- Support repositioning.

- Support an accessible keyboard alternative to drag-and-drop.

- Respect the user's preferred location.

The toolbar shall not become the only way to access Collaboration
functionality.

#### Command Search Integration

All applicable Collaboration commands shall be available through Command
Search.

Search results shall respect:

- Permissions.

- Current context.

- Collaboration availability.

- Feature flags.

#### Command Palette Integration

All applicable Collaboration commands shall be available through the
Command Palette.

The Command Palette shall remain accessible and shall not expose
unauthorized commands.

#### Global Context Menu Integration

When Collaboration is enabled, applicable context-sensitive
Collaboration commands may be added to the global context menu.

The context menu shall only display commands relevant to the current
context.

Do not fill the global context menu with every possible Collaboration
command.

#### Keyboard Shortcut Integration

Collaboration commands may have keyboard shortcuts where appropriate.

Shortcuts shall:

- Avoid conflicts with existing ART shortcuts.

- Be discoverable.

- Be configurable where appropriate.

- Work with keyboard-only interaction.

- Work appropriately with screen readers.

#### Shortcut Documentation

All Collaboration shortcuts shall be documented through existing ART
shortcut-discovery mechanisms.

Do not create a separate shortcut system solely for Collaboration.

#### Dialog Integration

Collaboration dialogs shall follow ART's existing dialog architecture.

Dialogs shall:

- Have accessible names.

- Have appropriate modal semantics.

- Trap focus appropriately when modal.

- Restore focus when closed.

- Support Escape where appropriate.

- Provide accessible error handling.

#### Dialog Focus Restoration

When a Collaboration dialog closes, return focus to the control that
opened it whenever practical.

Do not move focus to:

- The top of the page.

- The beginning of the application.

- An unrelated control.

#### Error Handling

Collaboration errors shall be understandable to users.

Examples include:

- Permission denied.

- Resource unavailable.

- Synchronization failure.

- Conflict detected.

- Authentication expired.

- Provider unavailable.

- Invitation failure.

Errors shall provide useful next steps where possible.

#### Error Accessibility

Errors shall:

- Be programmatically associated with the relevant control where
  appropriate.

- Be announced appropriately.

- Not interrupt unrelated typing.

- Not rely solely on color.

- Remain available until the user has had an opportunity to understand
  them.

#### Loading States

Collaboration loading states shall not unnecessarily block unrelated ART
functionality.

For example, failure to load Collaboration data should not prevent a
user from opening locally stored Reports unless the requested operation
specifically requires Collaboration.

#### Graceful Degradation

If Collaboration is temporarily unavailable:

- Local Reports should remain usable where possible.

- Local Workspace data should remain available where possible.

- Users should be informed that synchronization is unavailable.

- Local changes should be preserved.

- ART should not falsely indicate that changes have synchronized.

#### Local-First Preservation

The Collaboration Framework shall not undermine ART's local-first
architecture.

A user should continue to be able to:

- Create Reports locally.

- Edit Reports locally.

- Save Reports locally.

- Import Reports locally.

- Export Reports locally.

- Use templates locally.

- Use the WCAG Lookup Tool locally.

- Use Working Views locally.

Collaboration should enhance these capabilities rather than replace
them.

#### Export and Import Compatibility

Collaboration shall not prevent authorized users from exporting Reports.

Where appropriate, exported Reports shall contain the same report
content regardless of whether the Report was:

- Created locally.

- Created collaboratively.

- Edited synchronously.

- Edited asynchronously.

#### Collaboration Metadata in Exports

Do not automatically expose internal collaboration metadata in exported
Reports unless explicitly required.

Examples of information that should not automatically appear in exports
include:

- Internal user IDs.

- Synchronization IDs.

- Provider identifiers.

- Internal permission metadata.

- Private activity information.

#### Template Compatibility

Templates shall remain compatible with collaborative Reports.

Where templates are shared:

- Permissions shall be respected.

- Template changes shall be versioned where appropriate.

- Users shall not automatically receive edit permission merely because
  they can use a template.

#### Report Format Compatibility

Collaboration shall not alter the existing supported export formats
unless explicitly required.

Existing Report formats shall continue to function.

#### Version History Integration

Version history should integrate with existing Report and Workspace
concepts.

Users with appropriate permissions should be able to:

- View versions.

- Compare versions where supported.

- Restore versions where supported.

Restoration shall preserve auditability.

#### Restore Focus Behavior

After restoring a version:

- Provide an accessible confirmation.

- Preserve logical focus.

- Do not unexpectedly move the user to the top of the application.

#### Unsaved Changes

When a user has local changes that have not synchronized, ART shall
distinguish between:

- Saved locally.

- Pending synchronization.

- Successfully synchronized.

- Synchronization failed.

Do not represent a locally saved but unsynchronized change as fully
synchronized.

#### Browser Refresh Protection

Where practical, ART shall protect pending local changes from accidental
loss caused by:

- Refresh.

- Navigation.

- Closing the browser.

- Temporary provider failures.

#### Multiple Tabs

If a user opens the same collaborative resource in multiple browser
tabs, the application should handle the situation predictably.

Avoid silent data corruption caused by competing tabs.

If multiple-tab editing is unsupported, clearly communicate the
limitation.

#### Multiple Devices

A user should be able to access authorized collaborative resources from
multiple devices where supported.

Synchronization behavior shall remain consistent.

#### Time and Date Handling

Collaboration timestamps shall use a consistent underlying
representation.

Display timestamps according to the user's locale/time-zone preferences
where appropriate.

Do not use client-local timestamps as the authoritative source for
server-side event ordering.

#### Ordering of Collaborative Events

The system shall maintain a reliable ordering strategy for collaborative
events.

Where exact ordering cannot be established, the UI shall avoid
presenting misleading certainty.

#### Duplicate Event Handling

Collaboration clients shall safely handle duplicate synchronization
events.

Duplicate events shall not result in:

- Duplicate findings.

- Duplicate comments.

- Duplicate fields.

- Duplicate Working Views.

- Duplicate plugins.

- Duplicate packages.

#### Retry Handling

Failed operations may be retried where appropriate.

Retries shall not accidentally duplicate operations.

Operations that are not safely retryable shall use appropriate
idempotency mechanisms.

#### Idempotency

Critical Collaboration operations should be designed to be safely
retried where practical.

Examples include:

- Sharing.

- Permission updates.

- Comments.

- Resource creation.

- Synchronization events.

#### Offline Queue

If offline operations are queued:

- The queue shall be persisted appropriately.

- The queue shall survive normal application restarts where supported.

- The user shall be able to determine when changes are pending.

- Failed operations shall be recoverable.

- Duplicate operations shall be prevented.

#### Offline Accessibility

Offline state shall be accessible to screen-reader and keyboard users.

Do not communicate offline state only through a color change or icon.

#### Reconnection UX

When connectivity returns:

- ART should indicate that synchronization has resumed.

- Pending changes should synchronize automatically where appropriate.

- Conflicts should be surfaced when necessary.

- Routine synchronization should not repeatedly interrupt users.

#### Collaboration and Application Settings

Application Settings shall provide a coherent location for Collaboration
configuration.

Possible settings include:

- Enable/disable Collaboration.

- Collaboration Provider.

- Notification preferences.

- Presence preferences.

- Analytics visibility.

- Collaboration Toolbar visibility.

- Collaboration accessibility preferences.

Only settings that are actually implemented should be exposed.

#### Settings Accessibility

All Collaboration settings shall:

- Have accessible labels.

- Have appropriate descriptions.

- Be keyboard accessible.

- Expose their current state.

- Preserve logical focus.

- Avoid unexpected page navigation.

#### Settings Scope

Clearly distinguish:

- Application-wide Collaboration settings.

- Organization-level settings.

- Workspace-level settings.

- User-specific preferences.

Do not place an organization-wide policy in a user-only setting.

#### Help/User Guide Integration

Add Collaboration documentation to the existing ART Help/User Guide.

The Help/User Guide should explain the feature from a user perspective.

#### Help/User Guide Focus Restoration

Opening and closing the Help/User Guide shall preserve the user's
existing focus behavior.

Closing the Help/User Guide through:

- Close button.

- Escape key.

shall return focus to the location from which the Help/User Guide was
opened.

#### Accessibility Lookup Tool Integration

Collaboration-related accessibility standards and WCAG information
should continue to work with the existing Accessibility Lookup Tool.

Do not create a second accessibility-standard lookup mechanism.

#### Existing WCAG Lookup Behavior

The Collaboration Framework shall not modify unrelated WCAG Lookup Tool
behavior.

Existing:

- Search.

- Filtering.

- Results.

- Accessible names.

- Keyboard shortcuts.

- W3C links.

shall remain functional.

#### Existing Report Builder Integration

Collaboration shall integrate with the existing Report Builder without
changing unrelated Report Builder functionality.

Existing:

- Field configuration.

- Add Field.

- Move Up.

- Move Down.

- Keyboard shortcuts.

- Focus behavior.

- Validation.

shall continue to work.

#### Existing Working View Integration

The Collaboration Framework shall use the existing Working View model.

Do not create a separate collaboration-only Working View architecture.

Working Views shall remain primarily personal.

Shared Working Views shall be explicitly shared resources.

#### Existing Plugin Integration

Use the existing plugin architecture.

Do not create a duplicate plugin architecture solely for collaboration.

Plugins shall support appropriate personal/shared visibility.

#### Existing Package Integration

Use the existing Accessibility Standard package architecture.

Do not create a duplicate package architecture solely for collaboration.

Packages shall support appropriate personal/shared visibility.

#### Existing Audit Log Integration

Use the existing Audit Log architecture for collaboration-related events
where appropriate.

Do not create a redundant audit system.

#### Existing Analytics Integration

Use the existing Analytics tab and Analytics architecture.

Do not create a separate Collaboration Analytics application.

#### UI Clutter Prevention

Collaboration shall not significantly increase persistent UI clutter.

By default:

- Collaboration Toolbar is hidden.

- Optional Collaboration controls are not added to the main workspace
  unnecessarily.

- Collaboration commands are primarily available through menus and
  command-discovery mechanisms.

- Analytics sections are collapsed.

- Advanced controls are placed in appropriate menus/settings.

#### Progressive Disclosure

Advanced Collaboration functionality should use progressive disclosure.

Users should initially see only the controls needed for common
workflows.

More advanced capabilities may be accessed through:

- Menus.

- Command Search.

- Command Palette.

- Context menus.

- Settings.

- Expandable sections.

#### Consistent Terminology

Use consistent terminology throughout ART.

Preferred terminology shall remain consistent with existing ART
terminology.

For example:

- Project Workspace.

- Working View.

- Report.

- Report Builder.

- Report Viewer.

- Accessibility Standard.

- Finding.

- Issue Type.

- Analytics.

- Collaboration.

Do not introduce competing terminology for the same concept.

#### Terminology Accessibility

Labels shall be understandable to users and assistive technologies.

Avoid abbreviations that are not already established in ART.

#### Accessible Names

Every new Collaboration control shall have a meaningful accessible name.

Accessible names shall identify the control's purpose rather than its
implementation.

For example:

Share Report\
Manage Report Permissions\
Open Collaboration Menu\
View Workspace Activity

rather than:

Action\
Button\
Control\
More

#### Accessible Descriptions

Where a control requires additional explanation, provide an accessible
description or associated help text.

Do not place essential information only in tooltips.

#### Keyboard Navigation

The final integrated Collaboration experience shall maintain a logical
keyboard navigation order.

Dynamic Collaboration updates shall not:

- Move focus.

- Reorder focus unexpectedly.

- Trap focus outside the intended context.

- Return focus to the top of the page.

#### Screen Reader Behavior

Screen readers shall receive meaningful information about:

- Collaboration status.

- Permissions.

- Sharing.

- Comments.

- Conflicts.

- Synchronization.

- Presence.

- Analytics.

Routine background updates shall remain quiet.

#### Focus Preservation During Collaboration

Remote changes shall not steal focus from the local user.

For example, if User A is typing in a Report field and User B changes
another field:

- User A's focus remains on the active field.

- User A's insertion point remains stable.

- The remote change does not move the viewport unexpectedly.

#### Remote Changes

Remote changes should be visually distinguishable when necessary without
creating excessive visual or cognitive noise.

Accessibility equivalents shall be available.

#### Collaboration Conflict UX

Conflict resolution shall clearly explain:

- What changed locally.

- What changed remotely.

- What options are available.

- What will happen when an option is selected.

Do not require users to understand synchronization technology.

#### Conflict Accessibility

Conflict resolution shall be fully accessible.

Users shall be able to:

- Navigate conflicts.

- Review alternatives.

- Select an option.

- Confirm the resolution.

- Cancel.

- Return to the original context.

#### User Confirmation

Require confirmation for destructive or potentially irreversible
Collaboration actions when appropriate.

Examples include:

- Delete shared resource.

- Remove Workspace member.

- Transfer ownership.

- Revoke access.

- Delete shared plugin.

- Delete shared package.

Do not require unnecessary confirmation for routine non-destructive
operations.

#### Destructive Action Accessibility

Confirmation dialogs shall clearly identify:

- The action.

- The affected resource.

- The consequence.

- The available choices.

The destructive action shall not be communicated solely through color.

#### Collaboration Onboarding

If Collaboration requires setup, provide an accessible onboarding flow.

The onboarding process should explain:

- What Collaboration does.

- What data is synchronized.

- What remains local.

- What permissions mean.

- How sharing works.

- How to disable Collaboration.

Do not force onboarding on users who do not enable Collaboration.

#### First-Use Experience

The first-use experience should be concise.

Do not require users to complete extensive configuration before they can
use basic Collaboration features.

#### Provider Configuration UX

If users or administrators must select a Collaboration Provider, clearly
identify:

- Provider name.

- Connection status.

- Authentication requirements.

- Data storage implications.

- Supported capabilities.

Do not expose unnecessary technical implementation details to ordinary
users.

#### Provider Capability Detection

ART should determine which Collaboration capabilities are actually
supported by the configured provider.

For example, a provider may support:

- Asynchronous collaboration.

- Comments.

but not:

- Real-time editing.

- Presence.

The UI shall not expose unsupported functionality as if it were
available.

#### Capability-Aware UI

Unsupported capabilities should be:

- Hidden.

- Disabled with an accessible explanation.

- Or otherwise clearly identified as unavailable.

Do not display controls that appear functional but cannot work.

#### Provider Errors

Provider-specific errors should be translated into understandable ART
messages.

Do not expose raw provider-specific error messages unless they are
appropriate for an administrator/developer context.

#### Final Integration Regression

After integrating Collaboration, retest the entire ART application.

At minimum verify:

- Application startup.

- Dashboard.

- Menu bar.

- Command Search.

- Command Palette.

- Global context menu.

- Report Builder.

- Report Editor.

- Report Viewer.

- Working View.

- Project Workspace.

- Templates.

- Import.

- Export.

- Audit Log.

- Analytics.

- Accessibility Lookup Tool.

- Help/User Guide.

- Application Settings.

- Keyboard shortcuts.

- Local storage.

- Offline workflows.

#### Final Accessibility Regression

Perform a final accessibility regression covering:

- Keyboard-only operation.

- Screen-reader operation.

- Focus management.

- Accessible names.

- Accessible descriptions.

- Dialog behavior.

- Menu behavior.

- Command Search.

- Command Palette.

- Context menus.

- Dynamic status updates.

- Collaboration Toolbar.

- Analytics.

- Comments.

- Sharing.

- Permissions.

- Conflict resolution.

#### Final User Experience Review

Review the Collaboration Framework from the perspective of:

- Individual accessibility professionals.

- Contributors.

- Reviewers.

- Team leads.

- Workspace administrators.

- Organization administrators.

- Users who never use Collaboration.

- Keyboard-only users.

- Screen-reader users.

- Mouse users.

The interface shall remain understandable and uncluttered for all user
groups.

#### Final Local-Only Review

With Collaboration disabled, confirm that ART remains a complete and
useful application.

A user who never enables Collaboration should not encounter:

- Broken controls.

- Missing menus.

- Empty collaboration panels.

- Unnecessary authentication prompts.

- Provider errors.

- Collaboration configuration requirements.

#### Final Collaboration-Enabled Review

With Collaboration enabled, confirm that the user can discover
Collaboration through:

- Collaboration menu.

- Command Search.

- Command Palette.

- Global context menu where enabled.

- Optional Collaboration Toolbar.

The user should not need to know internal implementation details to
collaborate successfully.

#### Final Data Integrity Review

Confirm that all supported Collaboration workflows preserve:

- Report content.

- Findings.

- Issue Types.

- Report fields.

- Comments.

- Templates.

- Working Views.

- Plugins.

- Accessibility Standard packages.

- Version history.

- Audit information.

#### Final Security Review

Confirm:

- Authentication is secure.

- Authorization is enforced independently of the UI.

- Resource isolation works.

- Private resources remain private.

- Sharing works according to permissions.

- Revocation works.

- Sessions can be invalidated where supported.

- Sensitive information is not exposed.

- Production secrets are not included in the client.

#### Final Accessibility Review

Confirm that no major Collaboration workflow depends exclusively on:

- Mouse interaction.

- Color.

- Visual position.

- Animation.

- Hover.

- Tooltips.

- Visual presence indicators.

All critical information and operations shall have accessible
equivalents.

#### Final Documentation Review

Confirm that documentation accurately describes:

- Collaboration.

- Permissions.

- Sharing.

- Working Views.

- Plugins.

- Accessibility Standard packages.

- Synchronization.

- Offline behavior.

- Conflicts.

- Analytics.

- Activity.

- Provider configuration.

- Privacy.

- Security.

Documentation shall distinguish between capabilities that are:

- Implemented.

- Provider-dependent.

- Configuration-dependent.

- Planned.

- Unsupported.

#### Epic Closure Criteria

Epic 39 shall be closed only after all applicable requirements from
Parts 1–14 have been reviewed.

The implementation shall not be considered complete merely because the
code builds successfully.

Epic closure requires:

1.  Functional implementation.

2.  Integration with existing ART architecture.

3.  Accessibility validation.

4.  Security validation.

5.  Permission validation.

6.  Synchronization validation.

7.  Offline/reconnection validation.

8.  Conflict validation.

9.  Multi-user validation.

10. Regression validation.

11. Documentation.

12. Production-readiness review.

#### Implementation Status

At epic completion, clearly identify each major capability as one of:

**Implemented and Tested**

**Implemented but Requires External Infrastructure**

**Implemented but Provider-Dependent**

**Documented but Not Yet Implemented**

**Deferred**

**Not Supported**

Do not represent placeholders, mock implementations, or design concepts
as completed functionality.

#### Final Epic Summary

Produce a final summary that documents:

- What was built.

- What was integrated.

- What was tested.

- What was validated for accessibility.

- What was validated for security.

- What requires external infrastructure.

- What depends on the selected Collaboration Provider.

- What remains deferred.

- What limitations remain.

- What future development is recommended.

The final Collaboration Framework shall provide ART with a foundation
for Google Docs/Sheets-style collaboration while preserving the
application's core identity as an accessible, local-first accessibility
reporting platform.

The implementation shall support users who want to work independently
just as effectively as users who choose to collaborate.

Most importantly, Collaboration shall enhance ART without compromising:

- Accessibility.

- Privacy.

- Security.

- Data ownership.

- Local-first functionality.

- User choice.

- Modular permissions.

- Personal Working Views.

- Personal plugins.

- Personal Accessibility Standard packages.

- Existing ART workflows.

## Epic 40 – Reporting & Publishing Framework

### Part 1: Architecture, Scope, and Publishing Model

#### Overview

Design and implement a comprehensive **Reporting & Publishing
Framework** for ART.

The purpose of this Epic is to provide accessibility professionals with
flexible, professional, accessible, and reusable tools for transforming
ART reports into polished deliverables for clients, stakeholders,
managers, organizations, and other audiences.

The Reporting & Publishing Framework shall build upon ART's existing:

- Report Builder.
- Report Editor.
- Report Viewer.
- Report Templates.
- Report Branding.
- Analytics.
- Findings.
- Accessibility Standards.
- WCAG Success Criteria.
- Audit Log.
- Project Workspaces.
- Working Views.
- Import/Export functionality.

Do not create a separate reporting system that duplicates existing ART
functionality.

Instead, extend and refactor existing reporting capabilities where
appropriate so that reporting and publishing functionality is based on a
coherent architecture.

#### Primary Goals

The Reporting & Publishing Framework shall allow users to:

- Create professional reports.
- Customize report layouts.
- Configure report sections.
- Create reusable publishing profiles.
- Apply branding consistently.
- Create cover pages.
- Generate tables of contents.
- Add appendices.
- Configure page numbering.
- Apply report themes.
- Control which report content is published.
- Export reports in supported formats.
- Generate multiple report outputs efficiently.
- Compare reports where appropriate.
- Reuse publishing configurations.
- Preserve accessibility throughout the publishing process.

#### Local-First Requirement

The Reporting & Publishing Framework shall preserve ART's local-first
architecture.

Users shall be able to create, configure, preview, save, and export
reports without requiring:

- A Collaboration account.
- A server.
- An Internet connection.
- An external publishing service.

Collaboration-enabled publishing functionality may use the Collaboration
Framework where appropriate, but publishing shall not depend on
Collaboration.

#### Standalone Report Support

Publishing functionality shall support standalone Reports.

A user shall be able to create and publish a standalone Report without
placing it into a Project Workspace.

Standalone Reports shall be able to use:

- Report Branding.
- Publishing Profiles.
- Themes.
- Layouts.
- Cover Pages.
- Tables of Contents.
- Appendices.
- Page numbering.
- Supported export formats.

#### Project Workspace Support

Publishing functionality shall also support Reports contained within
Project Workspaces.

Workspace-level publishing resources may include:

- Shared Publishing Profiles.
- Shared Themes.
- Shared Branding.
- Shared Templates.
- Shared Layouts.

Workspace resources shall remain permission-controlled.

A user shall not automatically receive permission to modify shared
publishing resources merely because they can view or use them.

#### Personal Publishing Resources

Users should be able to create personal publishing resources where
supported.

Examples include:

- Personal Publishing Profiles.
- Personal Themes.
- Personal Layouts.
- Personal Branding configurations.

Personal resources shall remain private unless explicitly shared.

#### Shared Publishing Resources

Where Collaboration is enabled, users with appropriate permissions may
share publishing resources.

Shared resources may include:

- Publishing Profiles.
- Themes.
- Layouts.
- Branding.
- Templates.

The permission model shall distinguish between:

- Use permission.
- View permission.
- Edit permission.
- Create permission.
- Delete permission.
- Share permission.

#### Publishing Profile

Introduce a reusable **Publishing Profile** concept.

A Publishing Profile shall define how a Report is transformed into a
published deliverable.

A Publishing Profile may contain settings for:

- Report layout.
- Theme.
- Branding.
- Cover page.
- Table of contents.
- Page numbering.
- Headers.
- Footers.
- Appendices.
- Section visibility.
- Finding visibility.
- Analytics visibility.
- Metadata.
- Export format.
- Accessibility requirements.

The exact configuration options shall be determined by the capabilities
supported by the publishing architecture.

#### Publishing Profile Scope

Publishing Profiles shall support appropriate scopes:

- Personal.
- Report-specific.
- Project Workspace.
- Organization, where supported.

The scope shall be clearly displayed to the user.

#### Default Publishing Profile

Users should be able to identify a default Publishing Profile for
appropriate contexts.

Where supported, a Project Workspace may have a default Publishing
Profile for new Reports.

The default shall not override an explicitly selected Publishing Profile
without user confirmation or a clearly documented rule.

#### Publishing Profile Reuse

Users shall be able to apply an existing Publishing Profile to another
Report when they have appropriate permissions.

Applying a Publishing Profile shall not overwrite Report content unless
the profile explicitly controls content selection.

#### Publishing Profile Independence

Publishing Profiles shall define presentation and publishing behavior
without unnecessarily embedding Report-specific data.

A Publishing Profile should remain reusable across Reports.

Do not store the actual Report's findings, field values, or other
Report-specific content inside a reusable Publishing Profile unless
required by the design.

#### Publishing Profile Validation

Before publishing, validate that the selected Publishing Profile is
compatible with the current Report.

For example:

- Required sections exist.
- Required fields exist.
- Referenced branding exists.
- Referenced themes exist.
- Referenced templates exist.
- Selected export format supports the requested features.

#### Missing Resource Handling

If a Publishing Profile references a resource that is unavailable:

- Do not silently substitute an unrelated resource.
- Clearly identify the missing resource.
- Provide an accessible error or warning.
- Allow the user to select an alternative where appropriate.

#### Publishing Pipeline

Establish a consistent publishing pipeline.

The general process should be:

1.  Select Report.
2.  Select Publishing Profile.
3.  Resolve applicable branding/theme/layout resources.
4.  Resolve content and section configuration.
5.  Generate the publishable representation.
6.  Validate the output.
7.  Generate the selected export format.
8.  Provide the completed output to the user.

The architecture should allow additional publishing stages to be
introduced later without rewriting the entire publishing system.

#### Separation of Content and Presentation

Keep Report content separate from presentation configuration.

Report content includes information such as:

- Findings.
- Issue Types.
- WCAG Success Criteria.
- Accessibility Standards.
- Pages/screens/components.
- Severity.
- Recommendations.
- Descriptions.
- Evidence.
- Analytics.

Presentation configuration includes:

- Fonts.
- Colors.
- Spacing.
- Layout.
- Headers.
- Footers.
- Page numbering.
- Cover pages.
- Tables of contents.
- Section presentation.

Changing presentation settings shall not modify the underlying Report
data.

#### Separation of Report Data and Export Format

The publishing architecture shall not make the Report's internal data
model dependent upon a particular export format.

For example, the Report model should not contain PDF-specific layout
instructions merely because the user exports to PDF.

Instead:

``` text
Report Data
     ↓
Publishing Configuration
     ↓
Publishing Representation
     ↓
Export Format
```

### Part 2: Report Layouts, Themes, Branding, and Visual Structure

#### Overview

Implement the core visual presentation system for the Reporting &
Publishing Framework.

Users shall be able to control how published Reports look without
modifying the underlying Report data.

The layout system shall support both:

- Standalone Reports.
- Reports contained within Project Workspaces.

The implementation shall reuse existing ART Report Branding, Report
Builder, Report Viewer, Template, and export functionality wherever
practical.

#### Report Layout System

Create a reusable Report Layout configuration within the Publishing
Framework.

A Report Layout shall control the structural presentation of the
published Report, including where major sections appear and how they are
organized.

A Layout may define:

- Cover page placement.
- Executive summary placement.
- Table of contents placement.
- Report information.
- Findings.
- Analytics.
- Recommendations.
- Methodology.
- Appendices.
- References.
- Audit information.
- Footer content.
- Page numbering.
- Section breaks.

The Layout shall control presentation and organization rather than
changing the underlying Report data.

#### Layout Scope

Layouts shall support appropriate scopes:

- Personal Layouts.
- Report-specific Layouts.
- Project Workspace Layouts.
- Shared Layouts where Collaboration permissions allow.

Clearly identify the scope of each Layout.

#### Layout Reuse

Users shall be able to apply an existing Layout to another Report when
they have permission to use it.

Applying a Layout shall not modify the underlying Report data.

#### Layout Editing

Users with appropriate permissions shall be able to:

- Create a Layout.
- Edit a Layout.
- Rename a Layout.
- Duplicate a Layout.
- Delete a Layout.
- Apply a Layout.
- Save a Layout.
- Preview a Layout.

Do not expose editing commands to users who lack the required
permissions.

#### Layout Duplication

Duplicating a Layout shall create an independent Layout configuration.

Subsequent changes to the duplicated Layout shall not modify the
original Layout.

#### Layout Defaults

Users may designate a default Layout for:

- A Report.
- A Project Workspace.
- New Reports within a Project Workspace.

If a Workspace has a default Layout, it should be applied to new Reports
unless the user explicitly selects another Layout.

#### Existing Report Templates

Integrate Layouts with the existing Report Template system.

Do not create a separate template architecture if the existing
architecture can support the requirement.

Where a Template contains layout information, the Publishing Framework
should be able to use that information when creating or publishing a
Report.

#### Template and Layout Relationship

Clearly distinguish between:

- Report Template.
- Report Layout.
- Publishing Profile.

A useful conceptual relationship is:

``` text
Report Template
    ↓
Creates/configures Report structure

Report Layout
    ↓
Controls visual/section presentation

Publishing Profile
    ↓
Controls the complete publishing configuration
```

### Part 3: Cover Pages, Table of Contents, Headers, Footers, Page Numbering, and Document Structure

#### Overview

Implement the document-structure and navigation features required to
produce professional, consistent, and accessible published Reports.

This part builds upon the Layout, Theme, Branding, and Publishing
Profile architecture established in Parts 1 and 2.

All features in this part shall support:

- Standalone Reports.
- Reports within Project Workspaces.
- Existing Report Templates.
- Existing Report Branding.
- Publishing Profiles.
- Supported export formats.
- Keyboard-only users.
- Screen-reader users.

Do not create separate implementations for standalone Reports and
Workspace Reports when the same underlying functionality can be reused.

#### Cover Page System

Implement a configurable Cover Page system as part of the Publishing
Framework.

Users shall be able to enable or disable a Cover Page through the
applicable Publishing Profile or Report publishing configuration.

The Cover Page should support configurable content such as:

- Organization name.
- Organization logo.
- Report title.
- Report subtitle.
- Project name.
- Workspace name, when applicable.
- Client name, when applicable.
- Author.
- Report date.
- Report version.
- Report status.
- Additional supported metadata.

#### Cover Page Layout

The Cover Page shall use the selected Report Layout and Theme where
applicable.

Users should be able to configure:

- Content placement.
- Alignment.
- Spacing.
- Typography.
- Colors.
- Images.
- Branding.

Do not require users to manually recreate the Cover Page for every
Report.

#### Cover Page Semantics

The Cover Page shall use a logical semantic structure.

The Report title shall be represented using an appropriate heading level
in the published document.

Do not use heading levels solely to achieve a particular visual
appearance.

Visual styling shall be controlled through the selected Theme.

#### Cover Page Logo and Image Accessibility

All Cover Page images and logos shall follow the image accessibility
requirements established in Part 2.

Each non-decorative image shall have required Alt Text.

Alt Text shall be preserved in:

- Preview.
- Saved Reports.
- Templates.
- Saved Branding.
- Published output.
- Supported export formats.

#### Cover Page Date

Where a Report date is displayed, the published document should use a
meaningful textual representation.

Do not expose a raw machine-readable timestamp as the only
representation of the date.

#### Cover Page Metadata

Where metadata is displayed, ensure it has appropriate semantic
structure.

For example:

``` text
Report Title
Accessibility Evaluation Report

Organization
Example Organization

Evaluation Date
July 15, 2026
```

### Part 4: Findings Presentation, Analytics, Filtering, Sorting, and Report Content Selection

#### Overview

Implement the content-selection and presentation capabilities required
to control which Report information appears in a published Report.

Users shall be able to determine which findings, analytics, fields,
sections, and supporting information are included in the final published
output without modifying or deleting the underlying Report data.

This functionality shall work for:

- Standalone Reports.
- Reports within Project Workspaces.
- Reports using personal Publishing Profiles.
- Reports using Workspace Publishing Profiles.
- Reports using shared Publishing Profiles where permitted.
- Existing Report Templates.
- Existing Report Branding.
- Existing Analytics.
- Existing Working Views where applicable.

The Publishing Framework shall use ART's existing Report data model
wherever possible.

#### Non-Destructive Publishing

Content selection shall never delete or modify the underlying Report
data.

For example, if a user excludes a Finding from a published Report:

- The Finding remains in the Report.
- The Finding remains available in the Report Viewer.
- The Finding remains available for future publishing.
- The Finding remains available to authorized users.
- The Finding is simply excluded from the current published output.

#### Report Content Selection

Provide a clear mechanism for selecting which major categories of Report
content are published.

Potential categories include:

- Executive Summary.
- Scope.
- Methodology.
- Findings.
- Analytics.
- Recommendations.
- Conclusion.
- Audit information.
- Appendices.
- References.
- Supporting information.

The exact available categories shall reflect the content actually
supported by ART.

#### Content Selection and Publishing Profiles

Content-selection settings shall be stored as part of the Publishing
Profile where appropriate.

A user should be able to configure a Publishing Profile once and reuse
the same content-selection rules across multiple Reports.

Report-specific overrides may be supported where appropriate.

#### Content Selection Scope

Clearly identify whether a content-selection setting applies to:

- The current Report.
- A Publishing Profile.
- A Project Workspace.
- A shared Publishing Profile.

Do not allow users to mistakenly believe that changing a Publishing
Profile only affects the current Report if the change actually affects
other Reports.

#### Findings

The Publishing Framework shall provide control over how Findings are
included in published Reports.

Users should be able to configure:

- Whether Findings are included.
- Which Findings are included.
- Finding order.
- Finding grouping.
- Finding detail level.
- Finding metadata.
- Finding evidence.
- Finding recommendations.

#### Finding Inclusion

Where appropriate, users should be able to include or exclude Findings
based on:

- Severity.
- Issue Type.
- Accessibility Standard.
- WCAG Success Criterion.
- Page.
- Screen.
- Component.
- Status.
- Finding state.
- Other Report fields.

Filtering options shall dynamically reflect the fields available in the
current Report.

#### Dynamic Report Fields

Do not hard-code field names that may differ between Reports.

If the current Report contains custom fields, the publishing interface
should use the actual field names and values from that Report.

This requirement is especially important for:

- Filtering.
- Sorting.
- Grouping.
- Finding selection.
- Report sections.
- Analytics.
- Publishing rules.

#### Issue Type Terminology

ART uses **Issue Type** to represent an individual test criterion within
an Accessibility Standard.

The Publishing Framework shall preserve this terminology consistently.

Where Issue Type is displayed, do not incorrectly substitute unrelated
terminology such as:

- Finding Type.
- Problem Type.
- Error Type.

unless the underlying data model actually distinguishes those concepts.

#### WCAG Success Criteria

When WCAG Success Criteria are displayed in published Reports, preserve:

- Success Criterion ID.
- Success Criterion Name.
- Conformance Level.

For example:

``` text
1.1.1 Non-Text Content (Level A)
```

### Part 5: Export Formats, Accessible Document Generation, and Publishing Output

#### Overview

Implement the export and document-generation layer of the Reporting &
Publishing Framework.

The Publishing Framework shall allow users to generate professional,
accessible Reports in the supported output formats while preserving the
selected:

- Report Layout.
- Report Theme.
- Report Branding.
- Header and Footer configuration.
- Cover Page.
- Table of Contents.
- Page numbering.
- Section structure.
- Finding presentation.
- Analytics.
- Filtering.
- Sorting.
- Grouping.
- Links.
- Images.
- Alternative text.
- Semantic structure.

The exported Report shall reflect the user's selected Publishing Profile
and shall not modify the underlying Report data.

This functionality shall support both:

- Standalone Reports.
- Reports contained within Project Workspaces.

Do not create separate publishing architectures for standalone Reports
and Workspace Reports when the same underlying implementation can be
reused.

#### Supported Export Formats

The Publishing Framework shall support the export formats already
supported by ART and should provide an architecture that allows
additional formats to be added without redesigning the publishing
system.

At minimum, preserve support for applicable existing formats such as:

- Microsoft Word (`.docx`).
- PDF.
- HTML.

If ART supports additional report formats, integrate those formats into
the same Publishing Framework.

#### Format Capability Model

Different export formats have different capabilities.

The Publishing Framework shall maintain a clear capability model so that
a Publishing Profile does not request functionality that the selected
export format cannot support.

For example, a format may or may not support:

- Interactive links.
- Bookmarks.
- Dynamic page numbers.
- Repeating headers.
- Repeating footers.
- Embedded images.
- Semantic headings.
- Tables.
- Accessible document metadata.
- Interactive analytics.

Do not silently discard requested functionality when the selected format
cannot support it.

#### Unsupported Features

If a selected Publishing Profile contains a feature that cannot be
represented in the selected output format:

1.  Identify the unsupported feature.
2.  Explain the limitation in an accessible message.
3.  Provide an appropriate alternative where possible.
4.  Allow the user to continue only when doing so will not produce
    misleading or unusable output.

Do not silently omit important Report content.

#### Export Validation

Before generating an export, perform validation appropriate to the
selected output format.

Validation should identify applicable:

- Missing required Alt Text.
- Broken links.
- Missing images.
- Invalid document structure.
- Unsupported features.
- Heading hierarchy problems.
- Table accessibility problems.
- Invalid filters.
- Invalid grouping.
- Invalid sorting.
- Missing required publishing data.
- Other known export problems.

#### Export Validation Summary

Provide an accessible summary before publishing.

For example:

``` text
Publishing Validation

Errors: 0
Warnings: 2
Information: 1
```

### Part 6: Publishing Profiles, Templates, Presets, and Reusable Report Configurations

#### Overview

Implement the reusable configuration layer for the Reporting &
Publishing Framework.

Publishing Profiles shall allow users to define, save, reuse, and share
consistent Report publishing configurations without having to configure
the same options repeatedly.

A Publishing Profile may define:

- Output format.
- Layout.
- Theme.
- Branding.
- Cover Page.
- Table of Contents.
- Headers.
- Footers.
- Page numbering.
- Document structure.
- Content selection.
- Findings presentation.
- Filtering.
- Sorting.
- Grouping.
- Analytics.
- Navigation.
- Accessibility settings.
- Metadata.
- Other supported publishing options.

Publishing Profiles shall not contain or duplicate the underlying Report
data.

#### Publishing Profile Architecture

Implement Publishing Profiles as reusable configuration objects.

A Publishing Profile shall reference configuration rather than copying
Report content.

For example, a Publishing Profile may specify:

``` text
Layout: Executive Report
Theme: Corporate
Branding: Organization Default
Cover Page: Enabled
Table of Contents: Enabled
Analytics: Enabled
Findings: Detailed
Grouping: Severity
Sorting: Issue Type
```

### Part 7: Report Layouts, Themes, Branding, and Visual Presentation

#### Overview

Implement the reusable visual presentation layer of the Reporting &
Publishing Framework.

This part establishes the mechanisms that determine how Reports look and
are structured when viewed, previewed, and published.

The framework shall support reusable:

- Report Layouts.
- Report Themes.
- Report Branding.
- Header configurations.
- Footer configurations.
