### Derived Data

Where data is calculated or derived from other data, conflict resolution
should occur on the underlying source data.

After the source conflict is resolved:

- Derived metrics shall be recalculated.
- Cached values shall be invalidated where necessary.
- Dashboards shall refresh appropriately.

### Tasks and To-Do Integration

Epic 45 task functionality shall participate in this conflict framework.

Conflicts may involve:

- Assignment
- Reassignment
- Status
- Priority
- Due date
- Task text
- Comments
- Shared To-Do membership
- Status options

Personal To-Do membership and personal reminders shall remain
user-specific unless explicitly designed as shared data.

### Personal Data Protection

A user's personal To-Do List shall not become a merge conflict merely
because another user changes the underlying shared task.

Instead:

- Shared task data may require resolution.
- Personal To-Do membership remains personal.
- Personal reminders remain personal.
- Personal sorting preferences remain personal.

### Notifications After Resolution

When a conflict is resolved, ART may notify affected users where
appropriate.

For example:

> 

**Merge conflict resolved**\
The "Homepage Audit" report was updated after resolving conflicting
changes.

Notifications shall not reveal information to unauthorized users.

### Accessibility Testing

Conflict resolution shall be tested with:

- JAWS
- NVDA
- VoiceOver
- TalkBack where applicable
- Keyboard-only navigation
- Browser zoom
- High magnification
- Other supported assistive technologies

Testing shall include:

- Conflict detection
- Conflict notification
- Opening conflict dialog
- Reviewing differences
- Selecting versions
- Manual merging
- Applying resolution
- Canceling resolution
- Undo
- Redo
- Concurrent changes
- Deleted entities
- Text conflicts
- Structured field conflicts
- Task conflicts

### Acceptance Criteria

#### Conflict Detection

- ART detects conflicting revisions.
- Conflicts are identified using stable entity/revision information.
- Local changes are not silently overwritten.
- Shared changes are not silently overwritten.
- Non-conflicting changes can be automatically merged where safe.
- Unsafe changes require user intervention.

#### Conflict Resolution

- Users receive an accessible conflict notification.
- Users can open the conflict-resolution dialog.
- Users can review competing versions.
- Users can identify who made each change.
- Users can identify when changes were made.
- Users can resolve conflicts at the field level where supported.
- Users can keep their version.
- Users can keep the other version.
- Users can create a merged result where supported.
- Unresolved conflicts cannot be silently committed.
- Task creation, deletion, assignment, status changes, priority changes,
  due dates, comments/notes/instructions, and completion state shall be
  represented in a manner that allows the changes to be detected and
  resolved by the Merge Conflict system defined in Epic 46.
- - Two copies of the same project can be independently modified and
    merged without a server.
- Non-conflicting changes are automatically merged.
- Conflicting changes are identified.
- Users can resolve conflicting changes.
- Stable object identifiers remain intact after merging.
- Merged data can be exported and imported again without losing resolved
  changes.
- The merge architecture can later be used by server-based
  synchronization.

#### Accessibility

- Conflict dialogs are fully keyboard accessible.
- Tabs use correct tablist/tab/tabpanel semantics where applicable.
- Differences are accessible to screen readers.
- Conflict status is programmatically determinable.
- Focus is managed correctly.
- No keyboard traps exist.
- Visual differences are not communicated by color alone.
- Resolution controls have meaningful accessible names.

#### History

- Conflict resolution participates in the History Framework.
- Applicable resolution actions can be undone.
- Applicable resolution actions can be redone.
- Undo does not silently overwrite newer collaborative changes.
- Redo does not blindly apply stale data.

#### Collaboration

- Shared Progress Logs support conflict detection.
- Shared tasks support conflict detection.
- Task assignments support conflict detection.
- Task status changes support conflict detection.
- Task comments are preserved appropriately.
- Shared To-Do Lists support conflict detection.
- Concurrent changes are detected.
- Stale resolutions are rejected or recalculated.

#### Data Safety

- No silent data loss occurs.
- Delete/modify conflicts are detected.
- Conflicting versions are preserved.
- Import conflicts are handled safely.
- Derived statistics are recalculated from resolved source data.

### Regression Testing

Verify that Epic 46 does not regress:

- Audit Logs
- Executive Summaries
- Usability Reports
- Report Builder
- Report Viewer
- Progress Logs
- Shared Progress Logs
- Tasks
- Shared To-Do Lists
- Personal To-Do Lists
- Organization Statistics
- Dashboard
- Notifications
- History Framework
- Undo/Redo
- Global Context Menu
- Menu bar
- Customizable keyboard shortcuts
- Local-first storage
- Import/Export
- Permissions
- Existing collaboration functionality

### Non-Goals

This epic shall not:

- Require permanent locking of shared entities.
- Replace the existing History Framework.
- Replace the Notifications system.
- Replace Shared Progress Logs.
- Replace Tasks or To-Do Lists.
- Automatically choose a winner when changes are genuinely conflicting.
- Silently discard local changes.
- Silently discard shared changes.
- Expose private information to unauthorized users.
- Treat derived Organization Statistics as independently editable source
  data.
- Require users to resolve conflicts that can safely be merged
  automatically.

### Definition of Done

Epic 46 shall be considered complete when ART provides a reliable,
accessible, and permission-aware merge-conflict framework that:

1.  Detects conflicting collaborative changes.
2.  Automatically merges safe, non-conflicting changes.
3.  Preserves competing versions when automatic merging is unsafe.
4.  Clearly notifies users of conflicts.
5.  Provides an accessible conflict-resolution dialog.
6.  Supports field-level and manual resolution where appropriate.
7.  Integrates with Shared Progress Logs and Tasks.
8.  Integrates with Notifications.
9.  Integrates with the History Framework.
10. Supports Undo/Redo where safe.
11. Prevents silent data loss.
12. Handles concurrent changes safely.
13. Respects permissions and privacy.
14. Works with local-first/offline workflows.
15. Provides complete keyboard and screen-reader accessibility.
16. Preserves the integrity of derived information such as Organization
    Statistics.

The resulting architecture shall provide ART with a dependable
foundation for multi-user collaboration without sacrificing the
**local-first, accessibility-first, user-controlled design principles**
of the application.

## Epic 47 — Security, Privacy, and Enterprise Readiness

### Overview

ART shall provide a secure, privacy-conscious foundation capable of
supporting individual users, small organizations, educational
institutions, nonprofits, government organizations, accessibility
consultancies, and large enterprises.

Security shall be treated as a core product requirement rather than a
feature added after development is complete.

This epic establishes the security, privacy, authentication,
authorization, deployment, monitoring, testing, documentation, and
compliance foundations necessary for ART to support:

-Local and standalone use

- Hosted SaaS deployments
- Shared Project Workspaces
- Collaboration
- User accounts
- Organization-level data
- Self-hosted deployments
- Enterprise deployments
- Future integrations with third-party platforms
- Sensitive accessibility audit and organizational data

### Supported Deployment and Collaboration Models

ART shall be designed to support multiple deployment and collaboration
models:

1.  **Local ART**

    - No account required.
    - No collaboration server required.
    - Data remains on the user's device unless explicitly exported or
      otherwise transmitted.

2.  **File-Based Collaboration**

    - Users exchange ART project/workspace packages.
    - Collaboration occurs through export, import, and merge operations.
    - No centralized server is required.

3.  **Hosted ART**

    - ART is connected to an ART-hosted collaboration service.
    - User accounts, synchronization, permissions, notifications, and
      other server-dependent functionality may be provided.

4.  **Self-Hosted ART**

    - Organizations operate their own ART collaboration infrastructure.
    - The organization controls its infrastructure, data,
      authentication, and applicable security policies.

Security requirements shall be appropriate to each deployment model.

### General Requirements

- Security shall be considered throughout ART's architecture and
  development lifecycle.
- Security controls shall not unnecessarily interfere with
  accessibility.
- Security-related interfaces shall be fully keyboard accessible and
  compatible with assistive technologies.
- Security-sensitive operations shall provide appropriate accessible
  feedback.
- ART shall follow the principle of least privilege.
- Users shall only be able to access information and perform actions
  permitted by their account, role, organization, project, workspace,
  and applicable permissions.
- Security controls shall apply consistently across the web application,
  desktop application, APIs, integrations, hosted deployments, and
  self-hosted deployments where applicable.
- Local-first functionality shall continue to work without unnecessarily
  requiring an account or network connection.
- Features that require authentication, collaboration, synchronization,
  or hosted services shall clearly communicate those requirements.
- Security mechanisms shall not expose sensitive information through
  error messages, URLs, logs, browser storage, notifications, exports,
  or other unintended locations.
- Security-related changes shall be covered by appropriate automated and
  manual testing.

### Security Architecture

ART shall use a security architecture appropriate for an application
that may store accessibility findings, audit reports, organizational
information, tester information, project information, collaboration
data, and other potentially sensitive information.

The architecture shall address:

- Authentication
- Authorization
- Session management
- Identity management
- Organization isolation
- Project/workspace isolation
- Data protection
- Encryption
- Secure communications
- Secure storage
- API security
- Integration security
- Input validation
- Output encoding
- Error handling
- Logging
- Monitoring
- Backup and recovery
- Data deletion
- Data export
- Security incident response

Security-sensitive architectural decisions shall be documented.

### Threat Modeling

ART shall establish a repeatable threat-modeling process.

Threat modeling shall consider, at minimum:

- Unauthorized account access
- Privilege escalation
- Unauthorized organization access
- Unauthorized project/workspace access
- Cross-organization data exposure
- Cross-user data exposure
- Session hijacking
- Credential theft
- Token theft
- Malicious imports
- Malicious exports
- Malicious integrations
- API abuse
- Injection attacks
- Cross-site scripting
- Cross-site request forgery where applicable
- Insecure direct object references
- Data leakage
- Insecure file handling
- Supply-chain attacks
- Dependency vulnerabilities
- Denial-of-service risks
- Collaboration and synchronization attacks
- Merge/conflict manipulation
- Compromised third-party integrations
- Malicious or compromised self-hosted environments

Threat models shall be reviewed as ART's architecture and capabilities
evolve.

### Authentication

When user accounts are enabled, ART shall provide secure authentication
mechanisms.

Authentication shall only be required for functionality that requires
identity, authorization, synchronization, centralized collaboration, or
another authenticated service.

Local ART and file-based collaboration shall not require user accounts
solely to operate the application.

Authentication shall include appropriate support for:

- Account creation

- Secure login

- Logout\
  agement where passwords are supported

- Account recovery

- Session management

- Authentication failure handling

- Account security settings

- Optional multi-factor authentication where supported

- Authentication-provider integration where appropriate

Authentication shall not be required for functionality that is
intentionally designed to operate locally without an account.

### Authorization

ART shall implement role- and permission-based authorization.

Authorization shall determine whether a user may:

- View an organization
- Modify organization information
- View a project
- Modify a project
- Access a workspace
- Modify a workspace
- View reports
- Modify reports
- Export reports
- Create or modify tasks
- Assign or reassign tasks
- Modify Progress Logs
- Manage Shared Progress Logs
- Manage users
- Manage permissions
- Manage integrations
- View Organization Statistics
- Modify organization settings
- Perform administrative operations

Authorization shall be enforced server-side for hosted and collaborative
functionality and shall not rely solely on client-side controls.

### Least Privilege

ART shall follow the principle of least privilege.

Users shall receive only the permissions necessary to perform their
assigned responsibilities.

Administrative privileges shall not automatically grant access to
unrelated organizations or projects unless explicitly permitted.

### Organization Isolation

Because ART may support multiple organizations within a single hosted
environment, strong logical isolation shall be maintained between
organizations.

Data belonging to one organization shall not be accessible to another
organization unless explicitly shared or otherwise authorized.

Organization isolation shall apply to:

- Reports
- Findings
- Projects
- Workspaces
- Progress Logs
- Shared Progress Logs
- Tasks
- Users
- Organization Statistics
- Templates
- Files
- Notifications
- Integrations
- API requests
- Search
- Exports
- Backups

Cross-organization access shall be specifically tested.

Organization isolation is primarily applicable to hosted and shared
server deployments.

Local ART shall instead isolate data according to the local
project/workspace and user's device.

File-based collaboration shall rely on explicit sharing of
project/workspace packages and shall not create centralized
cross-organization access.

### Organization/Client Metadata

ART currently uses the Organization/Client value in report metadata to
identify the organization associated with reports when Organization
Statistics are being collected.

Security and privacy documentation shall clearly distinguish between:

- A report's Organization/Client metadata
- An authenticated user's organization membership
- A hosted ART organization/account
- A self-hosted organization's environment

Organization Statistics shall not assume that the Organization/Client
field is a security boundary.

The documentation shall continue to explain that Organization Statistics
can only be accurate when the Organization/Client field is consistently
and accurately populated.

### Data Protection

ART shall protect sensitive data throughout its lifecycle.

This shall include:

- Data at rest
- Data in transit
- Temporary data
- Cached data
- Backup data
- Exported data
- Imported data
- Shared data
- Integration data

Where encryption is appropriate, industry-accepted encryption mechanisms
shall be used.

### Secure Communications

Hosted ART services shall use secure communications.

Sensitive information shall not be transmitted through insecure
communication channels.

Certificates, TLS configuration, secure headers, and related
infrastructure shall be appropriately configured and maintained.

### Local Data Security

ART's local-first architecture shall be documented clearly.

The application shall explain:

- What data is stored locally
- Where it is stored
- What data leaves the user's device
- When network communication occurs
- What happens when synchronization is enabled
- What happens when collaboration is enabled
- How users can export their data
- How users can delete their local data

Local storage shall not be treated as inherently secure merely because
it is local.

### Browser Storage

ART shall review the security implications of storing data in
browser-based storage.

Sensitive information shall not be stored in locations that
unnecessarily expose it to:

- Cross-site attacks
- Malicious scripts
- Untrusted extensions
- Other users of the device
- Shared-device access

Where browser storage is used, the implementation shall follow
appropriate security practices.

### Desktop Application Security

When ART provides a downloadable/installable desktop application, the
desktop application shall follow appropriate platform security
practices.

This shall include:

- Secure updates
- Code-signing where appropriate
- Secure local storage
- Application permissions
- Protection against unauthorized modification
- Secure handling of imported/exported files
- Secure communication with hosted services
- Protection of authentication credentials and tokens

The desktop application shall not unnecessarily weaken the security
model of the web application.

### Self-Hosted Security

Self-hosted ART deployments shall provide documentation and
configuration guidance for secure deployment.

Documentation shall address:

- Supported deployment models
- Containerization
- Network configuration
- HTTPS/TLS
- Authentication
- Database security
- Secrets management
- Backups
- Updates
- Logging
- Monitoring
- Firewall configuration
- Access control
- Vulnerability management

ART shall clearly communicate which security responsibilities belong to
the ART software and which belong to the organization operating the
deployment.

### Containers, Wrappers, and Sandboxes

Self-hosted organizations may deploy ART within their own:

- Containers
- Sandboxes
- Wrappers
- Virtual machines
- Private clouds
- Enterprise environments

ART shall provide documentation describing supported deployment
approaches and security considerations.

The application shall not assume that every organization has the same
infrastructure.

### SaaS Security

If ART is offered as a hosted SaaS service, the hosted environment shall
provide appropriate protections for:

- User accounts
- Organizations
- Projects
- Workspaces
- Reports
- Databases
- Uploaded files
- Authentication credentials
- API credentials
- Integrations
- Backups
- Logs

Hosted infrastructure shall be designed to prevent unauthorized access
and cross-organization data exposure.

Hosted SaaS collaboration shall be an optional deployment model and
shall not be required for ART's core local functionality.

### Session Management

Authenticated sessions shall be securely managed.

ART shall provide appropriate controls for:

- Session creation
- Session expiration
- Session renewal
- Logout
- Session invalidation
- Concurrent sessions where supported
- Password or credential changes
- Suspicious session activity

Users shall have an accessible way to manage active sessions where
appropriate.

### Password Security

If ART supports password-based authentication:

- Passwords shall never be stored in plaintext.
- Passwords shall be protected using an appropriate password-hashing
  mechanism.
- Password requirements shall be documented.
- Password-reset mechanisms shall be secure.
- Password-reset tokens shall expire appropriately.
- Authentication errors shall not disclose unnecessary account
  information.

### Multi-Factor Authentication

ART should support multi-factor authentication for hosted and enterprise
deployments where appropriate.

MFA implementation shall consider:

- Accessibility
- Screen readers
- Braille
- Mobile devices
- Authentication applications
- Hardware security keys
- Recovery procedures

MFA shall not unnecessarily exclude users with disabilities.

### Identity Provider Integration

ART should eventually support enterprise identity providers where
appropriate.

Potential capabilities include:

- Single sign-on
- SAML
- OpenID Connect
- OAuth-based authentication
- Enterprise directory integration

Any identity-provider integration shall follow appropriate security
practices and shall clearly document responsibility boundaries.

### API Security

ART APIs shall use appropriate authentication and authorization.

API security shall address:

- Authentication
- Authorization
- Rate limiting
- Input validation
- Output filtering
- Request-size limits
- Error handling
- Token management
- Token expiration
- Revocation
- Logging
- Abuse prevention

APIs shall never expose data merely because a user can construct a valid
request.

### Integration Security

Third-party integrations shall use secure authentication mechanisms.

ART shall protect:

- API keys
- Access tokens
- Refresh tokens
- OAuth credentials
- Webhook credentials
- Integration configuration

Users shall be able to revoke integrations where supported.

ART shall clearly communicate what information is shared with each
integration.

### GitHub Issues Integration

When GitHub Issues integration is implemented, ART shall:

- Clearly identify the GitHub account/repository being accessed.
- Request only necessary permissions.
- Securely store credentials/tokens.
- Allow users to disconnect the integration.
- Prevent unauthorized users from using another user's GitHub
  credentials.
- Clearly identify which ART data is sent to GitHub.
- Handle GitHub API errors securely.
- Avoid exposing GitHub credentials in logs or exported reports.

### Jira, Azure, and Other Integrations

Equivalent security controls shall apply to:

- Jira
- Microsoft Azure / Azure DevOps
- Google Workspace
- Microsoft 365
- Other future integrations

Each integration shall document:

- Permissions requested
- Data shared
- Data received
- Authentication method
- Credential storage
- Revocation procedure
- Error handling
- Security responsibilities

### File and Import Security

ART supports importing and exporting data.

Imported files shall be treated as untrusted input.

ART shall validate:

- File type
- File size
- File structure
- Data types
- Expected fields
- Embedded content
- Potentially malicious content

Import functionality shall not allow malicious data to execute code or
compromise the application.

### Export Security

Exports may contain sensitive accessibility and organizational
information.

ART shall ensure that exports:

- Include only intended information.
- Respect applicable permissions.
- Do not unintentionally expose hidden/internal data.
- Do not include credentials or security tokens.
- Clearly identify potentially sensitive information where appropriate.

### Report Security

Reports may contain:

- Accessibility findings
- Screenshots
- URLs
- User information
- Tester information
- Organization information
- Internal project information
- Security-sensitive information

ART shall provide appropriate controls for viewing, exporting, sharing,
and deleting reports.

### Audit Logging

Security-sensitive actions should be logged appropriately.

Potential events include:

- Login
- Logout
- Authentication failures
- Password changes
- Permission changes
- Organization membership changes
- Report access
- Report deletion
- Data export
- Integration creation
- Integration removal
- Administrative actions
- Security configuration changes

Logs shall avoid storing unnecessary sensitive information.

### Security Log Protection

Security logs shall be protected from unauthorized modification or
deletion.

Where hosted services are provided, security logs should be retained
according to documented policies.

### Notifications and Security

ART notifications shall not expose sensitive information unnecessarily.

Notifications shall be evaluated for:

- Dashboard notifications
- Email notifications
- Task notifications
- @mentions
- Reminders
- Shared Progress Log updates
- Security alerts

Email notifications shall contain enough information to identify the
relevant event without unnecessarily exposing confidential report or
project information.

### Accessibility of Security Features

All security features shall be accessible.

This includes:

- Login
- Registration
- Password fields
- MFA
- Account settings
- Permission management
- Security settings
- Session management
- Integration authorization
- Security notifications
- Confirmation dialogs
- Error messages

Security features shall be tested with:

- JAWS
- NVDA
- Narrator
- VoiceOver
- ChromeVox
- TalkBack
- Braille displays
- Keyboard-only interaction
- Other relevant assistive technologies

### Security and the Global Context Menu

Security-sensitive commands available through ART's global context menu
shall:

- Respect permissions.
- Be keyboard accessible.
- Provide accessible names.
- Provide appropriate confirmation where necessary.
- Not expose commands to unauthorized users.

### Security and Keyboard Shortcuts

User-defined keyboard shortcuts shall not provide a mechanism for
bypassing authorization.

Security-sensitive keyboard commands shall:

- Respect permissions.
- Provide appropriate confirmation.
- Provide accessible feedback.
- Avoid accidental execution where the consequence is significant.

### Security and History / Undo / Redo

ART's History Framework shall not allow Undo/Redo to bypass security
controls.

For example, a user shall not be able to use History to:

- Restore data they are no longer authorized to access.
- Reverse a permission change they are not authorized to modify.
- Restore deleted information outside their permissions.
- Circumvent organization boundaries.

Security-sensitive historical actions shall be handled appropriately.

### Security and Collaboration

Collaborative features shall enforce authorization at every relevant
operation.

This includes:

- Shared workspaces
- Shared Progress Logs
- Assigned tasks
- Task reassignment
- Comments
- @mentions
- Notifications
- Report editing
- Organization Statistics
- Conflict resolution

A user shall not gain access to information simply because another user
references it in a collaborative action.

### Merge Conflict Security

Merge conflict resolution shall respect permissions.

A user shall only be able to resolve conflicts involving data they are
authorized to access and modify.

Conflict-resolution interfaces shall not expose hidden data from another
user, organization, or project.

### Security and Organization Statistics

Organization Statistics may aggregate information from many reports and
projects.

Access to statistics shall therefore be permission controlled.

ART shall prevent unauthorized users from using aggregated statistics to
infer information they are not permitted to access.

Statistics shall respect:

- Organization boundaries
- Project permissions
- Report permissions
- Workspace permissions
- User permissions

### Privacy

ART shall follow privacy-by-design principles.

The application shall collect only information necessary for the
functionality being used.

Users shall be informed about:

- What information is collected
- Why it is collected
- Where it is stored
- How it is used
- When it is shared
- How it can be exported
- How it can be deleted

### Data Minimization

ART shall avoid collecting unnecessary personal information.

Where possible, users should be able to operate ART without providing
personal information.

Account information required for hosted collaboration shall be limited
to what is necessary.

### Data Retention

ART shall establish configurable and documented data-retention practices
where appropriate.

Retention considerations shall include:

- Accounts
- Projects
- Reports
- Audit Logs
- Progress Logs
- Tasks
- Notifications
- Security logs
- Backups
- Deleted information

### Data Deletion

Users and authorized administrators shall have appropriate mechanisms
for deleting data.

Deletion shall respect:

- Permissions
- Dependencies
- Audit requirements
- Collaboration
- Backups
- Retention policies

Where deletion cannot immediately remove data from backups or immutable
logs, the documentation shall explain this behavior.

### Data Export and Portability

Users shall be able to export their ART data in documented formats.

Data portability shall be considered for:

- Reports
- Projects
- Workspaces
- Tasks
- Progress Logs
- Organization Statistics
- Templates
- Settings
- Other user-created content

Users shall not be unnecessarily locked into ART.

### Privacy Documentation

ART shall provide clear privacy documentation covering:

- Local storage
- Hosted storage
- Account information
- Collaboration
- Integrations
- Analytics
- Organization Statistics
- Notifications
- Security logs
- Cookies and browser storage where applicable
- Data deletion
- Data export

### Dependency Security

ART shall maintain an inventory of software dependencies.

Dependencies shall be:

- Regularly reviewed
- Updated
- Monitored for vulnerabilities
- Removed when unnecessary
- Pinned or otherwise controlled where appropriate

Critical vulnerabilities shall receive appropriate priority.

### Software Supply Chain Security

ART shall establish protections for the software supply chain.

This should include:

- Dependency scanning
- Package integrity verification
- Secure build processes
- Protected source repositories
- Protected release processes
- Build provenance where practical
- Signed releases where appropriate

### Secure Development Lifecycle

Security shall be integrated into ART development.

Development practices should include:

1.  Security requirements
2.  Threat modeling
3.  Secure implementation
4.  Code review
5.  Automated security testing
6.  Dependency scanning
7.  Manual security testing
8.  Release verification
9.  Vulnerability remediation
10. Post-release monitoring

### Code Review

Security-sensitive changes shall receive appropriate code review.

Additional review should be considered for:

- Authentication
- Authorization
- Cryptography
- Database access
- APIs
- Integrations
- File handling
- User permissions
- Organization isolation
- Data deletion
- Security configuration

### Automated Security Testing

ART shall incorporate automated security testing where practical.

Potential testing includes:

- Dependency scanning
- Static analysis
- Dynamic analysis
- Secret scanning
- Authentication tests
- Authorization tests
- API security tests
- Input-validation tests
- Cross-organization isolation tests
- Regression tests

### Penetration Testing

ART should undergo independent penetration testing before major
enterprise or hosted deployment.

Testing should cover:

- Web application
- APIs
- Authentication
- Authorization
- Collaboration
- Organization isolation
- Integrations
- Hosted infrastructure
- Desktop application where applicable

Identified vulnerabilities shall be tracked through remediation and
retesting.

### Vulnerability Management

ART shall establish a vulnerability-management process.

The process shall define:

-How vulnerabilities are reported

- Who receives reports
- Severity classification
- Response priorities
- Remediation procedures
- Disclosure procedures
- Retesting
- Security advisories

A security contact mechanism shall be published for responsible
vulnerability reporting.

### Security Incident Response

ART shall establish an incident-response process.

The process shall address:

- Detection
- Investigation
- Containment
- Eradication
- Recovery
- Communication
- Documentation
- Post-incident review

Hosted services shall have documented procedures for responding to
suspected data breaches.

### Backup and Disaster Recovery

Hosted and self-hosted deployments shall provide guidance for:

- Backups
- Backup encryption
- Backup testing
- Restoration
- Disaster recovery
- Recovery objectives
- Data integrity verification

Backups shall be protected from unauthorized access.

### Business Continuity

Hosted ART services should establish business-continuity plans
addressing:

- Infrastructure failures
- Database failures
- Security incidents
- Service outages
- Loss of personnel
- Provider outages
- Disaster scenarios

### Monitoring

Hosted deployments should provide appropriate monitoring for:

- Application health
- Authentication events
- API activity
- Database health
- Security events
- Infrastructure health
- Performance
- Errors

Monitoring shall avoid unnecessary collection of personal or sensitive
information.

### Security Alerts

Security alerts shall be accessible and understandable.

Where security alerts require user action, they shall clearly explain:

- What happened
- Why it matters
- What the user should do
- What options are available

### Enterprise Security Documentation

ART shall eventually provide documentation suitable for organizational
security reviews.

Documentation should include:

- Architecture
- Data flow
- Security controls
- Authentication
- Authorization
- Encryption
- Infrastructure
- Backup
- Disaster recovery
- Incident response
- Vulnerability management
- Privacy
- Data retention
- Subprocessors where applicable
- Integration security

### SOC 2 Readiness

ART shall establish a roadmap toward SOC 2 readiness if hosted services
and enterprise adoption warrant it.

The project shall evaluate applicable Trust Services Criteria,
including:

- Security
- Availability
- Processing integrity
- Confidentiality
- Privacy

The project shall establish appropriate policies, controls, evidence
collection, monitoring, and operational procedures before pursuing an
independent SOC 2 examination.

SOC 2 certification shall not be represented as completed until an
appropriate independent examination has been successfully completed.

### Other Security Frameworks

ART shall evaluate additional standards and frameworks based on target
markets and deployment requirements.

Potential frameworks include:

- ISO/IEC 27001
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework
- NIST SP 800-series guidance
- CIS Controls
- OWASP guidance
- Applicable government security requirements
- Applicable privacy regulations

ART shall not claim compliance or certification without appropriate
evidence.

### Government Readiness

If ART is adopted by government organizations, additional requirements
may apply.

The project shall evaluate applicable:

- Accessibility requirements
- Privacy requirements
- Security requirements
- Procurement requirements
- Data residency requirements
- Records-retention requirements
- Authorization requirements

Where applicable, the project shall evaluate whether government-hosted
deployments require additional authorization frameworks such as FedRAMP.

### Enterprise Vendor Assessments

ART should eventually support common enterprise vendor-security review
requirements.

Documentation should be prepared to address common questions regarding:

- Data location
- Encryption
- Authentication
- Access control
- Logging
- Incident response
- Backups
- Disaster recovery
- Vulnerability management
- Privacy
- Subprocessors
- Business continuity
- Security testing

### Security Testing Matrix

A comprehensive security test matrix shall be developed covering:

- Anonymous users
- Authenticated users
- Organization members
- Project members
- Workspace members
- Editors
- Administrators
- Other defined permission levels

Tests shall verify that each role can perform only permitted actions.

### Accessibility Security Testing

Security features shall be included in accessibility regression testing.

Testing shall verify that:

- Authentication is accessible.
- Permission-management interfaces are accessible.
- Security alerts are accessible.
- Error messages are accessible.
- MFA workflows are accessible.
- Account recovery is accessible.
- Security dialogs are accessible.
- Security settings are accessible.

### Security Documentation for Contributors

Developer documentation shall explain:

- Security architecture
- Authentication architecture
- Authorization model
- Data boundaries
- Secure coding requirements
- Secret management
- Dependency management
- Vulnerability reporting
- Security testing
- Release security

Contributors shall not be expected to infer security requirements from
the codebase.

### Security Documentation for Self-Hosted Administrators

Self-hosting documentation shall explain:

- Minimum system requirements
- Network requirements
- HTTPS/TLS
- Database configuration
- Authentication
- User management
- Backups
- Updates
- Monitoring
- Logging
- Security hardening
- Incident response
- Disaster recovery

### Security Documentation for Users

User-facing documentation shall clearly explain:

- Account security
- Password management
- MFA where available
- Sessions
- Data storage
- Sharing
- Collaboration
- Integrations
- Export
- Deletion
- Privacy

### Security Regression Testing

Security tests shall be included in the regression-testing process.

Security-sensitive functionality shall be retested whenever related
functionality changes.

### Security Release Checklist

Before significant releases, the project should evaluate:

- Authentication
- Authorization
- Organization isolation
- Dependency vulnerabilities
- Secret exposure
- API security
- File handling
- Integrations
- Data migration
- Backup/recovery
- Security logging
- Accessibility of security features
- Regression testing

### Security Acceptance Criteria

Epic 47 shall not be considered complete until:

1.  A documented ART security architecture exists.
2.  Authentication requirements are documented.
3.  Authorization and permission requirements are documented.
4.  Organization isolation requirements are implemented and tested.
5.  Hosted and self-hosted security responsibilities are documented.
6.  Local data-security considerations are documented.
7.  API security requirements are implemented.
8.  Integration-security requirements are established.
9.  Import/export security has been evaluated.
10. Security-sensitive actions respect permissions.
11. Collaboration security has been tested.
12. Merge conflict security has been tested.
13. Organization Statistics access controls have been tested.
14. Dependency and secret scanning are implemented where practical.
15. A vulnerability-reporting process exists.
16. A security incident-response process exists.
17. Backup and disaster-recovery procedures are documented for hosted
    deployments.
18. Security features have been tested with assistive technologies.
19. Self-hosting security documentation is available.
20. Enterprise security documentation is established.
21. A SOC 2 readiness roadmap has been established if applicable.
22. Appropriate independent security testing has been planned or
    completed before enterprise production deployment.
23. No known critical security vulnerabilities remain unresolved for
    release.
24. Security regression testing is incorporated into the development
    process.

### Deliverables

The completed epic shall produce:

- ART security architecture documentation
- Threat models
- Authentication architecture
- Authorization architecture
- Permission model
- Organization-isolation controls
- Secure session management
- API security controls
- Integration security controls
- Local-storage security guidance
- SaaS security architecture
- Self-hosting security guidance
- Desktop security requirements
- Security logging and monitoring requirements
- Vulnerability-management process
- Security incident-response process
- Backup and disaster-recovery guidance
- Security testing plan
- Automated security tests where practical
- Accessibility security-testing plan
- Enterprise security documentation
- Privacy documentation
- Data-retention and deletion guidance
- Data-portability guidance
- SOC 2 readiness roadmap where applicable
- Security contribution guidelines
- Security release checklist

### Non-Goals

This epic does not require ART to:

- Claim SOC 2 certification before an independent examination is
  completed.
- Claim compliance with a security framework without evidence.
- Require an account for local functionality that does not need one.
- Force every deployment model to use identical infrastructure.
- Collect unnecessary personal information.
- Replace an organization's existing enterprise security infrastructure.
- Guarantee security against every possible threat.
- Require one authentication provider for every organization.
- Require hosted deployment when self-hosting is appropriate.

### Long-Term Security Goal

ART shall provide a security foundation that allows the application to
grow from an accessible local reporting tool into a secure,
collaborative, enterprise-capable platform without sacrificing its
accessibility-first and privacy-conscious principles.

Security shall remain an ongoing responsibility of ART's architecture,
development, testing, deployment, documentation, and community rather
than a one-time implementation milestone.

The ultimate goal is to make ART capable of being trusted by individuals
and organizations ranging from independent accessibility professionals
to large enterprises, educational institutions, nonprofits, and
government organizations while allowing each organization to select an
appropriate deployment and security model.

## Epic 48 — Secure Passwordless User Accounts and Authentication

### Overview

Implement a secure, accessible, privacy-conscious, passwordless user
account and authentication system for ART.

The authentication system shall provide the foundation for future
server-dependent functionality, including:

- Shared Project Workspaces
- Server-based collaboration
- Shared Progress Logs
- User assignments
- Centralized notifications
- @mention notifications
- Organization membership
- Organization Statistics synchronization
- Server-based task synchronization
- Future integrations requiring authenticated access
- Hosted SaaS functionality
- Self-hosted ART deployments
- Future desktop application functionality

**Authentication shall not be required to use ART's fundamental
functionality.**

ART shall remain fully usable without an account or login. Users who
choose not to log in shall continue to have access to ART's core local
functionality, including creating, editing, testing, reporting,
importing, exporting, and managing local projects.

Logging in shall provide **additional capabilities**, rather than being
a prerequisite for using ART.

### Core Authentication Principle

ART shall follow this model:

``` text
                         ART
                          |
              +-----------+-----------+
              |                       |
       Not Logged In              Logged In
              |                       |
       Core ART Features         Core ART Features
              |                       |
       Local Projects            Local Projects
       Local Reports             Local Reports
       Local Tasks               Local Tasks
       Import/Export             Import/Export
                                  +
                           Collaboration
                           Shared Workspaces
                           Server Features
                           Accounts
                           Organizations
                           Synchronization
```

A user shall never be forced to create an account merely to use ART's
fundamental accessibility-testing and reporting capabilities.

### Passwordless Authentication

ART shall use **passwordless authentication as the preferred
authentication model**.

ART shall not require users to create or maintain an ART password.

The preferred native ART authentication mechanism shall be **passkeys
using WebAuthn/FIDO2**.

WebAuthn provides a standards-based browser API for strong public-key
authentication, while FIDO passkeys provide passwordless authentication
using authenticators such as device biometrics, device PINs, security
keys, and other supported authenticators.

The implementation shall use established standards rather than creating
a proprietary authentication mechanism.

### General Requirements

- Authentication shall use established, secure standards.
- WebAuthn/FIDO2 passkeys shall be the preferred native ART
  authentication mechanism.
- OAuth 2.0 and/or OpenID Connect shall be supported for external
  identity providers where appropriate.
- ART shall not require users to create an ART password.
- Password-based authentication shall not be implemented unless a future
  requirement demonstrates a compelling need.
- Authentication credentials shall never be stored in plain text.
- Passwords shall never be stored in plain text if password
  authentication is ever introduced.
- OAuth access tokens, refresh tokens, ID tokens, passkeys, private
  keys, session credentials, and other authentication secrets shall
  never be exposed through the user interface, reports, exports, URLs,
  logs, or browser-visible source code.
- ART shall remain fully usable without authentication for fundamental
  local functionality.
- Users shall be able to authenticate when they want access to
  server-dependent functionality.
- Users shall be able to log out.
- Authentication failures shall provide useful but appropriately limited
  information.
- Authentication shall follow the principle of least privilege.
- Authentication shall support both hosted SaaS and self-hosted ART
  deployments where practical.

### Passkeys and WebAuthn

ART shall support passkeys as the preferred passwordless authentication
method.

The implementation shall use the Web Authentication API and an
appropriate FIDO2/WebAuthn server implementation.

The architecture shall support appropriate passkey types, including:

- Synced passkeys
- Device-bound passkeys
- Platform authenticators
- Roaming authenticators
- Hardware security keys
- Mobile-device authenticators
- Cross-device authentication

FIDO identifies passkeys as FIDO credentials that can be unlocked using
a device's biometric authentication, PIN, pattern, or equivalent local
authentication mechanism.

ART shall not require users to understand the underlying cryptographic
technology in order to use passkeys.

### Passkey User Experience

The ART login interface should provide a simple option such as:

> **Sign in with a passkey**

or:

> **Use a passkey**

The exact user-facing wording shall be evaluated for accessibility and
platform consistency.

Users should be able to authenticate using:

- Fingerprint
- Face recognition
- Device PIN
- Device screen lock
- Hardware security key
- Supported mobile authenticator
- Other supported WebAuthn authenticator mechanisms

The user's local biometric information shall remain under the control of
the authenticator/device and shall not be transmitted to ART.

FIDO states that biometric information used by passkeys remains on the
user's device rather than being sent to the service.

### Multiple Passkeys

Users shall be able to register multiple passkeys with their ART
account.

This shall allow users to maintain access through multiple devices or
authenticators.

Examples include:

- Desktop computer
- Laptop
- Smartphone
- Tablet
- Hardware security key
- Secondary computer
- Backup authenticator

Users shall be able to:

- Add a passkey.
- Name a passkey.
- View registered passkeys.
- Remove a passkey.
- Identify when a passkey was last used where technically available.
- Replace lost or compromised passkeys.
- Maintain multiple active passkeys.

### Passkey Management

The account security interface shall provide an accessible
passkey-management area.

For each registered passkey, ART should display information such as:

- User-defined passkey name
- Registration date
- Last-used date where available
- Authenticator type where available
- Device/platform information where safely available

ART shall not expose private cryptographic key material.

### Cross-Device Authentication

ART should support cross-device passkey authentication where supported
by the browser, operating system, and authenticator.

This may include authentication using a nearby mobile device or another
supported authenticator.

FIDO2 supports external authenticators and cross-device authentication
mechanisms through CTAP and related technologies.

### Hardware Security Keys

ART should support FIDO2-compatible hardware security keys through
WebAuthn.

Examples include supported:

- USB security keys
- NFC security keys
- Bluetooth security keys

Hardware security keys shall be treated as authenticators and shall not
require users to maintain a password.

### Authentication Providers

ART shall initially support authentication through:

- Google
- Microsoft
- Amazon
- GitHub

These providers shall be treated as **external identity-provider
options**, rather than replacements for ART's native passkey
architecture.

### Google

Users shall be able to authenticate using a supported Google identity
through an appropriate OAuth 2.0 and/or OpenID Connect workflow.

### Microsoft

Users shall be able to authenticate using a supported Microsoft identity
through an appropriate OAuth 2.0 and/or OpenID Connect workflow.

The architecture shall allow future support for Microsoft Entra ID and
organizational Microsoft identities.

### Amazon

Users shall be able to authenticate using a supported Amazon identity
through an appropriate OAuth 2.0 workflow.

### GitHub

Users shall be able to authenticate using a supported GitHub identity
through an appropriate OAuth workflow.

GitHub authentication shall not automatically grant access to any ART
GitHub repository, organization, source code, or development resources.

### Authentication Architecture

The preferred architecture shall resemble:

``` text
ART User Account
       |
       +-------------------------+
       |                         |
 Native Passwordless        External Identity
 Authentication             Providers
       |                         |
   WebAuthn/FIDO2        Google / Microsoft
       |                 Amazon / GitHub
       |
   Passkeys
       |
 +-----+-----+---------+
 |           |         |
Device      Mobile   Security
Auth        Device     Key
```

Authentication shall establish **who the user is**.

Authorization shall separately determine **what the user may access**.

### Provider Abstraction

ART shall avoid tightly coupling its user-account architecture to one
authentication provider.

Where practical, the authentication architecture shall support:

- WebAuthn/FIDO2
- Google
- Microsoft
- Amazon
- GitHub
- Additional OAuth providers
- Additional OpenID Connect providers
- Enterprise identity providers
- Self-hosted identity providers where appropriate

The internal ART user identity shall not be identical to an external
provider's internal identifier.

### ART User Identity

ART shall maintain its own stable internal user identifier.

The internal user identifier shall:

- Be unique.
- Remain stable across sessions.
- Not expose sensitive personal information.
- Not be based solely on the user's email address.
- Be usable by collaboration, permissions, tasks, Progress Logs,
  Organization Statistics, notifications, and other server-dependent
  functionality.

Changing an email address or authentication provider shall not
unintentionally create a second ART identity.

### User Sign-Up Workflow

ART shall provide an accessible user sign-up workflow.

The workflow shall allow a new user to:

1.  Choose to create an ART account.
2.  Select an authentication method.
3.  Register a passkey or authenticate through a supported identity
    provider.
4.  Provide any additional ART-specific information that is required.
5.  Review applicable terms and privacy information.
6.  Complete account creation.
7.  Return to ART as an authenticated user.

The sign-up process shall collect only information necessary for the
functionality being provided.

### Passwordless Sign-Up

Where technically appropriate, the preferred sign-up experience shall
be:

``` text
Create your ART account

[ Create account with a passkey ]

or

[ Continue with Google ]
[ Continue with Microsoft ]
[ Continue with Amazon ]
[ Continue with GitHub ]

Already have an account? Sign in
```

Users should not be required to create an ART password.

### Passkey Registration

The passkey registration process shall:

- Clearly explain what a passkey is.
- Clearly explain what will happen when the user creates one.
- Invoke the browser/platform's standard WebAuthn interface.
- Allow the user to cancel.
- Handle unsupported devices gracefully.
- Handle authentication cancellation gracefully.
- Provide accessible success and error messages.
- Allow the user to name the newly created passkey.
- Allow registration of additional passkeys later.

### Existing Account Detection

ART shall distinguish between:

- New users
- Existing ART users
- Existing users authenticating through another provider
- Users registering an additional passkey
- Users linking an additional authentication provider
- Users requiring account recovery
- Suspended or disabled accounts

ART shall not create duplicate accounts merely because the user selects
a different authentication method.

### Account Linking

Where technically and securely appropriate, ART shall allow users to
associate multiple authentication methods with one ART account.

For example:

``` text
ART Account
    |
    +-- Passkey: Windows Laptop
    +-- Passkey: iPhone
    +-- Passkey: Security Key
    +-- Google
    +-- Microsoft
```

Account linking shall require appropriate authentication of the
identities being linked.

ART shall prevent an attacker from linking an authentication identity to
another user's account.

### Email-Based Account Identity

If an email address is obtained from an identity provider:

- It shall be treated as personal information.
- It shall not be displayed publicly without appropriate authorization.
- It shall not automatically become the user's display name.
- It shall not be used as the sole internal identity identifier.
- It shall only be used for account-management purposes where
  appropriate.

### Login Workflow

ART shall provide an accessible login workflow.

The preferred experience shall allow users to:

- Sign in with a passkey.
- Use another registered passkey.
- Authenticate through Google.
- Authenticate through Microsoft.
- Authenticate through Amazon.
- Authenticate through GitHub.
- Use an approved recovery mechanism.
- Cancel authentication.
- Continue using ART without logging in.

### Passkey-First Login

The login interface should prioritize passwordless authentication.

For example:

``` text
Sign in to ART

[ Sign in with a passkey ]

Other ways to sign in:

[ Google ]
[ Microsoft ]
[ Amazon ]
[ GitHub ]

[ Continue without signing in ]
```

The exact presentation shall be evaluated through accessibility and
usability testing.

### Continue Without Logging In

ART shall provide an obvious, accessible way to continue using ART
without logging in.

For example:

> **Continue without logging in**

This option shall not be hidden or presented as an error condition.

Selecting this option shall return the user to the normal local ART
experience.

### Authentication State

ART shall clearly communicate whether the user is:

- Not logged in
- Authentication in progress
- Logged in
- Session expired
- Authentication unavailable

Authentication state shall be exposed programmatically to assistive
technologies where it is presented in the user interface.

### Local Data and Authentication

Logging in shall not unnecessarily destroy, overwrite, or reset local
ART data.

If a user has created local projects before logging in:

- Those projects shall remain available.
- Logging in shall not automatically upload them.
- ART shall clearly communicate whether local data remains local.
- Synchronization shall require appropriate user action or clearly
  documented behavior.

### Local-to-Server Transition

When a user decides to use server-dependent functionality, ART shall
provide an understandable workflow for determining what local
information will be shared.

For example:

> You are about to add this project to a shared workspace. The project
> data will be synchronized with the configured ART server.

The user shall have an opportunity to understand and confirm the action
where appropriate.

### Logout

ART shall provide an accessible logout command.

Logout shall:

- Invalidate the appropriate authenticated session.
- Remove or invalidate locally stored session credentials as
  appropriate.
- Return the user to an unauthenticated state.
- Preserve local ART data unless the user explicitly chooses otherwise.
- Clearly communicate the resulting authentication state.

### Session Management

Authenticated sessions shall be securely managed.

ART shall support appropriate:

- Session expiration
- Session renewal
- Logout
- Session invalidation
- Token expiration
- Token refresh where applicable
- Revocation where supported
- Handling of expired sessions
- Handling of revoked credentials

### Token Security

OAuth access tokens, refresh tokens, ID tokens, session tokens, and
other authentication credentials shall be handled securely.

Tokens shall:

- Never be displayed to users.
- Never be written to reports.
- Never be included in exports.
- Never be exposed in URLs.
- Never be included in ordinary application logs.
- Never be committed to source control.
- Never be embedded in client-side source code when they are intended to
  remain confidential.
- Be stored using the safest storage mechanism appropriate to the
  architecture.

### Passkey Security

ART shall not receive or store users' private passkey keys.

ART shall store only the appropriate public credential information
required by WebAuthn.

The implementation shall protect:

- Credential IDs
- Public keys
- Sign counters
- User identifiers
- Credential metadata
- Authenticator information

The implementation shall follow the applicable WebAuthn security
requirements.

### WebAuthn Relying Party Configuration

ART shall securely configure its WebAuthn Relying Party identity.

The implementation shall correctly configure:

- RP ID
- Origin
- Challenge generation
- Challenge expiration
- User verification requirements
- Authenticator selection
- Attestation requirements where appropriate
- Credential registration
- Credential authentication

The implementation shall not accept credentials from unauthorized
origins.

### User Verification

Where appropriate, ART should require user verification for passkey
authentication.

The implementation shall account for the distinction between:

- User presence
- User verification
- Authenticator type
- Platform authenticators
- Roaming authenticators

Security requirements shall be appropriate to the sensitivity of the
requested operation.

### Step-Up Authentication

ART should support stronger authentication for sensitive operations.

Examples may include:

- Changing account authentication methods
- Adding a new passkey
- Removing the last remaining passkey
- Linking an external authentication provider
- Changing account recovery settings
- Changing organization ownership
- Performing sensitive organization administration
- Deleting an account

Step-up authentication should use an existing strong authentication
mechanism such as a passkey where practical.

### Authenticator Apps

ART shall support authenticator applications as an **optional additional
authentication/recovery mechanism**, rather than requiring passwords.

Where TOTP is implemented:

- Users shall be able to register a compatible authenticator
  application.
- The setup process shall provide a QR code.
- The setup process shall also provide an accessible manual-entry
  alternative.
- Users shall be able to enter a time-based verification code.
- TOTP secrets shall be stored securely.
- TOTP secrets shall never be exposed after enrollment.
- Users shall be able to remove an authenticator.
- Users shall be able to replace a lost authenticator using an
  appropriate recovery process.

ART shall not require users to use Microsoft Authenticator, Google
Authenticator, or any specific TOTP application.

### Authenticator-App Accessibility

Authenticator-app enrollment shall be accessible to users who:

- Cannot scan QR codes.
- Use screen readers.
- Use magnification.
- Use braille displays.
- Cannot use a smartphone camera.
- Use a desktop-only workflow.

The manual setup process shall provide equivalent information to the
QR-code workflow.

### Recovery Codes

ART shall provide secure recovery codes where appropriate.

Recovery codes shall:

- Be generated securely.
- Be displayed only when appropriate.
- Be downloadable or printable through an accessible mechanism.
- Never be included in application logs.
- Be single-use.
- Be revocable.
- Be replaceable.
- Clearly explain their importance.

Users should be encouraged to store recovery codes securely.

### Account Recovery

ART shall provide an accessible passwordless account-recovery process.

Recovery shall consider:

- Lost passkey
- Lost device
- Lost security key
- Lost authenticator application
- Changed device
- Lost access to an external identity provider
- Account compromise
- Organization administrators
- Enterprise identity providers
- Self-hosted deployments

Recovery shall not provide a mechanism for bypassing authentication.

### Recovery Security

Account recovery shall be treated as a high-security function.

ART shall avoid weak recovery mechanisms such as:

- Security questions
- Easily guessed personal information
- Unverified email-only recovery where stronger verification is required

Recovery mechanisms shall be designed to avoid becoming the weakest link
in an otherwise passwordless authentication system.

### Multi-Factor Authentication

Because passkeys can provide strong user verification through
authenticators, ART shall not require a traditional password-plus-MFA
architecture.

Instead, ART shall support strong authentication using combinations
appropriate to the deployment and security requirements, including:

- Passkeys
- Security keys
- Platform authenticators
- TOTP authenticator applications
- External identity-provider MFA
- Enterprise MFA

FIDO describes passkeys as passwordless credentials that can themselves
provide strong authentication using a device-held credential plus local
verification such as a PIN or biometric.

### Enterprise Authentication

The architecture should support future enterprise authentication
requirements.

Potential capabilities include:

- Microsoft Entra ID
- Google Workspace identity
- SAML
- OpenID Connect
- Enterprise single sign-on
- Enterprise-managed passkeys
- Enterprise security keys

Enterprise authentication shall be implemented as an extension of the
core identity architecture rather than requiring a complete redesign.

### Account Profile

Authenticated users shall have an accessible account/profile interface.

The interface should allow users to view and, where appropriate, modify:

- Display name
- Preferred name
- Email address where supported
- Profile information
- Registered passkeys
- Authentication providers
- Authenticator applications
- Recovery codes
- Account security settings
- Notification preferences
- Collaboration preferences
- Accessibility preferences
- Active sessions

### Account Security Dashboard

ART should provide a dedicated security section within account settings.

This section should provide access to:

- Passkey management
- Authenticator management
- Authentication-provider management
- Recovery-code management
- Active-session management
- Security-event history where appropriate

### Account Deletion

Users shall have an accessible mechanism for requesting or initiating
account deletion where appropriate.

The process shall clearly explain:

- What will be deleted
- What will remain
- What happens to shared projects
- What happens to comments
- What happens to task assignments
- What happens to organization membership
- What happens to audit history
- What happens to backups

### Account Suspension and Deactivation

Authorized administrators shall eventually be able to suspend or
deactivate accounts when appropriate.

A suspended user shall not be able to authenticate into server-dependent
functionality until the account is restored.

### Organization Membership

Authenticated users shall be capable of belonging to one or more
organizations when organizational collaboration is enabled.

Membership shall be separate from authentication.

``` text
ART Identity
    |
User Account
    |
Organization Membership
    |
Project / Workspace Permissions
```

### Permissions

Authentication shall integrate with ART's authorization model.

Authentication shall not automatically grant access to:

- Organizations
- Projects
- Workspaces
- Reports
- Progress Logs
- Tasks
- Organization Statistics
- Integrations

Permissions shall be evaluated separately.

### Collaboration Access

A user shall only gain access to server-dependent collaborative
functionality after successfully authenticating and receiving
appropriate authorization.

Examples include:

- Shared Project Workspaces
- Shared Progress Logs
- Server-based Tasks
- Organization Statistics
- Centralized Notifications
- @mention notifications
- Organization integrations
- Server synchronization

### Local Features Remain Available

The following shall remain usable without logging in unless a specific
future feature explicitly requires server functionality:

- Accessibility testing
- Report creation
- Report editing
- Report templates
- WCAG Lookup Tool
- Accessibility Standards lookup
- Usability Reports
- Executive Summaries
- Local Audit Logs
- Local Progress Logs
- Personal Tasks
- Personal To-Do Lists
- Local dashboards
- Local Organization Statistics where applicable
- Import
- Export
- Undo/Redo
- Keyboard shortcuts
- Custom working views

### Server-Dependent Feature Indicators

Features requiring authentication shall be clearly identified.

For example:

> **Shared Workspace — Login required**

or:

> **Sign in to use collaboration features**

The application shall not unexpectedly redirect a user to a login page
simply because they selected a local feature.

### Authentication Prompt Behavior

When a user attempts to access a server-dependent feature while logged
out, ART shall provide an accessible explanation.

The dialog should communicate:

- Which feature requires login.
- Why login is required.
- That core ART functionality remains available without login.
- An option to log in.
- An option to cancel and continue using local ART.

### Authentication Error Handling

Authentication errors shall be:

- Accessible
- Understandable
- Concise
- Actionable

Errors shall not expose sensitive information.

ART should avoid displaying account-enumeration information such as
whether a particular email address exists.

### Network Failure

ART shall handle authentication-service outages gracefully.

If the authentication provider or ART authentication service is
unavailable:

- ART shall clearly communicate the problem.
- Local ART functionality shall remain available.
- Existing local projects shall remain accessible.
- ART shall not corrupt local data.
- ART shall not repeatedly attempt authentication without user action.
- The user shall be able to retry authentication.

### Offline Operation

ART shall remain functional offline for local functionality.

If an authenticated user loses network connectivity:

- Local functionality shall remain available.
- ART shall clearly communicate that server-dependent functionality is
  temporarily unavailable.
- Unsynchronized changes shall not be silently discarded.
- Changes shall be synchronized when connectivity is restored, subject
  to the collaboration and merge architecture.

### Authentication and Merge Conflicts

Authentication shall integrate with the Merge Conflict system.

Where authenticated identity information is available, changes should be
associated with the appropriate ART user identity.

Where file-based collaboration occurs without authentication, ART shall
identify the change source using available local/project metadata
without requiring a fabricated authenticated identity.

### Authentication and History

The History Framework shall remain functional regardless of
authentication state.

Users shall be able to undo and redo local changes without logging in.

Server synchronization and collaboration actions shall not allow users
to bypass authorization through Undo/Redo.

### Accessibility Requirements

The entire authentication experience shall conform to ART's
accessibility-first design principles.

Testing shall include:

- JAWS
- NVDA
- Narrator
- VoiceOver
- ChromeVox
- TalkBack
- Refreshable braille displays
- Keyboard-only interaction
- Voice control
- Magnification
- High-contrast configurations
- Zoom
- Other relevant assistive technologies

### Keyboard Accessibility

All authentication controls shall be fully keyboard accessible.

Users shall be able to:

- Navigate the authentication workflow.
- Start authentication.
- Cancel authentication.
- Register a passkey.
- Authenticate with a passkey.
- Handle errors.
- Manage passkeys.
- Manage authenticator applications.
- Log out.
- Access account settings.
- Manage recovery options.

### Focus Management

Authentication dialogs and pages shall provide predictable focus
management.

When an authentication dialog opens:

- Focus shall move appropriately.
- The dialog shall have an accessible name.
- Focus shall remain within the dialog where appropriate.
- Closing the dialog shall return focus appropriately.
- Error messages shall be announced appropriately.
- Newly available controls shall be exposed correctly.

### Screen Reader Support

Authentication state changes shall be communicated programmatically.

Screen readers should be able to determine:

- Whether the user is logged in.
- Whether authentication is in progress.
- Whether authentication succeeded.
- Whether authentication failed.
- Whether the session expired.
- Whether login is required for a selected feature.
- Which authentication method is currently being used.
- Which passkeys are registered.

### Accessible Passkey Experience

ART shall test passkey registration and authentication with multiple
assistive technologies.

Testing shall include:

- Passkey registration
- Passkey authentication
- Passkey deletion
- Passkey naming
- Passkey replacement
- Cross-device authentication
- Hardware security-key authentication
- Recovery

ART shall not assume that biometric authentication is available to every
user.

Where a passkey provider presents multiple authentication methods, users
shall be able to use an accessible alternative supported by their
device.

### Accessible OAuth Provider Experience

If ART redirects users to an external identity provider, each selected
provider shall be evaluated for accessibility.

Testing shall consider:

- Google
- Microsoft
- Amazon
- GitHub

Each provider's authentication experience shall be tested with:

- Screen readers
- Keyboard navigation
- Magnification
- Braille
- Mobile assistive technologies

### Privacy

The account system shall follow privacy-by-design principles.

ART shall collect only personal information necessary for account and
collaboration functionality.

Potential account information may include:

- Internal ART user identifier
- Display name
- Email address
- Authentication-provider identifier
- Organization membership
- Account preferences
- Notification preferences

Unnecessary personal information shall not be collected.

### Biometric Privacy

ART shall not collect or store users' biometric data as part of passkey
authentication.

Where a biometric authenticator is used, the biometric verification
shall occur through the user's device or authenticator.

The ART server shall receive cryptographic authentication results rather
than the user's biometric information.

FIDO specifically states that biometric information used with passkeys
remains on the user's device.

### Authentication Logs

Security-related authentication events may be logged where appropriate.

Potential events include:

- Successful passkey authentication
- Failed authentication
- Logout
- Passkey registration
- Passkey removal
- Authenticator registration
- Authentication-provider linking
- Account recovery
- Account suspension

Logs shall not contain passwords, private keys, authentication secrets,
or unnecessary sensitive information.

### Rate Limiting and Abuse Prevention

Authentication endpoints shall implement appropriate protections
against:

- Brute-force attacks
- Automated account creation
- Token abuse
- Recovery abuse
- Denial-of-service attempts
- Credential-registration abuse

Rate limits shall not unnecessarily prevent legitimate users with
disabilities from completing authentication.

### Bot Protection

If bot protection is introduced during account creation or
authentication, it shall be accessible.

ART shall avoid inaccessible CAPTCHA mechanisms.

If CAPTCHA or equivalent protection is necessary, an accessible
alternative shall be provided.

### Secure Redirect Handling

Authentication redirects shall be validated.

ART shall prevent attackers from using authentication workflows to
redirect users to malicious destinations.

### Secrets Management

Authentication secrets used by ART's server infrastructure shall be
managed securely.

Secrets shall:

- Never be committed to source control.
- Never be included in client-side bundles.
- Never be stored in plain-text configuration files when a secure
  secret-management mechanism is available.
- Be rotated appropriately.
- Be revoked when compromised.

### Environment Separation

Authentication configuration shall distinguish between:

- Development
- Testing
- Staging
- Production

Development credentials shall never be used in production.

Production credentials shall never be included in development
repositories or test fixtures.

### Testing Environment

A dedicated test authentication environment should be established before
production deployment.

Testing shall not use real user credentials unnecessarily.

Automated tests shall use test accounts or appropriate mocks.

### Automated Testing

Automated tests shall cover:

- Passkey registration
- Passkey authentication
- Passkey removal
- Multiple passkeys
- Passkey recovery
- Google authentication
- Microsoft authentication
- Amazon authentication
- GitHub authentication
- Logout
- Session expiration
- Session renewal
- Authentication failure
- Permission checks
- Unauthorized access
- Token handling
- Authentication-provider callbacks
- Account linking
- Recovery mechanisms

### Security Testing

Authentication shall undergo security testing for:

- Authentication bypass
- Session fixation
- Session hijacking
- CSRF
- XSS
- Open redirects
- Token leakage
- Account enumeration
- Credential-registration abuse
- Privilege escalation
- Unauthorized organization access
- Unauthorized project access
- Passkey registration abuse
- Account recovery abuse
- Authentication-provider linking attacks

### Accessibility Testing

Authentication shall undergo manual accessibility testing with multiple
assistive technologies.

Testing shall include:

- Account creation
- Passkey registration
- Passkey login
- OAuth login
- Logout
- Authentication errors
- Recovery
- Authenticator-app enrollment if implemented
- Account settings
- Passkey management
- Session management
- Account deletion
- Organization membership

Each supported authentication provider shall be tested independently.

### Documentation

The user guide shall explain:

- ART can be used without logging in.
- Why a user may choose to log in.
- Which features require authentication.
- What passwordless authentication means.
- How to create an account.
- How to register a passkey.
- How to sign in with a passkey.
- How to register multiple passkeys.
- How to use a security key.
- How to use an authenticator application if enabled.
- How to recover access.
- How to log out.
- How to manage account settings.
- How authentication affects collaboration.
- How local data is handled when logging in.
- How to protect account credentials.
- How to report account-security concerns.
- Which authentication providers are currently supported.

### User Guide — Local vs. Authenticated ART

The documentation shall clearly distinguish between:

#### Without an Account

Users can use ART's fundamental local functionality without creating an
account.

#### With an Account

Users can access server-dependent capabilities such as:

- Collaboration
- Shared Workspaces
- Shared Progress Logs
- Server synchronization
- Organization membership
- Centralized notifications
- Other future server-based services

### User Guide — Passwordless Authentication

The documentation shall clearly explain that ART does not require users
to create an ART password.

It shall explain:

- What passkeys are.
- How passkeys work at a high level.
- How to create one.
- How to use one.
- How to register multiple passkeys.
- How to recover access.
- How security keys work.
- How authenticator apps may be used where supported.

### Security Documentation

Developer documentation shall describe:

- Authentication architecture
- WebAuthn implementation
- FIDO2 integration
- Passkey registration
- Passkey authentication
- Credential storage
- OAuth/OpenID Connect implementation
- Provider configuration
- Token handling
- Session management
- Identity mapping
- Authorization boundaries
- Security controls
- Secrets management
- Account recovery
- Testing requirements

### Authentication Provider Documentation

ART shall document each selected provider and clearly identify:

- Provider name
- Authentication protocols
- Required scopes
- Data received
- Data transmitted
- Account-management responsibilities
- Provider security responsibilities
- ART security responsibilities
- Provider limitations
- Cost considerations
- Migration considerations

### Provider Independence

ART shall avoid unnecessary vendor lock-in.

The architecture should allow authentication providers to be replaced or
supplemented without requiring the entire application to be redesigned.

Passkeys shall remain an independent authentication option rather than
being tied exclusively to Google, Microsoft, Amazon, GitHub, or another
external provider.

### Self-Hosted Authentication

Self-hosted ART deployments shall be able to use authentication
appropriate to the organization's environment.

Where technically feasible, self-hosted deployments should support:

- WebAuthn/passkeys
- Local authentication services
- OAuth/OpenID Connect
- Enterprise identity providers
- Organization-managed identity systems
- Security keys
- Enterprise-managed authenticators

Self-hosted administrators shall be responsible for configuring and
securing their selected authentication infrastructure.

### SaaS Authentication

Hosted ART shall provide secure authentication appropriate for a
multi-tenant environment.

The hosted service shall ensure:

- User isolation
- Organization isolation
- Secure sessions
- Secure credentials
- Secure API access
- Secure account recovery
- Appropriate logging
- Appropriate monitoring

### Data Migration

If the authentication architecture changes in the future, ART shall
