Where appropriate, provide integration commands through ART's existing
context-menu architecture.

Examples:

- Send to Jira.
- Create GitHub Issue.
- Create Azure Work Item.
- Open linked issue.
- Synchronize.
- Disconnect integration.

Avoid unnecessary permanent buttons that clutter the interface.

### Integration Menu Commands

When the Tasks modal, Report Viewer, Report Builder, or applicable
interface is open, provide relevant integration commands through menu
commands.

### Customizable Keyboard Shortcuts

Integration commands shall be compatible with ART's customizable
keyboard shortcut system.

Users may assign shortcuts to supported commands such as:

- Create external issue.
- Open linked issue.
- Synchronize.
- Refresh.
- Import.
- Export.

### Accessibility of Integrations

Every integration workflow shall be tested for:

- Keyboard accessibility.
- Screen-reader accessibility.
- Focus management.
- Accessible status messages.
- Accessible errors.
- Accessible authentication.
- Accessible permission selection.
- Accessible synchronization feedback.

### Live Status Messages

Provide accessible status messages for integration events.

Examples:

- "Jira connected."
- "GitHub repository connected."
- "Finding exported to Jira."
- "GitHub Issue created."
- "Synchronization complete."
- "Synchronization failed."
- "Three external changes detected."
- "Integration authorization expired."

### Integration Notifications

Where appropriate, users may receive notifications for:

- Synchronization failures.
- Authorization expiration.
- External changes.
- Conflicts.
- Completed synchronization.

### Privacy

Integrations shall comply with Epic 58.

Do not transmit ART data to external services unless required by the
selected integration and authorized by the user.

### Data Minimization

Transmit only the data necessary to perform the requested operation.

### Integration Transparency

Before enabling an integration, clearly explain:

- What information ART will access.
- What information ART may send.
- What permissions are requested.
- Where information will be stored.
- Whether synchronization is automatic.
- How the integration can be disconnected.

### Organization Controls

Organizations shall be able to control integrations where organization
administration is implemented.

Possible controls include:

- Enable/disable integrations.
- Restrict integrations.
- Require administrator approval.
- Define approved providers.
- Manage organization-level credentials where appropriate.

### Role-Based Integration Permissions

Integration access shall respect ART's authorization model established
in Epic 50.

For example:

- Organization administrators may configure integrations.
- Project members may use approved integrations.
- Users without appropriate permissions may not modify organization
  integrations.

Exact permissions shall follow the authorization policy service.

### Integration Logs

Where appropriate, maintain accessible integration activity information.

Include:

- User.
- Date/time.
- Integration.
- Action.
- Result.

Do not expose credentials or sensitive tokens.

### Offline Behavior

When ART is offline:

- External integrations may become unavailable.
- Local ART functionality shall continue.
- Pending integration actions should be preserved where safe.
- Synchronization should resume when connectivity returns.

### Queued Integration Actions

Where technically safe, allow integration operations to be queued while
offline.

Clearly identify:

- Pending.
- Successful.
- Failed.
- Retrying.

Do not silently lose queued actions.

### Duplicate Prevention

Prevent duplicate external records where practical.

Use stable external identifiers.

### External Record Identity

Maintain references such as:

``` text
Provider
Organization
Repository/Project
External Record ID
ART Record ID
```

### Integration Removal

If an integration is disconnected:

- Preserve ART data.
- Preserve historical references where appropriate.
- Clearly identify records that are no longer synchronized.
- Do not delete external records unless explicitly requested and
  authorized.

### API Rate Limits

Respect external API rate limits.

Provide appropriate handling for:

- Rate limiting.
- Retry-after responses.
- Temporary failures.
- Authentication expiration.

### API Version Changes

Monitor external API changes that could affect ART integrations.

Document unsupported or deprecated APIs.

### Integration Health

Provide an accessible indication of integration health.

Possible states:

- Connected.
- Not Connected.
- Authorization Required.
- Synchronizing.
- Error.
- Temporarily Unavailable.

### Developer Integration Framework

Create reusable integration interfaces for:

- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Data mapping.
- CRUD operations.
- Synchronization.
- Conflict handling.
- Error handling.
- Logging.
- Notifications.

### Integration SDK/Adapter Pattern

Where appropriate, implement integrations as adapters around a common
interface.

This should allow future integrations to be added without modifying
unrelated ART functionality.

### Integration Testing

Create automated tests for:

- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Connection.
- Disconnection.
- Data export.
- Data import.
- Synchronization.
- Conflict handling.
- Error handling.
- Rate limits.
- Token expiration.
- Duplicate prevention.
- Permission failures.

### Mock External Services

Use mocks/test environments where possible.

Do not make automated tests dependent on production external services.

### End-to-End Integration Testing

Perform end-to-end testing with supported external services.

Test:

1.  Connect integration.
2.  Authorize ART.
3.  Create ART data.
4.  Export/synchronize.
5.  Verify external record.
6.  Modify external record.
7.  Synchronize back to ART.
8.  Verify changes.
9.  Create a conflict.
10. Resolve the conflict.
11. Verify final state.

### Accessibility Integration Testing

Test integrations with:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox where applicable.
- Braille displays.
- Keyboard-only operation.
- Magnification/low-vision configurations.

### Security Testing

Verify:

- OAuth security.
- Token storage.
- API authorization.
- Permission enforcement.
- Data isolation.
- Organization isolation.
- Secure transmission.
- Token expiration.
- Revocation.
- Error handling.

### Privacy Testing

Verify:

- Only authorized data is transmitted.
- Disconnected integrations stop transmitting data.
- Logs do not expose sensitive information.
- External identifiers are handled appropriately.
- User consent is respected.

### Performance

Integration functionality shall not significantly degrade ART
performance.

Avoid unnecessary:

- Background polling.
- API calls.
- Synchronization operations.
- Network requests.

### Caching

Where caching is used:

- Clearly define cache lifetime.
- Avoid caching sensitive information unnecessarily.
- Invalidate stale data appropriately.

### Documentation

Document each supported integration.

For each integration, document:

- Supported functionality.
- Required permissions.
- Authentication method.
- Setup process.
- Data exchanged.
- Synchronization behavior.
- Conflict handling.
- Limitations.
- Disconnect procedure.
- Troubleshooting.

### User Documentation

Provide accessible Help documentation explaining:

- How to connect integrations.
- How to disconnect integrations.
- How synchronization works.
- How conflicts are handled.
- What data is shared.
- How to revoke access.
- How to troubleshoot failures.

### Integration Roadmap

Prioritize integrations based on:

1.  User demand.
2.  Accessibility.
3.  Security.
4.  API availability.
5.  Privacy.
6.  Technical feasibility.
7.  Organizational value.
8.  Maintenance burden.

### Definition of Done

Epic 62 shall be considered complete when:

- ART has a modular integration framework.
- Integrations are optional.
- ART remains fully functional without integrations.
- Integration management is available in Settings.
- Integration workflows are accessible.
- Secure authentication is implemented.
- OAuth is used where appropriate.
- Credentials and tokens are never stored in plain text.
- Minimum required permissions are requested.
- Users can connect and disconnect integrations.
- Integration status is accessible.
- Integration failures do not corrupt ART data.
- Integration conflicts have an accessible resolution process.
- Integration actions can be represented in ART's History Framework
  where appropriate.
- Jira integration is implemented to the supported scope.
- GitHub Issues integration is implemented to the supported scope.
- Microsoft Azure/Azure DevOps integration is implemented to the
  supported scope.
- Google Workspace integration is implemented to the supported scope.
- Microsoft 365 integration is evaluated and implemented to the
  supported scope.
- Cloud-storage integration supports the existing file-based
  collaboration model.
- Google Drive workflows are supported where implemented.
- OneDrive workflows are supported where implemented.
- Dropbox workflows are supported where implemented.
- External task/finding synchronization is supported where appropriate.
- @mentions are preserved where external platforms support equivalent
  functionality.
- ART comments remain accessible.
- External links are accessible.
- Integration commands are available through appropriate context menus
  and command menus.
- Integration commands can use customizable keyboard shortcuts where
  appropriate.
- Accessible live status messages communicate integration events.
- Privacy requirements from Epic 58 are preserved.
- Authorization requirements from Epic 50 are enforced.
- Offline ART functionality remains available.
- Safe queued integration operations are supported where practical.
- Duplicate external records are prevented where practical.
- External record identifiers are preserved.
- API rate limits are handled appropriately.
- External API changes can be accommodated through the integration
  architecture.
- Automated integration tests exist.
- Mock/test environments are used where practical.
- End-to-end integration testing is completed.
- Accessibility testing is completed.
- Security testing is completed.
- Privacy testing is completed.
- Performance testing is completed.
- Integration documentation is complete.

The resulting integration architecture shall make ART interoperable with
the tools organizations already use while keeping ART's core
functionality independent, accessible, secure, private, portable, and
user-controlled.

## Epic 63 — Enterprise Administration & Management

### Epic Overview

Implement comprehensive organization-level administration and management
capabilities for ART.

This epic builds upon the authenticated-user, organization-membership,
role, and authorization infrastructure established in Epic 50 and the
collaboration, synchronization, file-sharing, and identity capabilities
established in subsequent epics.

The purpose of this epic is to provide organizations with the
administrative controls necessary to manage ART safely and effectively
at scale while preserving ART's core principles of accessibility,
privacy, security, user choice, local-first functionality, and data
ownership.

Enterprise administration shall be available when ART is being used in
an organizational environment.

ART shall remain fully usable for individuals and small teams without
requiring enterprise administration.

### General Requirements

Implement only functionality necessary to provide secure and accessible
organization administration.

Preserve all existing ART functionality.

Do not require organizational administration for:

- Creating local reports.
- Editing reports.
- Importing reports.
- Exporting reports.
- Using the WCAG Lookup Tool.
- Using the dashboard.
- Managing personal tasks.
- Using personal settings.
- Using the desktop application.
- Using the web application.
- Using file-based collaboration where no organization account is
  required.

All administrative functionality shall respect the authorization policy
service established in Epic 50.

### Organization Administration

Provide an accessible Organization Administration area for authorized
users.

The Organization Administration area shall allow authorized
administrators to manage:

- Organization profile.
- Organization members.
- Roles.
- Permissions.
- Organization settings.
- Organization integrations.
- Shared resources.
- Organization-level collaboration settings.
- Organization-level security settings.
- Organization-level privacy settings.
- Organization-level data-management settings.

Only users with appropriate permissions shall be able to access
organization administration.

### Organization Profile

Allow authorized administrators to configure organizational information.

Possible fields include:

- Organization name.
- Organization display name.
- Organization description.
- Organization logo.
- Organization website.
- Organization contact information.
- Organization identifier.
- Organization-specific preferences.

Organization profile information shall be editable after creation.

### Organization Ownership

Define organization ownership and administrative responsibility.

An organization shall have one or more authorized administrators.

The system shall prevent an organization from becoming permanently
inaccessible because the only administrator account is removed,
disabled, or unavailable.

Provide an appropriate administrator-recovery or ownership-transfer
mechanism.

### Organization Members

Provide an accessible member-management interface.

Authorized administrators shall be able to:

- View organization members.
- Add members.
- Invite members.
- Remove members.
- Disable members where supported.
- Restore disabled members where supported.
- Change member roles.
- View member status.
- View member activity where authorized.
- Manage organization membership.

### Member Information

Display appropriate member information, such as:

- Name.
- Display name.
- Email address.
- Organization role.
- Account status.
- Invitation status.
- Last activity where appropriate and permitted.
- Connected devices where appropriate and permitted.

Do not expose sensitive information unnecessarily.

### Organization Invitations

Allow authorized users to invite people to join an organization.

Invitations shall:

- Be securely generated.
- Expire after a configurable period.
- Be usable only by the intended recipient where appropriate.
- Not expose passwords or authentication secrets.
- Provide accessible invitation workflows.

### Invitation Status

Administrators shall be able to identify:

- Pending invitations.
- Accepted invitations.
- Expired invitations.
- Revoked invitations.

Administrators shall be able to revoke pending invitations.

### Member Removal

When a member is removed:

- Their organization access shall be revoked.
- Their authorization shall immediately reflect the change where
  server-based functionality is available.
- Existing locally stored ART data shall not be unexpectedly deleted.
- Shared organization resources shall remain owned by the organization.
- Appropriate historical attribution shall be preserved.

### Disabled Accounts

Where account disabling is supported, administrators shall be able to
disable organizational access without necessarily deleting the user's
account.

Disabled users shall not be able to access organization resources.

### Roles

Implement organization roles using the authorization model established
in Epic 50.

Support, at minimum, roles equivalent to:

- Organization Owner.
- Organization Administrator.
- Project Manager or Coordinator.
- Contributor.
- Auditor/Reviewer.
- Read-Only Member.

The exact names may be configurable or refined based on ART's existing
terminology.

### Custom Roles

Where technically practical, allow organizations to create custom roles.

Custom roles shall be composed of specific permissions rather than
arbitrary access.

### Role Assignment

Authorized administrators shall be able to:

- Assign roles.
- Change roles.
- Remove roles.
- Review role assignments.

Role changes shall be recorded in the appropriate audit/history
mechanisms.

### Permission Management

Implement granular organization permissions.

Potential permissions include:

- View organization.
- Manage organization settings.
- Manage members.
- Invite members.
- Remove members.
- Manage roles.
- Manage projects.
- Create projects.
- Delete projects.
- Manage reports.
- View reports.
- Edit reports.
- Export reports.
- Manage shared tasks.
- Manage shared progress logs.
- View organization metrics.
- Manage integrations.
- Manage security settings.
- Manage privacy settings.
- Manage organization storage.

### Principle of Least Privilege

Users shall receive only the permissions necessary for their assigned
role.

Do not grant administrative permissions merely because a user belongs to
an organization.

### Permission Inheritance

Define predictable permission inheritance.

For example:

``` text
Organization
    |
    +-- Project
          |
          +-- Report
          +-- Tasks
          +-- Progress Log
```

Organization-level permissions may establish defaults, while
project-level permissions may provide additional restrictions or
delegated access.

Users shall never gain access to restricted content merely because they
can access a parent resource.

### Explicit Denials

Where the authorization model supports explicit deny rules, ensure that
denied access takes precedence over inherited access.

### Project Administration

Authorized users shall be able to manage organization projects.

Support:

- Create project.
- Rename project.
- Archive project.
- Restore project.
- Delete project where authorized.
- Manage project members.
- Manage project roles.
- Configure project permissions.
- Manage project resources.

### Project Ownership

Projects shall have clear ownership and administrative responsibility.

Project ownership shall remain meaningful even when individual members
leave the organization.

### Shared Resources

Allow organizations to manage shared:

- Reports.
- Tasks.
- To Do lists.
- Progress logs.
- Templates.
- Metrics.
- Documentation.
- Other ART resources supported by the application.

### Shared Tasks

Organization administrators shall be able to manage organization-level
shared tasks.

Respect the task functionality established in previous epics, including:

- Status.
- Priority.
- Due date/time.
- Reminders.
- Comments/notes/instructions.
- @mentions\.
- Assignment.
- Completion.
- History.

### Shared Progress Logs

Provide appropriate organization-level management of shared progress
logs.

Authorized users shall be able to:

- Create.
- View.
- Edit.
- Share.
- Archive.
- Export.
- Manage access.

### Organization Templates

Allow authorized administrators to manage organization templates.

Possible functionality includes:

- Create organization template.
- Edit template.
- Publish template.
- Archive template.
- Restrict template editing.
- Assign template access.

### Template Permissions

Organizations shall be able to determine whether members may:

- View templates.
- Use templates.
- Modify templates.
- Create templates.
- Delete templates.

### Organization Settings

Provide organization-level settings separate from individual user
settings.

Potential settings include:

- Default report preferences.
- Default task settings.
- Default project settings.
- Organization branding.
- Sharing defaults.
- Collaboration defaults.
- Integration settings.
- Security settings.
- Privacy settings.
- Notification settings.
- Data-retention settings where applicable.

### User Settings Versus Organization Settings

Clearly distinguish between:

- Personal settings.
- Project settings.
- Organization settings.

Organization administrators shall not automatically override personal
accessibility preferences.

### Accessibility Preferences

Users shall retain control over their personal accessibility preferences
unless an organizational policy is legitimately required.

Examples include:

- Text size.
- Zoom.
- Contrast.
- Visual settings.
- Screen-reader-related preferences.
- Keyboard shortcuts.
- Working views.
- Notifications.
- Sound settings.

### Organization-Wide Defaults

Where appropriate, organizations may define defaults without forcibly
overriding personal preferences.

For example:

- Default report type.
- Default project view.
- Default task sorting.
- Default notification settings.

### Security Administration

Provide organization-level security controls that build upon Epic 47 and
Epic 50.

Potential controls include:

- Authentication requirements.
- Session management.
- Account recovery.
- Device management.
- Integration restrictions.
- Security notifications.
- Organization access policies.

### Authentication Policies

Where server-based authentication is implemented, organizations may
require supported authentication methods.

Examples include:

- Passwordless authentication.
- Passkeys.
- OAuth identity providers.
- Multi-factor authentication where supported.

Do not weaken ART's passwordless security model merely to support
organizational requirements.

### Identity Provider Support

Where technically practical, support organizational identity providers
and enterprise authentication systems.

Potential future support includes:

- Microsoft Entra ID.
- Google Workspace identity.
- Other standards-compliant identity providers.

### Session Management

Authorized administrators shall be able to manage organizational
sessions where server-based functionality supports it.

Possible actions include:

- View active sessions.
- Revoke sessions.
- Revoke access following account compromise.
- Require reauthentication.

### Device Management

Where server-based functionality supports device identity, provide
appropriate organizational device-management capabilities.

Administrators may be able to:

- View authorized devices.
- Revoke a device.
- Require reauthentication.
- Remove an organization connection.

Do not expose unnecessary device information.

### Personal Device Identity

Respect the multi-device identity functionality established in Epic 50.

Organization administrators shall not gain unrestricted access to a
user's personal device information merely because the device is
associated with an organization account.

### Organization Integrations

Allow authorized administrators to manage organization-approved
integrations established in Epic 62.

Administrators shall be able to:

- Enable integrations.
- Disable integrations.
- Approve integrations.
- Restrict integrations.
- Review integration status.
- Configure organization-level integration settings.

### Integration Approval

Where appropriate, organizations may require administrator approval
before members connect external services.

### Integration Restrictions

Organizations may restrict specific providers where security or
compliance requirements dictate.

### Data Governance

Provide administrative controls for organizational data.

Potential controls include:

- Data retention.
- Data export.
- Data deletion.
- Data ownership.
- Data migration.
- Backup configuration where applicable.
- Storage configuration.

### Data Ownership

Clearly define organizational ownership of organization-created/shared
resources.

Removing a user from an organization shall not automatically transfer
ownership of personally owned resources unless explicitly configured.

### Resource Ownership

Define ownership for:

- Projects.
- Reports.
- Tasks.
- Progress logs.
- Templates.
- Metrics.
- Shared files.

### Organization Data Export

Authorized administrators shall be able to export organization data
where supported.

Exports shall preserve:

- Data integrity.
- Report structure.
- Metadata.
- Attribution.
- Relevant history.
- Collaboration information.

### Organization Data Deletion

Provide controlled organization-data deletion.

Deletion shall require appropriate authorization and confirmation.

Where deletion is destructive or irreversible, provide an accessible
confirmation dialog.

### Retention Policies

Where server-based functionality supports retention policies, allow
authorized administrators to define retention periods.

Clearly communicate the consequences of retention policies.

### Audit Logging

Provide organization-level administrative audit logging.

Log appropriate events such as:

- Member added.
- Member removed.
- Invitation created.
- Invitation revoked.
- Role changed.
- Permission changed.
- Organization setting changed.
- Integration connected.
- Integration disconnected.
- Project created.
- Project archived.
- Project deleted.
- Shared resource modified.
- Security setting changed.

### Audit Log Security

Audit logs shall:

- Be access controlled.
- Be protected from unauthorized modification.
- Avoid storing authentication secrets.
- Avoid storing passwords.
- Avoid exposing sensitive information unnecessarily.

### Audit Log Accessibility

The organization audit log shall be accessible using:

- Keyboard.
- Screen readers.
- Braille displays.
- Magnification.
- High-contrast settings.

Provide meaningful accessible names and table/list semantics.

### Administrative Notifications

Administrators may receive notifications for significant events.

Examples include:

- New member invitation accepted.
- Member removed.
- Administrator role changed.
- Integration authorization failure.
- Security event.
- Organization setting changed.
- Synchronization failure.

Notifications shall be configurable where appropriate.

### @Mentions

Preserve @mentions functionality throughout organization administration
and shared resources.

Users shall be able to mention authorized organization members where
@mentions are supported.

Mention functionality shall:

- Use accessible autocomplete behavior.
- Respect organization membership.
- Avoid exposing non-members.
- Preserve identity across file-based collaboration.
- Work within shared projects.
- Work within shared reports.
- Work within organization-shared resources.

### @Mention Permissions

Users shall not be able to @mention individuals who are not authorized
to access the associated resource unless the mention is intentionally
supported for external users.

### Organization Metrics Permissions

Access to organization metrics shall respect organization roles and
permissions.

Not every organization member should automatically receive access to
organization-wide metrics.

### Metrics Administration

Authorized administrators shall be able to configure:

- Metric visibility.
- Metric scope.
- Project inclusion.
- Organization inclusion.
- Reporting periods.
- Metric permissions.

### Shared Folder Administration

Where file-based organization collaboration is used, administrators
shall be able to define organization folder structures and permissions
where the external storage provider supports them.

ART shall respect permissions established by:

- Google Drive.
- OneDrive.
- Dropbox.
- Other supported storage systems.

ART shall never bypass external storage permissions.

### File-Based Organization Access

When a user opens an organization `.art` file:

- ART shall identify the organization where possible.
- ART shall verify the user's applicable identity information.
- ART shall apply available authorization information.
- ART shall respect file-level and folder-level permissions.
- ART shall preserve collaboration metadata.

### Offline Administration

Organization administration may be unavailable while ART is offline.

ART shall clearly communicate when an administrative operation requires
server connectivity.

Local functionality shall remain available.

### Cached Permissions

If permissions are cached locally:

- Cache them securely.
- Define appropriate expiration.
- Do not treat stale permissions as permanently authoritative.
- Require revalidation when necessary.

### Authorization Failures

If a user's organization permissions change while ART is offline, ART
shall handle the discrepancy safely when connectivity is restored.

Do not silently grant continued access to resources that are no longer
authorized.

### Organization Separation

Ensure strict separation between organizations.

A user belonging to multiple organizations shall not accidentally expose
data between them.

### Multiple Organizations

Support users who belong to more than one organization.

Users shall be able to:

- View organizations they belong to.
- Switch organization context.
- View organization-specific projects.
- View organization-specific tasks.
- View organization-specific resources.

### Organization Context

Clearly communicate the current organization context.

This is especially important when users belong to multiple
organizations.

### Organization Context Accessibility

Organization context shall be available programmatically to assistive
technologies.

Do not rely solely on visual indicators such as color or logos.

### Administrative Context Menus

Use ART's existing context-menu architecture for administrative actions
where appropriate.

Examples include:

- Change role.
- Remove member.
- Revoke invitation.
- Archive project.
- Manage permissions.
- Export organization data.

Avoid unnecessary interface clutter.

### Administrative Menu Bar

When the Organization Administration interface is open, provide relevant
administrative commands through the menu bar.

### Customizable Keyboard Shortcuts

Where appropriate, support customizable keyboard shortcuts for
administrative commands.

Potential commands include:

- Add member.
- Invite member.
- Change role.
- Open permissions.
- Export data.
- Open audit log.
- Search members.

### Confirmation Dialogs

Destructive administrative actions shall use accessible confirmation
dialogs.

Examples include:

- Remove member.
- Delete project.
- Delete organization resource.
- Revoke integration.
- Delete organization data.

Confirmation dialogs shall:

- Clearly identify the action.
- Explain consequences.
- Provide accessible focus management.
- Provide Cancel and confirmation controls.
- Support keyboard operation.
- Be announced correctly by screen readers.

### Search

Provide accessible administrative search where appropriate.

Users should be able to search:

- Members.
- Projects.
- Resources.
- Tasks.
- Audit events.
- Integrations.

### Filtering

Provide accessible filtering for large organizations.

Potential filters include:

- Role.
- Status.
- Project.
- Date.
- Activity.
- Resource type.

### Sorting

Administrative lists should support sorting by appropriate fields.

Examples:

- Name.
- Role.
- Status.
- Date added.
- Last activity.

Sorting controls shall be accessible to keyboard and screen-reader
users.

### Live Status Messages

Administrative operations shall provide accessible status messages.

Examples:

- "Member added."
- "Invitation sent."
- "Role updated."
- "Member removed."
- "Integration disabled."
- "Organization settings saved."

### Error Handling

Administrative errors shall:

- Be understandable.
- Identify the affected operation.
- Explain what the user can do next.
- Be announced accessibly.
- Not expose sensitive implementation details.

### Permission Errors

When access is denied, clearly communicate:

- That access is unavailable.
- The resource involved.
- Whether the user should contact an administrator.

Do not expose confidential information about restricted resources.

### Security Events

Security-sensitive administrative events shall be handled according to
Epic 47.

### Privacy

All organization administration shall comply with Epic 58.

Administrators shall receive only the information necessary to perform
their authorized duties.

### Privacy Boundaries

Organization administrators shall not automatically have access to:

- Personal reports.
- Personal tasks.
- Personal notes.
- Personal settings.
- Personal device information.

unless the user has shared them or an authorized organizational policy
explicitly permits access.

### Personal Versus Organization Resources

Clearly distinguish:

``` text
Personal
    |
    +-- Personal Reports
    +-- Personal Tasks
    +-- Personal Settings

Organization
    |
    +-- Shared Projects
    +-- Shared Reports
    +-- Shared Tasks
    +-- Shared Progress Logs
    +-- Organization Metrics
```

### Data Isolation

Ensure that personal data cannot accidentally enter organization
resources and that organization data cannot accidentally enter another
user's personal resources.

### Organization Branding

Allow organizations to optionally configure branding.

Possible branding includes:

- Organization logo.
- Organization name.
- Organization colors.
- Report branding.
- Export branding.

Branding shall not interfere with accessibility.

### Accessible Branding

Do not allow organization branding to produce inaccessible:

- Color combinations.
- Contrast.
- Text.
- Logos.
- Focus indicators.
- Interactive elements.

### Organization Defaults

Allow organizations to define reasonable defaults without preventing
users from accessing their personal accessibility settings.

### Administrative Dashboard

Provide an accessible organization administration dashboard.

Potential dashboard information includes:

- Member count.
- Active projects.
- Shared reports.
- Outstanding tasks.
- Organization metrics.
- Integration status.
- Security status.
- Recent administrative events.

### Dashboard Customization

Where appropriate, administrators may customize which administrative
widgets are displayed.

### Administrative Dashboard Accessibility

The dashboard shall support:

- Keyboard navigation.
- Screen readers.
- Braille displays.
- Magnification.
- Reflow.
- High contrast.
- Zoom.

### Performance

Organization administration shall remain usable for organizations with
large numbers of:

- Members.
- Projects.
- Reports.
- Tasks.
- Progress logs.
- Audit events.

Avoid loading unnecessary data into the interface.

### Pagination and Virtualization

Where appropriate, use pagination or virtualization for large datasets
without compromising accessibility.

### Bulk Operations

Where appropriate, authorized administrators may perform bulk actions.

Potential bulk actions include:

- Assign role.
- Remove members.
- Archive projects.
- Change permissions.

Bulk operations shall include accessible confirmation and status
reporting.

### Bulk Operation Safety

Bulk destructive operations shall provide:

- Clear scope.
- Number of affected items.
- Confirmation.
- Error reporting.
- Partial-failure handling where appropriate.

### History Framework Integration

Administrative changes shall integrate with ART's History Framework
where appropriate.

Support:

- Undo.
- Redo.

Do not allow undo/redo to bypass authorization.

For example, a user who loses permission to modify a resource shall not
be able to use an old undo operation to modify that resource after
permission has been revoked.

### History and Audit Distinction

Clearly distinguish:

- User-level undo/redo.
- Administrative history.
- Security audit logs.

Undoing an action shall not erase the security audit trail.

### Cross-Device Administration

Organization administration shall remain consistent across a user's
authorized devices.

Where server synchronization is available:

- Changes shall synchronize.
- Permissions shall be revalidated.
- Organization context shall remain consistent.

Where file-based collaboration is used:

- Organization metadata shall be preserved in supported `.art` files.
- Permission information shall not be treated as more authoritative than
  external file/folder permissions.

### Desktop Application

Enterprise administration shall be available in the ART desktop
application where applicable.

The desktop implementation shall provide equivalent functionality to the
web application.

Do not remove administrative functionality from the desktop version
merely because the feature is easier to implement on the web.

### Web Application

Enterprise administration shall be available in the web application
where applicable.

### Feature Parity

Web and desktop implementations shall maintain equivalent:

- Navigation.
- Keyboard shortcuts.
- Customization.
- Accessibility.
- Permissions.
- Organization management.
- Error handling.
- Notifications.

### Security Testing

Test:

- Authorization enforcement.
- Role changes.
- Permission changes.
- Member removal.
- Organization isolation.
- Multiple-organization access.
- Session revocation.
- Device revocation.
- Integration permissions.
- Administrative audit logs.

### Accessibility Testing

Test the complete administration interface with:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox where applicable.
- Braille displays.
- Keyboard-only navigation.
- Magnification and low-vision settings.

### Assistive Technology Testing

Verify administrative workflows with diverse assistive technologies and
users with different disabilities.

### End-to-End Testing

Test complete organizational workflows.

Example:

1.  Create organization.
2.  Create administrator.
3.  Invite member.
4.  Member accepts invitation.
5.  Assign role.
6.  Create project.
7.  Add member to project.
8.  Create shared report.
9.  Assign task.
10. Add @mention.
11. Modify permissions.
12. Remove member.
13. Verify access is revoked.
14. Verify shared resources remain available to authorized users.
15. Verify audit history.
16. Verify organization metrics.
17. Verify synchronization across devices.

### File-Based Organization Testing

Test organizational workflows using:

- Google Drive.
- OneDrive.
- Dropbox.
- Other supported shared storage.

Verify that ART respects external folder and file permissions.

### Multi-Organization Testing

Test a user belonging to multiple organizations.

Verify that:

- Organization data remains isolated.
- Organization context is clear.
- Switching organizations does not expose data.
- Permissions are evaluated against the correct organization.

### Performance Testing

Test organizations with realistic large datasets.

At minimum, test:

- Hundreds of members.
- Large project collections.
- Large report collections.
- Large task collections.
- Large audit logs.

The exact scalability targets may be refined based on production
requirements.

### Documentation

Provide accessible administrator documentation covering:

- Creating an organization.
- Inviting members.
- Managing members.
- Assigning roles.
- Managing permissions.
- Managing projects.
- Managing shared resources.
- Managing integrations.
- Managing security settings.
- Managing privacy settings.
- Exporting organization data.
- Removing members.
- Handling account/device access.
- Reviewing audit logs.

### Administrator Help

Provide contextual Help for complex administrative operations.

Help shall be accessible and shall not require users to understand
implementation details.

### Definition of Done

Epic 63 shall be considered complete when:

- An accessible Organization Administration area exists.
- Authorized users can manage organizations.
- Organization profiles can be configured.
- Organization ownership is safely managed.
- Members can be invited and managed.
- Invitations can be revoked and expire appropriately.
- Members can be removed or disabled.
- Organization roles are implemented.
- Custom roles are supported where practical.
- Granular permissions are implemented.
- Least-privilege access is enforced.
- Permission inheritance is predictable.
- Project administration is implemented.
- Shared resources can be managed.
- Shared tasks respect organization permissions.
- Shared progress logs respect organization permissions.
- Organization templates can be managed.
- Organization settings are separate from personal settings.
- Personal accessibility settings are preserved.
- Organization-wide defaults are supported where appropriate.
- Security administration is implemented.
- Supported authentication policies can be configured.
- Device/session management is implemented where supported.
- Organization integrations can be managed.
- Data governance controls are implemented where applicable.
- Organization data ownership is clearly defined.
- Organization data can be exported where supported.
- Destructive data operations require appropriate confirmation.
- Retention policies are supported where applicable.
- Administrative audit logging is implemented.
- Audit logs are protected and accessible.
- Administrative notifications are implemented where appropriate.
- @mentions work within authorized organization resources.
- Organization metrics respect permissions.
- Shared-folder workflows respect external storage permissions.
- Multiple organizations per user are supported.
- Organization context is clear and accessible.
- Administrative context menus are implemented where appropriate.
- Administrative menu commands are available.
- Appropriate administrative keyboard shortcuts are customizable.
- Destructive actions use accessible confirmation dialogs.
- Administrative search and filtering are accessible.
- Administrative sorting is accessible.
- Live status messages are accessible.
- Error handling is accessible and secure.
- Privacy boundaries from Epic 58 are preserved.
- Organization data is isolated from personal data.
- Organization branding does not create accessibility problems.
- Administrative dashboards are accessible.
- Large organizations can be managed efficiently.
- Bulk operations are supported where appropriate.
- Bulk operations are safe and accessible.
- Administrative actions integrate appropriately with the History
  Framework.
- Undo/redo cannot bypass authorization.
- Audit history cannot be erased through undo/redo.
- Organization data remains consistent across authorized devices.
- Web and desktop applications provide equivalent administrative
  functionality.
- Security testing is completed.
- Accessibility testing is completed.
- Assistive technology testing is completed.
- End-to-end organization workflows are tested.
- File-based organization workflows are tested.
- Multi-organization workflows are tested.
- Performance testing is completed.
- Administrator documentation is complete.

### Final Requirement

Enterprise Administration & Management shall provide organizations with
the controls necessary to safely manage ART at scale without
compromising the application's core principles.

ART shall remain:

- Accessible.
- Secure.
- Private.
- User-controlled.
- Local-first where applicable.
- Compatible with file-based collaboration.
- Compatible with server-based collaboration.
- Usable without enterprise administration.
- Consistent across web and desktop applications.

Enterprise functionality shall extend ART for organizations rather than
fundamentally changing the experience for individual users.

## Epic 64 — Organization Metrics & Analytics Expansion

### Epic Overview

Expand ART's organization-level metrics, analytics, dashboards, and
reporting capabilities so organizations can understand the status,
progress, quality, workload, accessibility findings, and overall
performance of their accessibility programs.

This epic builds upon:

- Organization membership, roles, and authorization from Epic 50.
- File-based collaboration and shared organization folders from Epic 49.
- Enterprise administration and permissions from Epic 63.
- Shared reports, tasks, and progress logs.
- ART's existing reporting and dashboard functionality.
- ART's local-first architecture.
- Server-based collaboration where available.

Organization Metrics shall work with both server-based and file-based
organizational workflows where technically possible.

### General Requirements

Implement organization metrics without compromising:

- Accessibility.
- Privacy.
- Security.
- Data ownership.
- User control.
- Local-first functionality.
- File-based collaboration.
- Server-based collaboration.
- Web/desktop feature parity.

Do not require an organization to use a server merely to calculate
metrics from locally available or shared `.art` files.

### Organization Metrics Sources

Metrics may be calculated from authorized organization data, including:

- Projects.
- Reports.
- Findings.
- WCAG Success Criteria.
- Accessibility Standards.
- Tasks.
- Shared Tasks.
- Progress Logs.
- Report status.
- Finding status.
- Finding priority.
- Task priority.
- Due dates.
- Assignees.
- Completion status.
- Project status.
- Audit activity.
- Other applicable ART data.

Only data the current user is authorized to access shall be included.

### File-Based Metrics

When an organization uses the file-based collaboration model, ART shall
be able to calculate organization metrics from authorized files and
folders where technically possible.

For example:

``` text
Acme Co A11y Audits
    |
    +-- Project A
    |     +-- Report A1.art
    |     +-- Report A2.art
    |
    +-- Project B
    |     +-- Report B1.art
    |
    +-- Shared Tasks
    +-- Progress Logs
```

ART may use the contents of the shared organization folder to calculate
applicable organization-level metrics.

### Shared Folder Discovery

Where supported by the storage environment, ART may identify:

- Organization parent folder.
- Project folders.
- `.art` files.
- Shared task files.
- Progress logs.
- Other supported ART resources.

ART shall not access files outside the authorized scope merely to
calculate metrics.

### External Storage Permissions

ART shall respect permissions established by:

- Google Drive.
- OneDrive.
- Dropbox.
- Box.
- Other supported storage providers.

ART shall not bypass external storage permissions.

### Server-Based Metrics

When server infrastructure is available, organization metrics may be
calculated from centralized organizational data.

Server-based metrics shall:

- Respect authorization.
- Respect organization boundaries.
- Respect project permissions.
- Respect privacy settings.
- Use only authorized data.

### Hybrid Metrics

Where both file-based and server-based data exist, ART shall clearly
identify the data source and avoid double-counting information.

### Data Freshness

Clearly communicate when metrics were last calculated or synchronized.

Examples:

- "Updated just now."
- "Updated 5 minutes ago."
- "Last calculated July 28, 2026."
- "Some shared files have not been synchronized."

### Stale Data

If metrics are based on files that may have changed externally, ART
shall detect or communicate stale information where possible.

### Recalculation

Provide an accessible command to recalculate metrics.

This command may be available through:

- Context menu.
- Menu bar.
- Command menu.
- Customizable keyboard shortcut.

Avoid unnecessary permanent controls that clutter the interface.

### Automatic Updates

Where practical, update metrics automatically when underlying authorized
data changes.

Automatic updates shall not create excessive processing or network
activity.

### Manual Refresh

Provide a manual refresh/recalculate command.

The command shall provide an accessible live status message.

Example:

> "Organization metrics are being recalculated."

Followed by:

> "Organization metrics updated."

### Organization Metrics Dashboard

Provide an accessible Organization Metrics dashboard.

The dashboard may include:

- Overall project status.
- Open findings.
- Resolved findings.
- Outstanding tasks.
- Completed tasks.
- High-priority tasks.
- Overdue tasks.
- Findings by priority.
- Findings by status.
- Findings by WCAG version.
- Findings by Success Criterion.
- Findings by accessibility standard.
- Findings by project.
- Findings by assignee.
- Audit progress.
- Testing progress.
- Retesting progress.
- Report completion.
- Project activity.

### Dashboard Customization

Allow authorized users to customize their personal view of organization
metrics.

Users may be able to:

- Show/hide metric panels.
- Rearrange panels.
- Change default filters.
- Change date ranges.
- Save working views.

Customization shall not change the underlying organization data.

### Organization-Defined Dashboards

Where appropriate, authorized administrators may define
organization-wide dashboard defaults.

Personal user preferences shall remain available unless an organization
policy explicitly requires otherwise.

### Working Views

Support customizable working views for organization metrics.

Users may create views such as:

- Executive Overview.
- Active Audits.
- High-Priority Findings.
- Overdue Tasks.
- WCAG 2.2 Findings.
- Projects Assigned to Me.
- Recent Activity.

### Saved Views

Users may save customized metric views.

Saved views may include:

- Filters.
- Sorting.
- Visible metrics.
- Date ranges.
- Project scope.

### Shared Views

Where appropriate, authorized users may share metric views with other
organization members.

Shared views shall respect permissions.

### View Permissions

A shared view shall never grant access to data that the recipient could
not otherwise access.

### Filtering

Provide accessible filters for metrics.

Potential filters include:

- Organization.
- Project.
- Report.
- Report type.
- Finding status.
- Finding priority.
- Task status.
- Task priority.
- Assignee.
- Date.
- Due date.
- WCAG version.
- Success Criterion.
- Accessibility Standard.
- Testing status.

### Filtering and Permissions

Filter options shall not expose restricted projects, reports, users, or
data.

### Sorting

Support sorting by appropriate metric dimensions.

Examples:

- Priority.
- Due date.
- Date created.
- Date modified.
- Status.
- Project.
- Assignee.
- Finding count.

### Default Sorting

Where a task or finding metric is displayed as a list, highest priority
items should appear first unless the user has selected another sorting
method.

### Sorting Commands

Sorting commands should be available through:

- Context menus.
- Menu commands.
- Customizable keyboard shortcuts where appropriate.

### Date Ranges

Support configurable date ranges.

Examples:

- Today.
- This week.
- This month.
- This quarter.
- This year.
- Custom date range.
- All available data.

### Time Zones

Where date/time information is displayed, use the user's configured time
zone appropriately.

For organization-wide reports, clearly identify the applicable time
zone.

### Finding Metrics

Provide metrics for accessibility findings.

Potential metrics include:

- Total findings.
- Open findings.
- Closed findings.
- Deferred findings.
- Needs Review findings.
- False positives.
- Findings by severity.
- Findings by priority.
- Findings by WCAG version.
- Findings by Success Criterion.
- Findings by project.
- Findings by tester.
- Findings by status.

### Finding Status

Metrics shall respect ART's existing finding-status model.

Do not create duplicate status systems unnecessarily.

### Finding Priority

Finding priority shall remain programmatically available and shall be
included in applicable metrics.

### Task Metrics

Provide metrics for tasks and To Do lists.

Potential metrics include:

- Total tasks.
- Open tasks.
- Completed tasks.
- Blocked tasks.
- Deferred tasks.
- Not Applicable tasks.
- Needs Review tasks.
- Need Assistance tasks.
- Overdue tasks.
- High-priority tasks.
- Tasks by assignee.
- Tasks by project.

### Task Status

Support all existing task statuses.

Metrics shall not assume that a task is complete merely because it has
been checked unless the ART task model identifies the checkbox state as
completion.

### Completed Tasks

Completed tasks shall remain available in the Completed Tasks view
established in previous task-management functionality.

Metrics shall be able to distinguish:

- Active tasks.
- Completed tasks.
- Reopened tasks.

### Task Reopening

If a completed task is returned to an active status, metrics shall
update accordingly.

### Progress Metrics

Calculate project and organization progress where sufficient data
exists.

Potential measurements include:

- Audit completion percentage.
- Finding remediation percentage.
- Task completion percentage.
- Retesting completion.
- Report completion.
- Project completion.

### Progress Calculation Transparency

Where ART calculates a percentage or score, provide enough information
for users to understand what is being measured.

Do not present a calculated percentage without identifying its
underlying scope.

### Project Metrics

Provide metrics for individual projects.

Potential metrics include:

- Project status.
- Reports.
- Findings.
- Tasks.
- Progress.
- Due dates.
- Assigned users.
- Activity.
- Completion.

### Cross-Project Metrics

Authorized users may view aggregated metrics across multiple projects.

Aggregation shall only include projects the user is authorized to
access.

### Organization-Wide Metrics

Authorized users may view organization-wide metrics.

Organization-wide metrics shall not automatically be available to every
organization member.

### Metrics Permissions

Use the authorization policy service established in Epic 50.

Possible permissions include:

- View organization metrics.
- View project metrics.
- View personal metrics.
- Export metrics.
- Share metrics.
- Configure metrics.
- Manage organization dashboards.

### Personal Metrics

Users should be able to view metrics related to their own:

- Tasks.
- Findings.
- Projects.
- Progress.
- Assigned work.

Personal metrics shall remain separate from organization-wide metrics.

### Assignee Metrics

Where permitted, provide metrics by assignee.

Avoid presenting individual performance metrics in a way that could
expose information the organization has not authorized users to see.

### Privacy-Aware Metrics

Metrics shall avoid unnecessarily exposing sensitive information.

For example, a user without permission to view individual assignments
may receive aggregate counts without seeing individual names.

### Minimum Group Size

Where organizational privacy requirements require aggregation
thresholds, support configurable minimum group sizes before
individual-level metrics are displayed.

### Anonymous Aggregation

Where appropriate, support aggregate metrics without identifying
individual users.

### Organization Activity

Provide appropriate organization activity metrics.

Potential metrics include:

- Reports created.
- Findings created.
- Findings resolved.
- Tasks created.
- Tasks completed.
- Projects created.
- Reports modified.
- Progress log updates.

### Activity Timeline

Provide an accessible activity timeline where appropriate.

Activity shall respect permissions and privacy.

### Historical Metrics

Where historical data exists, allow users to view changes over time.

Potential comparisons include:

- Findings opened versus closed.
- Tasks completed.
- Audit progress.
- Remediation progress.

### Trend Analysis

Provide accessible trends where sufficient data exists.

Examples:

- Increasing/decreasing findings.
- Increasing/decreasing remediation.
- Task completion trends.
- Project completion trends.

### Metric Definitions

Every metric shall have an accessible definition.

Users should be able to determine:

- What is being measured.
- What data is included.
- What time period is used.
- What filters are active.

### Metric Details

Provide a way to inspect the underlying records contributing to a metric
where the user has permission to access them.

For example:

> "42 open findings"

could allow the user to view the 42 applicable findings.

### Drill-Down

Metric drill-down shall:

- Preserve active filters.
- Preserve organization context.
- Respect authorization.
- Be keyboard accessible.
- Be usable with screen readers.

### Charts and Visualizations

Where charts are used, provide equivalent accessible information in text
or structured data.

Do not make a chart the sole means of communicating a metric.

### Accessible Data Tables

Provide accessible tabular representations of metric data where
appropriate.

Tables shall have:

- Appropriate headers.
- Programmatic relationships.
- Meaningful captions or labels.
- Accessible sorting.
- Accessible filtering.

### Screen Reader Announcements

Changes to metrics shall be communicated through accessible status
messages where appropriate.

Example:

> "Organization metrics updated. 128 findings across 6 projects."

### Live Updates

If server-based real-time collaboration updates a metric, provide
accessible notification without repeatedly interrupting users.

### User Control of Live Updates

Where practical, allow users to control automatic metric refresh
behavior.

### Export

Authorized users shall be able to export organization metrics.

Potential formats include:

- CSV.
- XLSX.
- PDF.
- HTML.
- DOCX.
- Other supported ART formats.

### Export Accessibility

Exports shall preserve meaningful structure and accessibility wherever
the target format supports it.

### Export Scope

Users shall be able to export:

- Current view.
- Filtered results.
- Selected projects.
- Organization-wide metrics where authorized.
- Specific date ranges.

### Export Security

Exports shall contain only data the user is authorized to access.

### Report Integration

Where appropriate, organization metrics may be included in ART reports.

### Executive Reporting

Provide appropriate executive-level summaries without requiring
executives to understand the underlying ART data model.

Possible information includes:

- Overall accessibility program status.
- Number of active projects.
- Number of open high-priority findings.
- Remediation progress.
- Outstanding tasks.
- Major risks.
- Recent activity.

### Executive Metrics Permissions

Executive summaries shall respect organization permissions and privacy
settings.

### WCAG Metrics

Provide WCAG-specific metrics.

Potential metrics include:

- Findings by WCAG version.
- Findings by conformance level.
- Findings by Success Criterion.
- Findings by principle.
- Findings by guideline.
- Findings by severity/priority.

### Accessibility Standard Metrics

Support metrics for standards beyond WCAG.

Examples may include:

- Section 508.
- EN 301 549.
- ADA-related requirements.
- Organization-specific standards.

Do not assume that every standard has the same structure as WCAG.

### Multi-Standard Findings

Where findings are associated with multiple standards, avoid
double-counting them unless the selected metric explicitly intends to
count standard associations.

### Report Type Metrics

Support metrics by report type where appropriate.

Examples include:

- Audit Reports.
- Usability Reports.
- Executive Summary Reports.
- Progress Reports.
- Other ART report types.

### Report Output Metrics

Where practical, measure report generation and export activity without
storing unnecessary personal information.

### File-Based Synchronization

When metrics depend on shared files, ART should detect newly added or
modified files when technically possible.

### Shared Folder Refresh

Provide an accessible command to refresh organization metrics from the
shared folder.

### File Conflict Handling

If a report has unresolved merge conflicts, clearly identify that the
metric data may be incomplete or pending resolution.

### Incomplete Data

Do not silently present incomplete organization metrics as complete.

Clearly communicate conditions such as:

- "Metrics may be incomplete."
- "2 reports contain unresolved conflicts."
- "3 files could not be accessed."
- "Some project data has not been synchronized."

### Missing Data

Where source data is unavailable, identify the affected metric where
practical.

### Duplicate Data

Prevent duplicate counting when the same report or resource is
discovered through multiple paths.

### Archived Projects

Allow organizations to determine whether archived projects are:

- Included.
- Excluded.
- Included only in historical metrics.

### Deleted Resources

Define how deleted reports, projects, and tasks affect historical
metrics.

### Data Retention

Respect organization data-retention policies established through
enterprise administration.

### Metric Calculation Performance

Metrics shall remain responsive for large organizations.

Use:

- Incremental calculation.
- Caching.
- Background processing.
- Pagination.
- Virtualization.

where appropriate.

### Desktop Application

Organization Metrics shall be available in the ART desktop application
where applicable.

The desktop application shall provide equivalent metric functionality to
the web application.

### Web Application

Organization Metrics shall be available in the web application where
applicable.

### Feature Parity

Web and desktop applications shall maintain equivalent:

- Metrics.
- Dashboards.
- Filters.
- Sorting.
- Exports.
- Accessibility.
- Keyboard commands.
- Customization.

### Context Menus

Use context menus for appropriate metric actions.

Examples:

- Refresh metrics.
- Filter.
- Sort.
- Drill down.
- Export.
- Open source records.
- Save view.

### Menu Bar

When the Organization Metrics dashboard is displayed, provide
appropriate commands through the menu bar.

### Customizable Keyboard Shortcuts

Support customizable shortcuts for frequently used metric commands where
appropriate.

Examples:

- Refresh metrics.
- Clear filters.
- Apply saved view.
- Export.
- Search.
- Open metric details.

### Search

Provide accessible search across applicable metric data.

Users may search:

- Projects.
- Reports.
- Findings.
- Tasks.
- Standards.
- Success Criteria.
- Users where permitted.

### Search Permissions

Search shall never reveal restricted resources.

### Organization Context

Clearly communicate which organization the metrics represent.

This is especially important for users belonging to multiple
organizations.

### Multiple Organizations

Users belonging to multiple organizations shall be able to switch
between organizations without mixing metric data.

### Organization Switching

When switching organizations:

- Clear or appropriately update filters.
- Recalculate metrics.
- Update organization context.
- Prevent stale metrics from another organization from being displayed
  as current.

### History Framework

Metric-related actions that modify data shall integrate with ART's
History Framework.

Examples:

- Changing task status.
- Updating finding status.
- Modifying priority.
- Editing project information.

Viewing or recalculating metrics should not create unnecessary undo
history entries.

### Undo/Redo

Actions initiated from the metrics dashboard that modify ART data shall
support Undo/Redo where appropriate.

Undo shall not bypass authorization.

### Privacy

All organization metrics shall comply with Epic 58.

Do not use organization metrics to expose private information
unnecessarily.

### Security

All organization metrics shall comply with Epic 47 and the authorization
architecture established in Epic 50.

### Authorization Changes

If a user's permissions change, metrics shall be recalculated using
their new permissions.

A user shall not continue seeing metrics derived from resources they can
no longer access.

### Caching Security

Cached metrics shall not allow a user to infer restricted information
after permissions change.

### Audit Logging

Administrative configuration changes to organization metrics should be
recorded in the appropriate audit mechanisms.

Examples include:

- Dashboard configuration changed.
- Metric visibility changed.
- Organization metric permissions changed.
- Shared view created.
- Shared view modified.

### Accessibility Testing

Test Organization Metrics with:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox where applicable.
- Braille displays.
- Keyboard-only operation.
- Magnification.
- High-contrast settings.
- Zoom.

### Accessible Charts

Verify that users who cannot see charts receive equivalent information
through accessible text and tables.

### Accessible Filters

Verify that filtering and sorting controls are fully accessible.

### Accessible Drill-Down

Verify that users can navigate from a metric to its underlying records
using only the keyboard and assistive technology.

### End-to-End Testing

Test complete workflows.

Example:

1.  Create an organization.
2.  Add members.
3.  Create multiple projects.
4.  Create reports.
5.  Add findings.
6.  Assign priorities.
7.  Create tasks.
8.  Complete tasks.
9.  Add progress-log information.
10. Share reports through an organization folder.
11. Modify reports.
12. Synchronize changes.
13. Recalculate metrics.
14. Verify project metrics.
15. Verify organization metrics.
16. Apply filters.
17. Sort results.
18. Drill into a metric.
19. Export results.
20. Change user permissions.
21. Verify restricted data is removed from the user's metrics.
22. Verify organization data remains isolated.

### File-Based Metrics Testing

Test organization metrics using shared folders on:

- Google Drive.
- OneDrive.
- Dropbox.
- Other supported storage providers.

Verify:

- File discovery.
- Permission handling.
- Change detection.
- Recalculation.
- Duplicate prevention.
- Conflict handling.
- Incomplete-data handling.

### Server-Based Metrics Testing

Where server infrastructure exists, verify:

- Centralized calculation.
- Synchronization.
- Permission enforcement.
- Organization isolation.
- Multi-user updates.
- Real-time or near-real-time updates where supported.

### Multi-Device Testing

Verify metrics across:

- Web ART.
- Desktop ART.
- Multiple authorized devices.

Ensure metrics remain consistent after synchronization.

### Multiple-Organization Testing

Verify that users belonging to multiple organizations cannot
accidentally combine:

- Projects.
- Reports.
- Findings.
- Tasks.
- Metrics.

### Performance Testing

Test with increasingly large datasets.

Include scenarios with:

- Hundreds of reports.
- Thousands of findings.
- Thousands of tasks.
- Multiple projects.
- Large audit histories.
- Large organizations.

### Failure Testing

Test:

- Missing files.
- Corrupted files.
- Unavailable cloud storage.
- Permission changes.
- Network interruption.
- Synchronization failure.
- Merge conflicts.
- Duplicate files.
- Deleted resources.
- Partial data availability.

### Documentation

Provide accessible documentation explaining:

- Organization Metrics.
- Metric definitions.
- Dashboard configuration.
- Filtering.
- Sorting.
- Saved views.
- Shared views.
- Drill-down.
- Exporting.
- File-based metrics.
- Server-based metrics.
- Data freshness.
- Incomplete data.
- Permissions.
- Privacy.

### Definition of Done

Epic 64 shall be considered complete when:

- Organization Metrics functionality is implemented.
- Metrics can be calculated from authorized organization data.
- File-based metrics are supported where technically feasible.
- Server-based metrics are supported where applicable.
- Hybrid data sources are handled safely.
- Data freshness is communicated.
- Stale and incomplete data are identified.
- Metrics can be recalculated.
- Automatic metric updates are supported where practical.
- An accessible Organization Metrics dashboard exists.
- Dashboard views can be customized.
- Saved views are supported.
- Shared views are supported where appropriate.
- Filtering is implemented.
- Sorting is implemented.
- Date ranges are supported.
- Finding metrics are implemented.
- Task metrics are implemented.
- Progress metrics are implemented.
- Project metrics are implemented.
- Cross-project metrics are implemented.
- Organization-wide metrics respect authorization.
- Personal metrics remain distinct from organization metrics.
- Assignee metrics respect privacy and permissions.
- Historical metrics are supported where data exists.
- Trends are supported where meaningful.
- Metric definitions are accessible.
- Metric drill-down is implemented.
- Charts have accessible alternatives.
- Metric data can be presented in accessible tables.
- Live metric updates are accessible.
- Users have appropriate control over automatic updates.
- Authorized users can export metrics.
- Exported metrics contain only authorized data.
- Executive-level metrics are supported.
- WCAG metrics are supported.
- Multiple accessibility standards are supported.
- Multi-standard findings are not incorrectly double-counted.
- Report-type metrics are supported where appropriate.
- Shared-folder metric calculation is supported.
- File changes can trigger metric updates where practical.
- Merge conflicts are accounted for.
- Incomplete metric data is clearly communicated.
- Duplicate resources are not double-counted.
- Archived projects can be handled according to organization settings.
- Deleted resources are handled predictably.
- Retention policies are respected.
- Metric calculation performs acceptably at organizational scale.
- Web and desktop implementations maintain feature parity.
- Context-menu commands are available where appropriate.
- Menu-bar commands are available where appropriate.
- Relevant keyboard shortcuts can be customized.
- Search is accessible and permission-aware.
- Organization context is clear.
- Multiple organizations are properly isolated.
- History Framework integration is implemented where appropriate.
- Undo/Redo cannot bypass authorization.
- Privacy requirements are satisfied.
- Security requirements are satisfied.
- Authorization changes are reflected in metrics.
- Cached metrics do not expose restricted information.
- Administrative metric changes are auditable.
- Accessibility testing is completed.
- Assistive technology testing is completed.
- End-to-end testing is completed.
- File-based testing is completed.
- Server-based testing is completed where applicable.
- Multi-device testing is completed.
- Multiple-organization testing is completed.
- Performance testing is completed.
- Failure and recovery testing is completed.
- Accessible documentation is complete.

### Final Requirement

Organization Metrics & Analytics shall provide organizations with
meaningful, trustworthy, accessible, and privacy-conscious insight into
their accessibility programs.

Metrics shall help organizations understand their work without becoming
a surveillance mechanism.

The system shall make it easy for authorized users to answer questions
such as:

- What accessibility work is currently active?
- Which projects need attention?
- Which findings have the highest priority?
- Which tasks are overdue?
- How much remediation has been completed?
- Which Success Criteria have the most findings?
- How are projects progressing?
- What work remains?
- What has changed since the previous reporting period?

All metrics shall remain grounded in the underlying ART data and shall
clearly communicate their scope, freshness, and limitations.

## Epic 65 — Performance & Scalability Optimization

### Epic Overview

Optimize ART so that it remains fast, responsive, reliable, accessible,
and usable as the size and complexity of reports, projects,
organizations, shared resources, integrations, collaboration activity,
and stored data increase.

ART shall provide a responsive experience for individual users while
also being capable of supporting larger organizations, large
accessibility audits, substantial report histories, extensive task
lists, shared progress logs, organization metrics, integrations, and
concurrent collaboration.

Performance optimization shall never be achieved by sacrificing:

- Accessibility.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Data integrity.
- Functionality.
- Usability.
- Keyboard accessibility.
- Screen-reader support.
- Web/desktop feature parity.
- Local-first functionality.
- File-based collaboration.
- Server-based collaboration.

### General Requirements

Identify and address performance bottlenecks throughout ART.

Performance work shall cover:

- Web application.
- Desktop application.
- Local storage.
- File processing.
- `.art` file operations.
- Report rendering.
- Report editing.
- Dashboard rendering.
- Organization metrics.
- Task management.
- Progress logs.
- Collaboration.
- Synchronization.
- Merge processing.
- Search.
- Filtering.
- Sorting.
- Import/export.
- Integrations.
- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Database operations.
- Server communication.
- Desktop application startup.
- Application updates.

### Performance Principles

ART shall:

- Load efficiently.
- Respond promptly to user interaction.
- Avoid unnecessary processing.
- Avoid unnecessary network requests.
- Avoid unnecessary file operations.
- Avoid unnecessary database queries.
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Avoid blocking the user interface.
- Provide feedback for operations that take longer than expected.

### Accessibility and Performance

Performance optimizations shall preserve accessibility.

Do not use performance techniques that cause:

- Lost keyboard focus.
- Missing screen-reader announcements.
- Broken virtual cursor behavior.
- Incorrect accessible names.
- Inaccessible virtualized content.
- Missing live-region updates.
- Unpredictable focus movement.
- Inaccessible loading states.

### Perceived Performance

Optimize not only measured performance but also perceived
responsiveness.

Where operations take time:

- Provide immediate feedback.
- Display accessible progress information.
- Keep the interface responsive.
- Allow cancellation where safe.

### Loading States

Provide accessible loading states for operations that cannot complete
immediately.

Examples include:

- Loading report.
- Calculating metrics.
- Synchronizing files.
- Loading organization data.
- Importing a large report.
- Exporting a large report.

### Live Status Messages

Long-running operations shall provide accessible status messages.

Examples:

> "Loading report."

> "Report loaded."

> "Calculating organization metrics."

> "Organization metrics updated."

### Progress Indicators

Where meaningful, provide progress indicators for long-running
operations.

Progress indicators shall have accessible programmatic information.

Do not rely solely on animation or color.

### Cancellation

Where technically safe, allow users to cancel long-running operations.

Examples include:

- Large imports.
- Large exports.
- Metric calculations.
- Synchronization.
- File scanning.

### Local Storage Performance

Optimize ART's use of browser and local storage.

Avoid:

- Excessive serialization.
- Repeated full-database reads.
- Unnecessary writes.
- Large blocking operations.

### Incremental Storage Updates

Where appropriate, update only changed data instead of rewriting entire
datasets.

### Local Data Indexing

Create appropriate indexes for frequently accessed local data.

Potential indexes include:

- Report identifiers.
- Project identifiers.
- Finding identifiers.
- Task identifiers.
- Dates.
- Statuses.
- Priorities.
- Assignees.

### Large `.art` Files

Optimize loading and saving of large `.art` files.

ART shall avoid unnecessary duplication of large data structures in
memory.

### `.art` File Integrity

Performance optimizations shall not compromise `.art` file integrity.

A failed save shall not silently produce a corrupted report.

### Atomic File Operations

Where supported by the environment, use safe/atomic save strategies.

### File Change Detection

Optimize external file-change detection so that shared-folder
collaboration does not continuously consume excessive system resources.

### File-Based Collaboration

Optimize:

- File comparison.
- Change detection.
- Version identification.
- Merge processing.
- Conflict detection.
- Conflict resolution.

### Incremental Merge Processing

Where practical, compare only changed portions of a report rather than
comparing the entire document.

### Merge Performance

Merge processing shall remain usable for reports containing:

- Large numbers of findings.
- Large task lists.
- Large progress logs.
- Extensive history.
- Multiple collaborators.

### Merge Conflicts

Conflict detection shall not unnecessarily block unrelated report
functionality.

Where conflicts exist:

- Clearly identify them.
- Preserve the user's work.
- Provide an accessible resolution workflow.

### Concurrent File Access

Optimize handling of reports being edited by multiple users through
shared storage.

### Server Performance

Where ART is deployed using a server, optimize:

- API response time.
- Database queries.
- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Synchronization.
- Collaboration.
- Metrics.
- File operations.
- Integration requests.

### API Performance

Avoid unnecessary API calls.

Where appropriate:

- Batch requests.
- Cache safe information.
- Use incremental synchronization.
- Use pagination.
- Use efficient payloads.

### API Response Sizes

Avoid transmitting unnecessary data.

Request only the fields required for the current operation.

### Pagination

Use pagination for large datasets.

Potential examples include:

- Organization members.
- Reports.
- Findings.
- Tasks.
- Progress logs.
- Audit logs.
- Metrics.

Pagination must remain accessible.

### Infinite Scrolling

If infinite scrolling is used, ensure it remains fully accessible and
usable with:

- Keyboard navigation.
- Screen readers.
- Braille displays.
- Magnification.

Do not use infinite scrolling where it creates accessibility or
usability problems.

### Virtualization

Where virtualization is necessary for performance, ensure virtualized
content remains accessible.

Users shall be able to:

- Navigate all available records.
- Determine their position within the list.
- Access content with screen readers.
- Navigate using the keyboard.

### Database Performance

Optimize database architecture and queries.

Identify:

- Slow queries.
- Missing indexes.
- Excessive joins.
- Repeated queries.
- Inefficient aggregations.
- Unnecessary database access.

### Database Indexes

Create appropriate indexes for high-frequency operations.

Potential indexed fields include:

- User ID.
- Organization ID.
- Project ID.
- Report ID.
- Finding ID.
- Task ID.
- Status.
- Priority.
- Created date.
- Modified date.

### Database Query Isolation

Ensure performance optimizations do not weaken organization or user data
isolation.

### Organization Scale

ART shall remain usable as organizations grow.

Performance testing shall consider organizations with:

- Hundreds of users.
- Hundreds of projects.
- Thousands of reports.
- Thousands of findings.
- Thousands of tasks.
- Large audit histories.

Exact capacity targets may be refined based on actual deployment
requirements.

### Multi-Tenant Performance

For server-based ART, ensure one organization cannot consume
disproportionate resources to the detriment of other organizations.

### Resource Isolation

Where appropriate, use:

- Rate limits.
- Request quotas.
- Resource controls.
- Background processing.

### Organization Metrics Performance

Optimize organization metric calculations.

Use appropriate techniques such as:

- Incremental calculation.
- Caching.
- Background processing.
- Precomputed aggregates.
- Indexed queries.

### Metric Recalculation

Avoid recalculating all organizational metrics after every minor change
when incremental calculation is possible.

### Large Metrics Datasets

Organization metrics shall remain responsive when processing:

- Large numbers of reports.
- Large numbers of findings.
- Large task collections.
- Long historical periods.

### Dashboard Performance

Optimize dashboard loading and rendering.

Do not load every possible dashboard widget when the user has chosen to
hide them.

### Custom Working Views

Only load data required by the current working view.

### Saved Views

Saved views shall load efficiently without unnecessarily reprocessing
unrelated data.

### Task Performance
