Optimize task management for large task collections.

Support large numbers of:

- Tasks.
- Completed tasks.
- Assignments.
- Comments.
- @mentions\.
- Status changes.
- Due dates.
- Priorities.

### Task Sorting

Sorting by:

- Priority.
- Due date/time.
- Date added.
- Status.

shall remain responsive for large task lists.

### Task Filtering

Filtering shall not require loading unnecessary records into memory.

### Completed Tasks

Completed Tasks shall remain accessible without unnecessarily slowing
the active To Do list.

### Progress Log Performance

Optimize large Progress Logs.

Support:

- Large numbers of entries.
- Multiple contributors.
- Long project histories.
- Shared progress logs.

### Search Performance

ART's search capabilities shall remain responsive as data grows.

Search shall support:

- Reports.
- Projects.
- Findings.
- Tasks.
- Users.
- Standards.
- Success Criteria.
- Progress logs.
- Other applicable resources.

### Search Indexing

Where appropriate, implement indexing to improve search performance.

### Search Accessibility

Search optimizations shall preserve:

- Keyboard accessibility.
- Screen-reader announcements.
- Accessible result counts.
- Accessible autocomplete.
- Focus management.

### Search Result Virtualization

If search results are virtualized, ensure all results remain accessible.

### Filtering Performance

Optimize filtering across large datasets.

### Sorting Performance

Optimize sorting without unnecessarily duplicating large datasets.

### Report Rendering

Optimize rendering of large reports.

Large reports may contain:

- Hundreds of findings.
- Large tables.
- Extensive descriptions.
- Numerous links.
- Screenshots.
- Attachments.
- Comments.
- History.

### Lazy Rendering

Where appropriate, render non-visible report sections only when needed.

Lazy rendering shall not make content inaccessible to assistive
technologies.

### Report Editor Performance

The report editor shall remain responsive while editing large reports.

Avoid:

- Excessive re-rendering.
- Unnecessary DOM updates.
- Blocking operations.
- Repeated full-document processing.

### Auto-Save Performance

If auto-save is implemented:

- Avoid excessive writes.
- Use debouncing/throttling where appropriate.
- Preserve data integrity.
- Clearly communicate save status.

### Save Status

Provide accessible save-state information such as:

- Saving.
- Saved.
- Save failed.
- Changes pending.

### History Framework Performance

Optimize ART's History Framework.

Large editing sessions shall not cause excessive memory use.

### History Compression

Where appropriate, combine or compress compatible history operations
without changing user-visible Undo/Redo behavior.

### Undo/Redo

Undo and Redo shall remain responsive even after substantial editing.

### History Retention

Define appropriate limits for history data where necessary.

Do not silently discard important data without clear design
requirements.

### Collaboration Performance

Optimize server-based collaboration.

Support efficient:

- Change transmission.
- Presence updates.
- Synchronization.
- Conflict detection.
- Merge processing.

### Real-Time Collaboration

Where real-time collaboration is supported, avoid excessive network
traffic.

Use efficient update mechanisms.

### Presence

Collaborator presence information shall not generate excessive network
activity.

### File-Based Collaboration Performance

Optimize file-based collaboration independently of real-time server
functionality.

File-based collaboration shall remain practical even without a server.

### Synchronization Frequency

Avoid excessive polling.

Prefer efficient file-system notifications or event-driven mechanisms
where available.

### Background Processing

Use background processing for operations that would otherwise block the
user interface.

Potential operations include:

- Metrics.
- Large imports.
- Large exports.
- Search indexing.
- Synchronization.
- Merge preparation.
- File scanning.

### Worker Processes

Where supported, use worker threads/processes appropriately.

Do not move accessibility-critical UI operations into inaccessible
background processes.

### Desktop Application Performance

The desktop application shall remain responsive during:

- Startup.
- Report loading.
- Saving.
- Exporting.
- Importing.
- Synchronization.
- Collaboration.
- Metrics calculation.

### Desktop Startup

Optimize startup time.

Avoid loading optional functionality until needed.

### Desktop Memory Usage

Monitor memory consumption during:

- Large report editing.
- Collaboration.
- Multiple reports.
- Long-running sessions.

### Desktop CPU Usage

Avoid excessive CPU use during:

- Idle periods.
- File watching.
- Synchronization.
- Metrics calculation.

### Desktop Battery Usage

Where applicable, minimize unnecessary CPU and background processing to
preserve battery life.

### Web Performance

Optimize ART for modern browsers.

Evaluate:

- Initial page load.
- JavaScript execution.
- Rendering.
- Network requests.
- Memory.
- Responsiveness.

### Code Splitting

Use code splitting where appropriate.

Do not delay critical accessibility functionality unnecessarily.

### Lazy Loading

Lazy-load non-critical features where appropriate.

Critical application functionality shall remain available without
confusing users or creating inaccessible loading behavior.

### Asset Optimization

Optimize:

- JavaScript.
- CSS.
- Images.
- Fonts.
- Other application assets.

Do not sacrifice accessibility or readability for asset size.

### Caching

Use appropriate caching for static resources and safe application data.

### Cache Invalidation

Ensure users receive current application versions and data when
required.

### Security and Caching

Never cache sensitive information in a manner that could expose it to
unauthorized users.

### Integration Performance

Optimize external integrations established in Epic 62.

Avoid unnecessary API calls to:

- Jira.
- GitHub.
- Azure.
- Google Workspace.
- Microsoft 365.
- Cloud-storage providers.
- Other supported platforms.

### Integration Rate Limits

Respect provider rate limits.

Use:

- Request batching.
- Caching.
- Incremental synchronization.
- Backoff.
- Retry strategies.

### Integration Queues

Where appropriate, queue non-urgent integration operations.

Clearly communicate pending operations.

### Failed Integrations

A failed integration shall not block normal ART functionality.

### Import Performance

Optimize large imports.

Support large:

- `.art` files.
- CSV files.
- JSON data.
- Other supported formats.

### Export Performance

Optimize large exports.

Provide accessible progress information for exports that take
significant time.

### Export Cancellation

Allow cancellation where safe.

### File Compression

Where appropriate, consider compression for large data structures.

Compression shall not compromise:

- Portability.
- File integrity.
- Interoperability.
- Accessibility.

### Network Resilience

ART shall remain responsive during poor network conditions.

Handle:

- High latency.
- Temporary disconnects.
- Packet loss.
- Server unavailable.
- Integration unavailable.

### Offline Performance

ART's local functionality shall remain responsive without network
connectivity.

### Reconnection

When connectivity returns:

- Reconnect safely.
- Synchronize changes.
- Detect conflicts.
- Preserve user work.

### Error Recovery

Performance-related failures shall fail safely.

Examples include:

- Out-of-memory conditions.
- Storage limitations.
- Network failure.
- Database timeout.
- Integration timeout.

### Graceful Degradation

When resources are constrained, ART should degrade gracefully rather
than becoming completely unusable.

### Performance Monitoring

Where server infrastructure exists, collect appropriate performance
metrics.

Potential metrics include:

- API response time.
- Database query time.
- Error rates.
- Synchronization latency.
- Resource utilization.
- Background job duration.

### Privacy-Aware Monitoring

Performance monitoring shall not collect unnecessary personal
information.

### Client-Side Diagnostics

Where appropriate, collect anonymized technical performance information.

Users shall be informed when diagnostic data is collected.

### Performance Budgets

Establish reasonable performance targets for critical workflows.

Potential targets include:

- Application startup.
- Report loading.
- Report saving.
- Search.
- Task operations.
- Dashboard loading.
- Metrics calculation.
- Synchronization.

Exact targets shall be determined based on realistic ART workloads.

### Performance Regression Testing

Create automated performance tests for critical workflows.

Run performance tests during development and release processes where
practical.

### Large Dataset Testing

Create representative large datasets for testing.

Include:

- Large reports.
- Large projects.
- Large organizations.
- Large task collections.
- Large finding collections.
- Large histories.

### Stress Testing

Test ART under unusually heavy workloads.

Examples include:

- Many simultaneous users.
- Large synchronization operations.
- Large imports.
- Large exports.
- Many concurrent file changes.

### Load Testing

For server-based deployments, perform load testing representative of
expected usage.

### Concurrency Testing

Test multiple users simultaneously:

- Editing reports.
- Modifying tasks.
- Updating progress logs.
- Synchronizing changes.
- Calculating metrics.
- Using integrations.

### Accessibility Under Load

Verify accessibility while ART is under heavy processing.

Users shall still be able to:

- Navigate.
- Use keyboard shortcuts.
- Operate controls.
- Receive live status messages.
- Maintain focus.
- Use screen readers.

### Assistive Technology Performance

Test with:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox where applicable.
- Braille displays.

Verify that performance optimizations do not create delays or
accessibility regressions.

### Low-Vision Performance

Test ART using:

- Zoom.
- Magnification.
- High-contrast settings.
- Increased text size.
- Other supported visual settings.

### Keyboard Performance

Verify that keyboard interaction remains responsive when processing
large datasets.

### Desktop/Web Parity

Performance improvements implemented in one application should be
evaluated for applicability to the other.

Do not allow the desktop application to become significantly less
responsive than the web application or vice versa.

### Documentation

Document:

- Performance architecture.
- Performance targets.
- Known limitations.
- Scaling strategies.
- Caching strategies.
- Background processing.
- Database optimization.
- Large dataset considerations.
- Troubleshooting.

### Definition of Done

Epic 65 shall be considered complete when:

- Major ART performance bottlenecks have been identified.
- Critical performance bottlenecks have been addressed.
- Web application performance has been optimized.
- Desktop application performance has been optimized.
- Local storage performance has been optimized.
- Large `.art` files can be handled efficiently.
- File integrity remains protected.
- File-based collaboration remains responsive.
- Merge processing has been optimized.
- Server APIs have been optimized where applicable.
- API payloads are appropriately minimized.
- Pagination is implemented where appropriate.
- Virtualization is accessible where used.
- Database queries have been optimized.
- Appropriate database indexes exist.
- Organization-scale workloads have been tested.
- Multi-tenant server performance has been considered.
- Organization metrics calculation has been optimized.
- Dashboards load efficiently.
- Working views remain responsive.
- Task management remains responsive with large task collections.
- Progress logs remain usable at scale.
- Search remains responsive with large datasets.
- Search indexing is implemented where appropriate.
- Report rendering has been optimized.
- Report editing remains responsive.
- Auto-save does not create excessive overhead.
- Save status is accessible.
- History Framework performance has been optimized.
- Undo/Redo remains responsive.
- Server-based collaboration has been optimized.
- Real-time collaboration does not generate unnecessary traffic.
- File-based collaboration does not require a server.
- Background processing is used where appropriate.
- Desktop startup performance has been optimized.
- Desktop memory usage has been evaluated.
- Desktop CPU usage has been evaluated.
- Web application loading has been optimized.
- Code splitting/lazy loading is implemented where appropriate.
- Assets are optimized.
- Caching is implemented safely.
- Integration performance has been optimized.
- Import performance has been optimized.
- Export performance has been optimized.
- Network resilience has been implemented.
- Offline performance remains strong.
- Reconnection behavior is safe.
- Error recovery is implemented.
- Graceful degradation is supported.
- Server performance monitoring exists where applicable.
- Performance monitoring respects privacy.
- Appropriate performance targets have been established.
- Performance regression tests exist.
- Large dataset testing is complete.
- Stress testing is complete where applicable.
- Load testing is complete for server deployments.
- Concurrency testing is complete.
- Accessibility-under-load testing is complete.
- Assistive technology performance testing is complete.
- Low-vision performance testing is complete.
- Keyboard performance testing is complete.
- Web/desktop performance parity has been evaluated.
- Performance documentation is complete.

### Final Requirement

ART shall remain fast and responsive as its capabilities and user base
grow.

Performance optimization shall never become an excuse to remove
functionality, simplify accessibility features, weaken privacy or
security, or create a fundamentally different experience for users of
assistive technologies.

ART shall scale from:

- A single accessibility professional working locally,
- to a small testing team sharing `.art` files,
- to organizations managing multiple projects,
- to large organizations using server-based collaboration, integrations,
  metrics, and centralized administration.

The objective is not merely to make ART faster.

The objective is to ensure that ART remains **usable, accessible,
reliable, and responsive at every stage of its growth.**

## Epic 66 — Accessibility Remediation & Conformance Hardening

### Epic Overview

Perform a comprehensive accessibility remediation and
conformance-hardening pass across the entire Accessibility Reporting
Tool (ART).

This epic shall identify, prioritize, remediate, and verify
accessibility issues throughout ART's web application, desktop
application, shared collaboration features, dashboards, reports, task
management, settings, editors, dialogs, menus, integrations,
authentication workflows, organization features, metrics,
imports/exports, and other user-facing functionality.

The objective is to ensure that accessibility is not merely addressed in
individual components, but is consistently implemented throughout the
entire ART ecosystem.

ART shall be usable by people with a wide range of disabilities and with
a wide range of assistive technologies.

### General Requirements

Implement accessibility remediation without sacrificing:

- Functionality.
- Performance.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Data integrity.
- Collaboration.
- File-based workflows.
- Server-based workflows.
- Web/desktop feature parity.
- User customization.
- Keyboard accessibility.
- Screen-reader accessibility.
- Low-vision usability.
- Native desktop functionality.

All remediation shall follow applicable accessibility standards and
established ART accessibility requirements.

### Standards

Accessibility remediation shall consider, as applicable:

- WCAG 2.2.
- WCAG 2.1 where legacy compatibility is required.
- Section 508.
- EN 301 549.
- WAI-ARIA specifications.
- Applicable platform accessibility requirements.
- Applicable desktop accessibility requirements.

ART shall prioritize WCAG 2.2 Level A and AA conformance.

### Accessibility Architecture Review

Review ART's accessibility architecture as a whole.

Identify systemic problems affecting multiple areas of the application.

Examples include:

- Incorrect heading structures.
- Inconsistent focus management.
- Inconsistent accessible naming.
- Incorrect ARIA usage.
- Inaccessible custom controls.
- Inconsistent keyboard shortcuts.
- Inaccessible dialogs.
- Inconsistent status messages.
- Incorrect programmatic relationships.
- Inaccessible dynamic content.

Where a systemic issue exists, correct the underlying architecture
rather than repeatedly patching individual instances.

### Semantic HTML

Prefer native semantic HTML wherever possible.

Use:

- Native buttons.
- Native links.
- Native form controls.
- Native headings.
- Native lists.
- Native tables.
- Native dialogs where appropriate.

Do not replace native controls with custom controls without a specific
reason.

### Headings

Ensure heading structures are logical and hierarchical.

ART shall:

- Use headings in logical order.
- Avoid unnecessary heading-level jumps.
- Avoid using visual styling alone to represent headings.
- Ensure headings have meaningful accessible names.

The application's highest appropriate heading level shall follow ART's
established heading strategy.

### Landmarks

Use appropriate landmarks, including where applicable:

- Header.
- Navigation.
- Main.
- Aside.
- Footer.
- Search.
- Form regions.

Landmarks shall have meaningful accessible names when multiple landmarks
of the same type exist.

### Page and Modal Titles

Ensure pages, views, dialogs, and panels have meaningful titles.

Titles shall clearly communicate the user's current context.

### Keyboard Accessibility

Every interactive feature shall be operable using the keyboard.

Verify:

- Tab navigation.
- Shift+Tab navigation.
- Enter.
- Space.
- Arrow keys.
- Home.
- End.
- Escape.
- Application-specific shortcuts.

### Keyboard Focus

Ensure focus is:

- Visible.
- Predictable.
- Programmatically determinable.
- Preserved when appropriate.
- Moved appropriately after dynamic changes.

### Focus After Dialog Opening

When a modal opens:

- Move focus to the appropriate first control.
- Ensure the dialog has a meaningful accessible name.
- Keep focus within the modal while it is active.

### Focus After Dialog Closing

When a modal closes, return focus to the control that opened it unless
another destination is explicitly required by the workflow.

### Focus Management for Dynamic Content

When ART creates or removes content dynamically, focus shall be managed
predictably.

Examples include:

- Adding a task.
- Adding a finding.
- Adding an evaluation item.
- Opening a merge dialog.
- Creating a report.
- Adding a project.
- Opening a context menu.

### Focus Trapping

Modal dialogs shall maintain appropriate focus trapping.

Users shall not unintentionally navigate into content behind an active
modal.

### Escape Key

Where appropriate, Escape shall close dialogs, menus, and temporary
overlays.

Escape behavior shall not discard user data without appropriate
confirmation.

### Keyboard Shortcuts

Review all ART keyboard shortcuts.

Verify:

- Shortcuts work consistently.
- Shortcut commands have equivalent menu commands where appropriate.
- User-defined shortcuts work correctly.
- Shortcut conflicts are prevented or clearly identified.
- Modifier combinations are accessible.
- Shortcuts do not interfere unnecessarily with assistive technology
  commands.

### Keyboard Shortcut Documentation

Ensure users can discover available keyboard shortcuts.

### Screen Reader Accessibility

Test ART with multiple screen readers.

Required testing includes:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox where applicable.

### Screen Reader Compatibility

Verify:

- Roles.
- Names.
- States.
- Properties.
- Relationships.
- Dynamic updates.
- Form validation.
- Dialog behavior.
- Menus.
- Tables.
- Lists.
- Tree structures where applicable.

### Accessible Names

Every interactive control shall have a meaningful accessible name.

Examples include:

- Buttons.
- Links.
- Textboxes.
- Checkboxes.
- Radio buttons.
- Select controls.
- Comboboxes.
- Menus.
- Menu items.
- Dialog controls.

### Visible Text and Accessible Names

Do not unnecessarily replace meaningful visible text with unrelated
accessible names.

Where additional information is needed for assistive technology users,
use appropriate accessible-name or description techniques without
unnecessarily changing the visible interface.

### Links

Verify that links:

- Have meaningful names.
- Clearly communicate their destination.
- Are keyboard accessible.
- Have appropriate focus indication.
- Do not rely solely on surrounding visual context.

### New-Tab Links

Links that open a new tab or window shall communicate this information
appropriately to assistive technology users without unnecessarily
duplicating the information in visible link text.

### Buttons

Buttons shall:

- Have meaningful names.
- Perform the action indicated by their accessible name.
- Use appropriate button semantics.
- Have appropriate disabled states where applicable.

### Form Controls

All form controls shall have:

- Accessible labels.
- Appropriate descriptions where necessary.
- Programmatic state information.
- Accessible validation messages.

### Required Fields

Required fields shall communicate required status programmatically.

Do not rely solely on an asterisk or visual styling.

### Validation Errors

Validation errors shall:

- Be clearly communicated.
- Be programmatically associated with the applicable control.
- Be announced appropriately.
- Provide actionable information.
- Preserve user-entered data where possible.

### Live Status Messages

ART shall use accessible live status messages for dynamic events.

Examples include:

- Report saved.
- Report loaded.
- Task created.
- Task completed.
- Task deleted.
- Merge completed.
- Merge conflict detected.
- Synchronization completed.
- Export completed.
- Import completed.
- Metrics updated.

### Live Region Behavior

Live regions shall:

- Avoid excessive announcements.
- Use appropriate politeness levels.
- Not interrupt critical screen-reader output unnecessarily.
- Communicate meaningful changes.

### Loading States

Loading states shall be accessible.

Users shall be able to determine:

- What is loading.
- Whether the application is still processing.
- When the operation completes.
- Whether an operation failed.

### Progress Indicators

Progress indicators shall have accessible programmatic information.

Do not communicate progress through color or animation alone.

### Color

Color shall never be the sole means of communicating:

- Status.
- Priority.
- Errors.
- Warnings.
- Success.
- Selection.
- Focus.

### Contrast

Verify sufficient contrast for:

- Text.
- Icons.
- Controls.
- Focus indicators.
- Borders where necessary.
- Disabled-state indicators where applicable.
- Interactive components.

### Visual Settings

Test ART's visual accessibility settings.

Where supported, verify:

- Zoom.
- Text scaling.
- Contrast settings.
- High contrast.
- Reduced motion.
- Other visual preferences.

### Low-Vision Testing

Conduct testing with:

- Screen magnification.
- Browser zoom.
- Windows magnification.
- High-contrast settings.
- Increased text size.
- Reduced viewport dimensions.

### Reflow

Verify that content remains usable when the viewport is resized or
zoomed.

### Responsive Layout

Ensure responsive layouts do not:

- Hide required functionality.
- Create inaccessible horizontal scrolling.
- Change the logical reading order.
- Make controls unreachable.

### Reduced Motion

Respect the user's reduced-motion preference where applicable.

Avoid unnecessary animation.

### Tables

All data tables shall have appropriate:

- Headers.
- Captioning where appropriate.
- Programmatic relationships.
- Row/column associations.

### Sortable Tables

Accessible sorting shall communicate:

- Which column is sorted.
- Sort direction.
- Available sorting options.

### Filterable Tables

Filters shall be:

- Keyboard accessible.
- Screen-reader accessible.
- Clearly labeled.
- Programmatically associated with the data they filter.

### Task Management Accessibility

Review the entire Tasks interface.

Verify accessibility of:

- To Do list.
- Completed Tasks tab.
- Task creation.
- Task editing.
- Task deletion.
- Task priority.
- Due date/time.
- Assignee.
- Task status.
- Comments.
- @mentions\.
- Context menus.
- Sorting.
- Filtering.

### Task Priority

Task priority shall be:

- Visually understandable.
- Programmatically available.
- Exposed to assistive technologies.
- Included in accessible names/descriptions where appropriate.

### Task Sorting

Ensure sorting commands are accessible.

Supported sorting shall include, where applicable:

- Priority.
- Due date/time.
- Date added.

### Completed Tasks

Ensure users can:

- Navigate the Completed Tasks panel.
- Change completion status.
- Return completed tasks to the To Do list.

### Task Deletion

Task deletion shall include an accessible confirmation dialog.

The dialog shall:

- Clearly identify the task being deleted.
- Provide an accessible confirmation message.
- Provide Cancel.
- Provide Delete.
- Manage focus correctly.
- Return focus appropriately after closing.

### @Mentions

@mentions shall be accessible.

Verify:

- Keyboard operation.
- Screen-reader announcements.
- Accessible suggestions.
- User identification.
- Selection.
- Editing.
- Deletion.
- Notifications where applicable.

### Collaboration Accessibility

Review collaboration functionality for accessibility.

Test:

- Shared reports.
- Shared projects.
- Shared folders.
- Shared tasks.
- Shared progress logs.
- File-based collaboration.
- Server-based collaboration.
- Synchronization.
- Conflict detection.
- Merge conflicts.
- Merge dialogs.

### Merge Conflict Accessibility

Merge conflict dialogs shall:

- Clearly identify the conflicting changes.
- Identify affected users where appropriate.
- Provide accessible controls for choosing changes.
- Preserve focus.
- Provide keyboard operation.
- Communicate the resolution state.

### Collaboration Status

Communicate collaboration and synchronization status accessibly.

Examples include:

> "Changes synchronized."

> "Changes from another user are available."

> "Merge conflict detected."

### Authentication Accessibility

Review authentication workflows.

Verify accessibility of:

- Sign-in.
- Sign-up.
- Passwordless authentication.
- OAuth provider selection.
- Authenticator applications where supported.
- Account recovery.
- Device linking.
- Personal identity token configuration.

### OAuth

Ensure OAuth workflows are accessible for:

- Google.
- Microsoft.
- Amazon.
- GitHub.

ART shall not create inaccessible authentication dependencies.

### Passwordless Authentication

Verify that passwordless authentication is accessible to keyboard and
screen-reader users.

### User Identity Settings

Review the ART user-personalization settings established in Epic 49.

Verify accessibility of fields for:

- Name.
- Email address.
- Display name.
- Job title.
- Role.
- Personal token/code/passphrase.

### Device Linking

Device-linking workflows shall be accessible.

Users shall be able to:

- Generate or enter their personal token.
- Understand whether the token is valid.
- Complete device linking.
- Remove or revoke linked devices.

### Organization Accessibility

Review organization-management interfaces.

Verify accessibility of:

- Organization selection.
- Organization creation.
- Organization membership.
- Roles.
- Permissions.
- Invitations.
- Administration.
- Organization settings.

### Authorization Information

Users shall be able to determine their current role and applicable
permissions where appropriate.

### Enterprise Administration Accessibility

Review administrative interfaces created through Epic 63.

Verify accessibility of:

- User management.
- Role management.
- Permission management.
- Organization configuration.
- Audit logs.
- Policies.
- Administrative settings.

### Organization Metrics Accessibility

Review Organization Metrics from Epic 64.

Verify:

- Charts have accessible alternatives.
- Tables are accessible.
- Filters are accessible.
- Sorting is accessible.
- Drill-down is accessible.
- Metric definitions are accessible.
- Dynamic updates are announced appropriately.

### Charts

Charts shall not be the sole source of information.

Provide equivalent accessible information through:

- Tables.
- Text summaries.
- Accessible data views.

### Dashboard Accessibility

All dashboards shall have:

- Logical heading structures.
- Predictable navigation.
- Accessible controls.
- Keyboard access.
- Screen-reader support.

### Customizable Views

Users shall be able to customize working views without creating
inaccessible layouts.

### Drag and Drop

If drag-and-drop functionality exists, provide an accessible keyboard
alternative.

Users shall not be required to drag an item to perform a task.

### Context Menus

Context menus shall:

- Be keyboard accessible.
- Have appropriate menu semantics.
- Be reachable using standard keyboard interaction.
- Close appropriately.
- Return focus appropriately.

### Menu Bar

The ART menu bar shall be fully keyboard accessible.

Verify:

- Menus.
- Submenus.
- Menu items.
- Keyboard shortcuts.
- Checked states.
- Disabled states.

### Search

Search functionality shall be accessible.

Verify:

- Search labeling.
- Search instructions.
- Autocomplete.
- Result counts.
- Result navigation.
- Loading states.
- No-results messaging.

### Accessibility Standards Lookup

Review the WCAG Lookup Tool and other accessibility-standard lookup
functionality.

Verify:

- Search.
- Filters.
- WCAG version selection.
- Results.
- Links to W3C documentation.
- Accessible names.
- Keyboard navigation.

### Editors

Review all ART editors.

Verify:

- Keyboard accessibility.
- Screen-reader behavior.
- Formatting controls.
- Headings.
- Lists.
- Links.
- Tables.
- Images.
- Code.
- Status messages.

### Report Viewer

Review the Report Viewer for:

- Reading order.
- Headings.
- Links.
- Tables.
- Findings.
- Success Criteria.
- Accessibility Standards.
- Comments.
- Tasks.
- Interactive controls.

### Report Export Accessibility

Review exported:

- DOCX.
- PDF.
- HTML.
- CSV.
- XLSX.
- Other supported formats.

Where the target format supports accessibility, exported documents shall
preserve appropriate structure.

### PDF Accessibility

Where ART generates PDFs, verify:

- Tagged structure.
- Reading order.
- Headings.
- Lists.
- Tables.
- Links.
- Document language.
- Metadata.
- Alternative text where applicable.

### Word Accessibility

DOCX exports shall preserve:

- Heading structure.
- Lists.
- Tables.
- Links.
- Document metadata.
- Appropriate reading order.

### HTML Export Accessibility

HTML exports shall use appropriate semantic HTML.

### CSV/XLSX Accessibility

Spreadsheet exports shall use:

- Meaningful column headers.
- Logical table structures.
- Appropriate worksheet names.
- Accessible data relationships where supported.

### Images

All meaningful images shall have appropriate alternative text.

Decorative images shall not create unnecessary screen-reader output.

### Screenshots

Screenshots used in findings or reports shall have appropriate
descriptions or alternative text where needed.

### Icons

Meaningful icons shall have accessible names or equivalent text.

Decorative icons shall not create redundant announcements.

### Tooltips

Tooltips shall not be the sole means of communicating essential
information.

Tooltip content shall be accessible where used.

### Notifications

Notifications shall:

- Be accessible.
- Not rely solely on color.
- Not disappear before users can reasonably perceive them.
- Be announced appropriately when necessary.

### Error Handling

Errors shall be:

- Clearly communicated.
- Accessible.
- Actionable.
- Persistent long enough to understand.
- Associated with the relevant control where appropriate.

### Offline Errors

Offline and synchronization errors shall clearly explain:

- What happened.
- Whether the user's work was saved.
- What the user can do next.

### Network Errors

Network errors shall not cause inaccessible or silent failure states.

### Integration Accessibility

Review integrations established in Epic 62.

Ensure that integration workflows remain accessible when interacting
with:

- Jira.
- GitHub Issues.
- Microsoft Azure.
- Google Workspace.
- Other supported platforms.

### Import/Export Accessibility

Import and export workflows shall provide:

- Accessible file selection.
- Accessible progress information.
- Accessible success/error messages.
- Keyboard operation.

### Desktop Accessibility

The desktop application shall provide the same accessibility level as
the web application.

### Native Desktop Integration

Where ART uses native operating-system functionality, ensure the
resulting controls remain accessible.

### Desktop Installer Accessibility

The ART desktop installer shall provide an accessible installation
workflow.

### Desktop Update Accessibility

The Help → Check for Updates workflow shall be accessible.

Users shall be able to:

1.  Activate Check for Updates.
2.  Determine whether an update is available.
3.  Choose Update Now or Cancel.
4.  Complete the update using the keyboard.

### Web/Desktop Parity

Accessibility improvements shall be evaluated in both:

- Web ART.
- Desktop ART.

No accessibility feature shall be intentionally omitted from one
platform without a documented technical reason.

### Assistive Technology Coverage

In addition to screen readers, test ART with other assistive
technologies where available.

Potential technologies include:

- Screen magnifiers.
- Braille displays.
- Alternative keyboards.
- Switch access.
- Speech recognition.
- Voice control.
- Keyboard emulation.
- Other relevant accessibility technologies.

### Disability Testing

Where practical, recruit testers with diverse disabilities.

Testing should include people with:

- Blindness.
- Low vision.
- Deafness.
- Hard of hearing.
- Mobility disabilities.
- Dexterity limitations.
- Cognitive disabilities.
- Learning disabilities.
- Speech disabilities.
- Multiple disabilities.

### User Testing

Accessibility conformance testing shall be supplemented with real-world
usability testing.

### Automated Testing

Use automated accessibility testing tools where appropriate.

Potential tools include:

- axe.
- WAVE.
- Lighthouse.
- Other applicable automated testing tools.

Automated testing shall not be treated as a replacement for manual
testing.

### Manual Testing

Perform manual testing for:

- Keyboard access.
- Focus.
- Screen readers.
- Accessible names.
- Programmatic relationships.
- Dynamic content.
- Reading order.
- Error handling.
- Dialog behavior.

### Accessibility Regression Testing

Create automated and manual regression tests for previously corrected
accessibility defects.

### Regression Prevention

Accessibility fixes shall be incorporated into development practices so
the same defects are less likely to return.

### Component-Level Testing

Reusable ART components shall be tested independently.

Components may include:

- Buttons.
- Dialogs.
- Menus.
- Form fields.
- Tables.
- Tabs.
- Tooltips.
- Notifications.
- Dropdowns.
- Comboboxes.
- Date pickers.

### Accessibility Test Cases

Maintain accessibility test cases for critical workflows.

### Critical Workflow Testing

At minimum, test:

1.  Launch ART.
2.  Create a report.
3.  Open an existing report.
4.  Edit a report.
5.  Save a report.
6.  Import a report.
7.  Export a report.
8.  Create a finding.
9.  Edit a finding.
10. Create a task.
11. Edit a task.
12. Complete a task.
13. Reopen a completed task.
14. Delete a task.
15. Add an @mention.
16. Create a project.
17. Open project information.
18. Use Organization Metrics.
19. Use search.
20. Use filters.
21. Use sorting.
22. Use context menus.
23. Use the menu bar.
24. Use keyboard shortcuts.
25. Customize keyboard shortcuts.
26. Open Settings.
27. Customize user information.
28. Sign in.
29. Sign up.
30. Link a device.
31. Join an organization.
32. Use permissions.
33. Share a report.
34. Synchronize a report.
35. Resolve a merge conflict.
36. Use shared tasks.
37. Use shared progress logs.
38. Use integrations.
39. Check for desktop updates.
40. Use Undo.
41. Use Redo.

### Accessibility Performance

Accessibility functionality shall remain responsive under large
workloads.

Test screen-reader and keyboard interaction while:

- Loading large reports.
- Calculating metrics.
- Synchronizing files.
- Processing merge conflicts.
- Searching large datasets.
- Exporting large reports.

### Accessibility and Security

Accessibility fixes shall not weaken security controls.

Do not expose restricted information merely to make it available to
assistive technologies.

### Accessibility and Privacy

Accessible names, announcements, and notifications shall not
unnecessarily expose private information.

### Accessibility and Collaboration

Collaborative notifications shall reveal only information the user is
authorized to receive.

### Accessibility Documentation

Document known accessibility behaviors and supported technologies.

Include:

- Keyboard shortcuts.
- Screen-reader support.
- Accessibility settings.
- Known limitations.
- Supported browsers.
- Supported desktop environments.
- Supported assistive technologies.

### Accessibility Statement

ART shall provide an accessible Accessibility Statement describing:

- Accessibility goals.
- Standards targeted.
- Supported technologies.
- Known limitations.
- Testing practices.
- Contact method for accessibility feedback.

### Accessibility Feedback

Provide an accessible mechanism for users to report accessibility
problems.

Feedback should capture, where appropriate:

- Description.
- Steps to reproduce.
- Assistive technology.
- Browser or operating system.
- ART version.

### Remediation Prioritization

Accessibility defects shall be prioritized based on:

1.  Impact on users.
2.  Severity.
3.  Frequency.
4.  Number of affected workflows.
5.  Availability of workarounds.
6.  WCAG conformance impact.

### Critical Accessibility Defects

Critical accessibility defects that prevent users from completing
fundamental ART workflows shall receive the highest priority.

### WCAG Conformance Review

Perform a comprehensive WCAG 2.2 A/AA review.

Review applicable Success Criteria across:

- Perceivable.
- Operable.
- Understandable.
- Robust.

### Conformance Evidence

Maintain evidence of accessibility testing.

Evidence may include:

- Test cases.
- Results.
- Screenshots.
- Screen-reader output.
- Automated test results.
- Manual audit findings.
- Remediation records.

### Final Accessibility Audit

After remediation is complete, perform a full accessibility audit of
ART.

The audit shall cover both:

- Web application.
- Desktop application.

### Independent Review

Where possible, have accessibility reviewed by qualified independent
accessibility professionals.

### User Acceptance Testing

Conduct accessibility-focused user acceptance testing with real users
before declaring this epic complete.

### Definition of Done

Epic 66 shall be considered complete when:

- A comprehensive accessibility review has been completed.
- Systemic accessibility problems have been identified.
- Critical accessibility defects have been remediated.
- WCAG 2.2 A/AA requirements have been reviewed.
- Semantic HTML has been reviewed.
- Heading structures are correct.
- Landmarks are appropriate.
- Keyboard navigation works throughout ART.
- Focus management is correct.
- Modal dialogs are accessible.
- Context menus are accessible.
- Menu bars are accessible.
- Keyboard shortcuts work correctly.
- Custom keyboard shortcuts remain accessible.
- Screen-reader support has been tested.
- JAWS testing is complete.
- NVDA testing is complete.
- Narrator testing is complete.
- VoiceOver testing is complete.
- TalkBack testing is complete.
- ChromeVox testing has been performed where applicable.
- Braille-display testing has been performed.
- Low-vision testing has been completed.
- Magnification testing has been completed.
- Color and contrast requirements have been reviewed.
- Reflow and zoom have been tested.
- Reduced-motion behavior has been reviewed.
- Forms are accessible.
- Validation errors are accessible.
- Live status messages are accessible.
- Task management is accessible.
- Task priority is programmatically available.
- Completed Tasks functionality is accessible.
- Task deletion confirmation is accessible.
- @mentions are accessible.
- Collaboration functionality is accessible.
- File-based collaboration is accessible.
- Server-based collaboration is accessible.
- Merge conflict workflows are accessible.
- Authentication workflows are accessible.
- OAuth workflows are accessible.
- Passwordless authentication is accessible.
- Device linking is accessible.
- Organization management is accessible.
- Authorization information is accessible where appropriate.
- Enterprise administration is accessible.
- Organization Metrics are accessible.
- Charts have accessible alternatives.
- Tables are accessible.
- Dashboards are accessible.
- Search is accessible.
- Accessibility Standards Lookup is accessible.
- Editors are accessible.
- Report Viewer is accessible.
- Report exports have been reviewed for accessibility.
- DOCX exports preserve appropriate structure.
- PDF exports preserve appropriate accessibility where supported.
- HTML exports are accessible.
- Spreadsheet exports have meaningful structures.
- Images have appropriate alternative text.
- Notifications are accessible.
- Errors are accessible.
- Integrations remain accessible.
- Import/export workflows are accessible.
- Desktop ART is accessible.
- Desktop installation is accessible.
- Desktop update workflows are accessible.
- Web/desktop accessibility parity has been verified.
- Additional assistive technologies have been tested where available.
- Testing with people with diverse disabilities has been performed where
  practical.
- Automated accessibility testing has been performed.
- Manual accessibility testing has been performed.
- Accessibility regression testing exists.
- Critical workflows have been tested.
- Accessibility under load has been tested.
- Security and privacy have been preserved.
- Accessibility documentation is complete.
- An Accessibility Statement is available.
- Accessibility feedback mechanisms are available.
- A final accessibility audit has been completed.
- Accessibility issues discovered during testing have been remediated or
  formally documented with an appropriate plan.
- Independent accessibility review has been performed where available.
- Accessibility user acceptance testing has been completed.

### Final Requirement

ART shall not simply claim to be accessible because it follows
accessibility guidelines.

ART shall demonstrate accessibility through:

- Standards-based implementation.
- Manual testing.
- Automated testing.
- Assistive technology testing.
- Real-user testing.
- Regression testing.
- Continuous remediation.

The final product shall provide an accessibility-first experience across
the entire ART ecosystem.

A user who is blind, has low vision, has a mobility disability, uses a
screen reader, uses a braille display, relies on keyboard navigation,
uses magnification, or uses another assistive technology shall be able
to perform the same fundamental ART workflows without being forced into
a reduced-functionality version of the application.

Accessibility shall remain a core product requirement rather than an
optional enhancement.

## Epic 67 — Documentation, Help & User Onboarding

### Epic Overview

Create a comprehensive, accessible, maintainable, and user-friendly
documentation and onboarding system for the Accessibility Reporting Tool
(ART).

As ART has evolved into a full accessibility reporting, project
management, collaboration, reporting, metrics, integration, and
organization-management platform, users shall have clear documentation
explaining how to use its features and workflows.

Documentation shall support:

- New users.
- Experienced accessibility professionals.
- Testing teams.
- Project managers.
- Organization administrators.
- Report reviewers.
- Collaborators.
- Developers.
- Self-hosted deployments.
- Web application users.
- Desktop application users.
- Users working offline.
- Users using file-based collaboration.
- Users using server-based collaboration.

Documentation shall be fully accessible and usable with keyboard
navigation, screen readers, magnification, braille displays, and other
assistive technologies.

### General Requirements

ART documentation shall:

- Be written in clear, concise language.
- Use consistent terminology.
- Use logical heading structures.
- Provide task-oriented instructions.
- Include examples where useful.
- Avoid unnecessary technical jargon.
- Clearly distinguish required steps from optional steps.
- Clearly identify differences between web and desktop versions.
- Identify functionality that requires a server.
- Identify functionality that works without a server.
- Explain file-based collaboration.
- Explain server-based collaboration.
- Explain security and privacy considerations.

### Documentation Architecture

Create a centralized documentation system for ART.

The documentation system shall provide organized access to:

- Getting Started.
- Installation.
- User Guide.
- Report Creation.
- Report Management.
- Findings.
- Tasks.
- Progress Logs.
- Projects.
- Collaboration.
- Synchronization.
- Organization Management.
- Metrics.
- Integrations.
- Accessibility.
- Settings.
- Keyboard Shortcuts.
- Import/Export.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Troubleshooting.
- Frequently Asked Questions.
- Developer Documentation.

### Documentation Navigation

Documentation shall provide predictable navigation.

Users shall be able to:

- Navigate by headings.
- Navigate by sections.
- Search documentation.
- Use a table of contents.
- Return to the documentation home.
- Navigate to related topics.

### Documentation Search

Provide accessible documentation search.

Search shall support:

- Keyword searches.
- Feature names.
- Workflow names.
- Error messages.
- Common user questions.

### Search Results

Search results shall communicate:

- Result title.
- Relevant section.
- Search relevance where applicable.

### Keyboard Accessibility

Documentation navigation shall be fully keyboard accessible.

### Screen Reader Accessibility

Documentation shall be tested with:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox where applicable.

### Braille Accessibility

Documentation shall remain understandable when accessed through braille
displays.

### Documentation Headings

Use logical heading hierarchy.

The documentation shall not skip heading levels unnecessarily.

### Links

Links shall have meaningful accessible names.

Avoid vague link text such as:

- "Click here."
- "Read more."
- "Learn more."

when the destination can be described more specifically.

### External Links

External links shall clearly identify when they leave ART documentation.

Links that open a new tab shall communicate this appropriately to
assistive technology users.

### Code Examples

Code examples shall:

- Be accessible.
- Preserve formatting.
- Be copyable.
- Identify the programming language where appropriate.

### Screenshots

Screenshots may be used when they materially improve understanding.

Every meaningful screenshot shall have an appropriate alternative text
or equivalent textual description.

### Video Documentation

Where instructional videos are provided, they shall include:

- Captions.
- Accessible controls.
- Audio descriptions where appropriate.
- Text alternatives for essential information.

Videos shall not be the only way to learn a critical ART workflow.

### Getting Started

Create a Getting Started guide that explains:

1.  What ART is.
2.  Who ART is designed for.
3.  How to launch ART.
4.  How to create a report.
5.  How to save a report.
6.  How to open an existing report.
7.  How to export a report.
8.  How to import a report.
9.  How to use the Tasks system.
10. How to access Settings.
11. How to customize ART.
12. How to obtain help.

### Web Application

Document how to use ART through the web application.

Include:

- Launching ART.
- Browser requirements.
- Local storage.
- File operations.
- Offline functionality.
- Server-dependent functionality.

### Desktop Application

Document the ART desktop application.

Include:

- Downloading ART.
- Installing ART.
- Launching ART.
- Creating shortcuts.
- Updating ART.
- Uninstalling ART.
- Desktop-specific features.

### Desktop Download

Document the official ART website download workflow.

Users shall be able to understand:

1.  Where to obtain ART.
2.  How to download the installer.
3.  How to start installation.
4.  How to complete installation.
5.  How to launch ART.

Users shall not be required to obtain ART directly from GitHub merely to
install the standard desktop application.

### Desktop Updates

Document:

**Help → Check for Updates**

Explain:

1.  Activate Check for Updates.
2.  If an update is available, choose Update Now or Cancel.
3.  ART completes the update.

### Web/Desktop Synchronization

Explain how ART's web and desktop versions remain aligned.

Clearly communicate that functionality should remain consistent across
both platforms.

### Installation Requirements

Document supported:

- Operating systems.
- Browsers.
- Hardware considerations.
- Accessibility technologies.

### Local-First Usage

Explain that ART can be used without creating an account.

Document which capabilities are available without authentication.

### Server-Dependent Features

Clearly identify functionality requiring server connectivity.

Examples include:

- Real-time collaboration.
- Server synchronization.
- Server-based account services.
- Centralized organization management.
- Server-dependent integrations.

### File-Based Collaboration

Provide comprehensive documentation for ART's file-based collaboration
model.

Explain that users may collaborate through shared storage such as:

- Google Drive.
- Microsoft OneDrive.
- Dropbox.
- Network drives.
- Other compatible shared storage.

### File-Based Collaboration Workflow

Document how users can:

1.  Create a report.
2.  Save the `.art` file.
3.  Place it in a shared folder.
4.  Allow another user to open the report.
5.  Make changes.
6.  Save the updated file.
7.  Reopen or refresh the report.
8.  Detect changes.
9.  Compare changes.
10. Resolve conflicts.
11. Continue working.

### File-Based Collaboration Limitations

Clearly explain that file-based collaboration does not provide true
real-time collaboration.

Users shall understand that changes become available to other users when
the file is saved and subsequently accessed or synchronized.

### Server-Based Collaboration

Explain the differences between file-based and server-based
collaboration.

### Real-Time Collaboration

Document:

- Presence.
- Shared editing.
- Synchronization.
- Conflict handling.
- Merge behavior.

### Merge Conflicts

Provide a detailed explanation of ART's merge-conflict workflow.

Explain:

- What causes conflicts.
- How ART detects conflicts.
- How users are notified.
- How the Merge Changes modal works.
- How to select changes.
- How ART preserves non-conflicting changes.

### @Mentions

Document @mentions.

Explain where @mentions can be used, including:

- Shared reports.
- Shared projects.
- Shared organization folders.
- Shared tasks.
- Shared progress logs.

### Shared Tasks

Document:

- Creating shared tasks.
- Assigning tasks.
- Changing task status.
- Completing tasks.
- Reopening tasks.
- @mentions\.
- Collaboration behavior.

### Completed Tasks

Explain how completed tasks are moved to the Completed Tasks panel.

Document how users can:

- View completed tasks.
- Change completion status.
- Return a task to the To Do list.

### Shared Progress Logs

Document:

- Creating progress-log entries.
- Editing entries.
- Sharing entries.
- Collaborating on progress logs.
- @mentions\.

### Projects

Document:

- Creating projects.
- Opening projects.
- Managing reports.
- Managing tasks.
- Managing progress logs.
- Sharing projects.

### Organization Folders

Document organization folder functionality.

Explain how a shared parent folder can contain:

- Projects.
- Reports.
- Tasks.
- Progress logs.
- Other project resources.

### Folder Permissions

Explain that shared-folder permissions are generally managed by the
underlying storage provider.

Examples include:

- Google Drive.

- ART does not force account creation merely to access fundamental
  functionality.
- Documentation can be accessed from within ART.

- Accessible release notes exist.
- Documentation is maintained alongside major feature changes.
- Documentation accessibility testing is complete.
- Documentation user testing has been performed where practical.

- Accessibility contribution guidance exists.
- Documentation governance has been established.

### Final Requirement

ART documentation shall make the application understandable without
requiring users to already be accessibility experts, software
developers, or collaboration-platform specialists.

A new user should be able to discover ART, install or launch it, create
a report, save and reopen that report, manage tasks, customize the
application, and begin collaborating without requiring direct
assistance.

An experienced accessibility professional should be able to quickly
locate detailed information about advanced features.

An organization administrator should be able to understand
authentication, organization management, permissions, collaboration,
security, privacy, integrations, and deployment options.

A contributor or developer should be able to understand the
architecture, development workflow, accessibility requirements, testing
expectations, and contribution process.

Documentation shall be treated as part of the ART product—not as an
afterthought.

It shall be **accessible, accurate, searchable, maintainable, and
useful.**

## Epic 68 — Community Beta, Feedback & Adoption

### Epic Overview

Establish a structured community beta program for the Accessibility
Reporting Tool (ART) to allow accessibility professionals, testing
teams, organizations, educators, nonprofits, government offices,
developers, assistive technology users, and other interested
participants to use ART in real-world scenarios.

The purpose of this epic is to move ART from primarily development and
internal testing into controlled community use while establishing a
sustainable process for:

- Recruiting beta testers.
- Distributing ART.
- Collecting feedback.
- Reporting defects.
- Identifying usability problems.
- Identifying accessibility problems.
- Evaluating real-world workflows.
- Prioritizing improvements.
- Tracking beta progress.
- Communicating changes.
- Building an ART community.
- Preparing ART for broader adoption.

### General Requirements

The beta program shall:

- Be voluntary.
- Clearly communicate that ART is in beta.
- Provide users with appropriate expectations regarding stability.
- Encourage accessibility feedback.
- Encourage usability feedback.
- Encourage feature requests.
- Encourage security and privacy feedback.
- Protect participant privacy.
- Avoid requiring an account merely to evaluate ART's fundamental
  functionality.
- Support both web and desktop versions where available.

### Beta Program Goals

The beta program shall evaluate whether ART is:

- Useful.
- Accessible.
- Understandable.
- Reliable.
- Performant.
- Secure.
- Private.
- Convenient.
- Compatible with real-world accessibility workflows.
- Suitable for individual accessibility professionals.
- Suitable for small testing teams.
- Suitable for larger organizations.

### Beta Participants

Recruit participants with diverse backgrounds.

Potential participants include:

- Accessibility professionals.
- Digital accessibility analysts.
- Accessibility consultants.
- Accessibility testers.
- QA professionals.
- UX professionals.
- Developers.
- Project managers.
- Accessibility program managers.
- Educational institutions.
- Government offices.
- Nonprofit organizations.
- For-profit organizations.
- Startups.
- Large enterprises.
- Open-source contributors.
- Assistive technology users.

### Accessibility Beta Participants

Actively recruit participants with disabilities.

Where possible, include people who:

- Are blind.
- Have low vision.
- Are deaf.
- Are hard of hearing.
- Have mobility disabilities.
- Have dexterity limitations.
- Have cognitive disabilities.
- Have learning disabilities.
- Have speech disabilities.
- Have multiple disabilities.

### Assistive Technology Participants

Encourage testing with users of:

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox.
- Braille displays.
- Screen magnification.
- Voice control.
- Alternative input devices.
- Switch access.
- Other assistive technologies.

### Beta Recruitment

Create an accessible method for volunteers to express interest in
participating.

The recruitment process shall clearly explain:

- What ART is.
- What beta testing involves.
- What participants are expected to test.
- How feedback will be collected.
- What information participants may need to provide.
- How privacy will be protected.

### Beta Enrollment

Provide an accessible enrollment workflow.

Enrollment should collect only information necessary to administer the
beta program.

### Privacy

Do not unnecessarily collect:

- Personal information.
- Accessibility/disability information.
- Assistive technology information.
- Usage information.

When testing information is collected, clearly explain why it is needed.

### Beta Agreement

If a beta agreement is required, it shall:

- Be accessible.
- Clearly explain expectations.
- Explain data handling.
- Explain confidentiality requirements where applicable.
- Avoid unnecessarily restrictive requirements that discourage
  participation.

### Beta Distribution

Provide a simple method for participants to obtain ART.

Where the desktop application is available, participants should be able
to obtain the installer from the official ART website.

Users should not be required to navigate GitHub merely to download the
standard desktop application.

### Web Beta

Provide access to the web version through the official ART website.

### Desktop Beta

Provide appropriate installers for supported operating systems.

### Beta Version Identification

Clearly identify beta releases.

Users shall be able to determine:

- ART version.
- Build/release information.
- Whether they are using a beta version.

### Release Notes

Provide accessible release notes for each beta release.

Release notes shall describe:

- New functionality.
- Improvements.
- Accessibility fixes.
- Bug fixes.
- Known issues.
- Breaking changes where applicable.

### Beta Testing Scope

Participants should be encouraged to test complete workflows rather than
isolated controls.

### Core Workflow Testing

Test:

2.  Creating a report.
3.  Opening a report.

6.  Importing a report.

24. Using Organization Metrics.
25. Using dashboards.
26. Using custom working views.
27. Using search.
28. Using filters.
29. Using sorting.
30. Using keyboard shortcuts.
31. Customizing keyboard shortcuts.

### File-Based Collaboration Testing

- Google Drive.
- Microsoft OneDrive.
- Dropbox.

- Other shared storage systems.

### File-Based Collaboration Scenarios

Test:

- Sequential editing.
- Multiple users editing the same report.

- Resolving conflicts.

- Deployment requirements.

### Feedback System

Create a centralized mechanism for collecting beta feedback.

Feedback categories should include:

- Bug.
- Accessibility issue.
- Usability issue.
- Performance issue.
- Security concern.
- Privacy concern.
- Feature request.
- Documentation issue.
- Integration issue.
- Other.

### Feedback Form

Feedback submissions should capture, where appropriate:

- Description.
- Steps to reproduce.
- Expected behavior.
- Actual behavior.
- ART version.
- Web or desktop application.
- Browser.
- Operating system.
- Assistive technology.
- Frequency.
- Severity.

Only request information that is relevant to resolving the issue.

### Accessibility Feedback

Provide a dedicated accessibility feedback category.

### Assistive Technology Information

Allow users to identify the assistive technology involved without
requiring disclosure of disability status.

### Reproduction Information

Encourage users to provide:

- Steps.
- Sample data where safe.
- Screenshots where appropriate.
- Screen-reader output where appropriate.
- Error messages.

### Privacy of Submitted Data

Warn users not to submit:

- Passwords.
- Authentication tokens.
- API keys.
- Private client information.
- Confidential audit information.
- Other sensitive information.

### Security Reporting

Provide a separate mechanism for reporting security vulnerabilities.

Security reports should not be treated as ordinary public bug reports.

### Vulnerability Disclosure

Establish a responsible security-reporting process.

### Bug Triage

Create a structured process for reviewing beta feedback.

### Triage Categories

Classify issues by:

- Severity.
- Accessibility impact.
- Security impact.
- Privacy impact.
- Frequency.
- Reproducibility.
- Number of users affected.

### Critical Defects

Critical issues affecting:

- Data integrity.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Fundamental accessibility.
- Report loss.
- Authentication.
- Authorization.

shall receive the highest priority.

### Accessibility Defect Priority

Accessibility defects that prevent users from completing fundamental
workflows shall receive high priority.

### Duplicate Reports

Identify and consolidate duplicate feedback.

### Reproduction

Attempt to reproduce reported defects before assigning final severity
when practical.

### Issue Tracking

Convert validated beta feedback into actionable development issues.

Each issue should contain:

- Problem description.
- Expected behavior.
- Actual behavior.
- Reproduction steps.
- Environment.
- Severity.
- Priority.
- Accessibility impact where applicable.

### Feature Requests

Feature requests shall be evaluated separately from defects.

### Feature Request Evaluation

Consider:

- User demand.
- Accessibility benefit.
- Number of affected users.
- Product alignment.
- Technical feasibility.
- Security implications.
- Privacy implications.
- Maintenance cost.

### Community Voting

Where appropriate, allow community members to indicate interest in
feature requests.

Community voting shall inform—not automatically determine—development
priorities.

### Feedback Transparency

Where appropriate, publish aggregate information about:

- Common issues.
- Planned improvements.
- Frequently requested features.
- Accessibility improvements.

Do not expose private participant information.

### Beta Dashboard

Where practical, maintain internal beta metrics.

Potential metrics include:

- Number of participants.
- Number of active testers.
- Number of reports submitted.
- Number of bugs.
- Number of accessibility issues.
- Number of feature requests.
- Number of resolved issues.
- Average resolution time.

### Privacy-Aware Metrics

Beta metrics shall avoid unnecessary personal tracking.

### Beta Surveys

Conduct periodic surveys.

Potential topics include:

- Ease of use.
- Accessibility.
- Performance.
- Reliability.
- Collaboration.
- Documentation.
- Report quality.
- Overall usefulness.

### Accessibility Surveys

Include questions about:

- Screen-reader usability.
- Keyboard accessibility.
- Low-vision usability.
- Braille usability.
- Visual settings.
- Assistive technology compatibility.

### Usability Testing

Conduct structured usability sessions where practical.

Observe users completing realistic workflows.

### Task-Based Testing

Create representative tasks such as:

- Create an audit report.
- Add findings.
- Assign Success Criteria.
- Create remediation tasks.
- Share a project.
- Resolve a merge conflict.
- Export a report.

### Accessibility Usability Testing

Conduct task-based testing with assistive technology users.

### Beta Documentation

Provide beta-specific documentation.

Include:

- Getting started.
- Known issues.
- How to report bugs.
- How to report accessibility problems.
- How to report security concerns.
- How to update ART.
- How to provide diagnostic information safely.

### Known Issues

Maintain a current list of known issues.

Known issues should identify:

- Affected version.
- Affected platform.
- Description.
- Workaround where available.
- Planned resolution where appropriate.

### Beta Support

Provide an accessible support mechanism.

Potential methods include:

- GitHub Issues.
- Discussion forums.
- Email.
- Community channels.
- Other accessible support mechanisms.

### Community Discussions

Where community discussion systems are used, establish moderation and
accessibility expectations.

### Contributor Path

Allow beta testers to transition into contributors.

Potential contributions include:

- Bug reports.
- Accessibility testing.
- Documentation.
- Code.
- Translations.
- User research.
- Assistive technology testing.
- Design feedback.

### Community Recognition

Where appropriate, recognize contributors and beta testers.

Do not publicly identify participants without appropriate permission.

### Community Accessibility

All community resources used by ART shall themselves be accessible.

### Feedback Loop

Establish a continuous cycle:

1.  Release.
2.  Test.
3.  Collect feedback.
4.  Triage.
5.  Prioritize.
6.  Fix.
7.  Retest.
8.  Release.
9.  Communicate results.

### Regression Testing

Fixes resulting from beta feedback shall be added to regression testing
where appropriate.

### Accessibility Regression Testing

Accessibility defects discovered during beta testing shall become
regression tests whenever practical.

### Beta Release Cadence

Establish a manageable release cadence.

Do not release updates so frequently that participants cannot reasonably
evaluate changes.

### Desktop Updates

Where automatic desktop updates are supported, beta participants should
be able to use:

**Help → Check for Updates**

and choose:

- Update Now.
- Cancel.

### Web Updates

Web releases should follow the established deployment process.

### Web/Desktop Synchronization

Where technically possible, web and desktop releases should remain
synchronized.

### Version Compatibility

Clearly communicate compatibility between:

- Web versions.
- Desktop versions.
- `.art` files.
- Server versions.

### Backward Compatibility

Where practical, preserve compatibility with previously created `.art`
files.

### Data Migration

If a beta release requires data migration, provide:

- Clear notification.
- Backup guidance.
- Accessible progress information.
- Error recovery.

### Beta Data Protection

Beta participants shall not be expected to risk production data.

Encourage users to maintain backups of important reports.

### Production Data Warning

Clearly communicate whether a beta release is appropriate for production
accessibility audits.

### Safe Testing

Provide guidance for testing beta releases without jeopardizing
important audit data.

### Beta Exit Criteria

Define criteria for determining when beta testing can conclude.

Potential criteria include:

- Critical defects resolved.
- Major accessibility barriers resolved.
- Major usability issues resolved.
- Performance targets achieved.
- Security issues addressed.
- Privacy requirements satisfied.
- Documentation complete.
- User feedback indicates readiness.

### Community Readiness

Before broad release, evaluate whether ART is sufficiently stable for
general adoption.

### Adoption Preparation

Use beta feedback to prepare ART for adoption by:

- Accessibility teams.
- Companies.
- Government organizations.
- Educational institutions.
- Nonprofits.
- Consultants.
- Independent accessibility professionals.

### Enterprise Readiness Feedback

Use beta participation from larger organizations to identify:

- Procurement concerns.
- Security requirements.
- Privacy requirements.
- Deployment requirements.
- Authentication requirements.
- Integration requirements.
- Administration requirements.

### Government Readiness Feedback

Use government participation to identify:

- Accessibility requirements.
- Security requirements.
- Privacy requirements.
- Deployment restrictions.
- Procurement requirements.

### Accessibility Conformance Feedback

Use beta testing to identify any remaining WCAG-related issues.

### Documentation Feedback

Use beta testing to identify unclear or missing documentation.

### Roadmap Updates

Use validated beta feedback to update the ART roadmap.

### Release Prioritization

Prioritize post-beta development based on:

- Severity.
- User impact.
- Accessibility impact.
- Security impact.
- Privacy impact.
- Technical feasibility.
- Strategic value.

### Community Beta Report

At the conclusion of the beta phase, prepare a summary report.

The report should include:

- Number of participants.
- Types of participants.
- Major workflows tested.
- Major accessibility findings.
- Major usability findings.
- Major technical findings.
- Major performance findings.
- Major security findings.
- Major privacy findings.
- Major improvements made.
- Remaining known issues.
- Recommendations for general release.

### Accessibility Beta Report

Include a dedicated accessibility summary covering:

- Screen readers.
- Keyboard access.
- Low vision.
- Magnification.
- Braille.
- Other assistive technologies.
- Testing with people with disabilities.
- Remaining accessibility limitations.

### Community Communication

Communicate major beta milestones.

Examples include:

- Beta launch.
- Major releases.
- Major fixes.
- Accessibility improvements.
- Beta completion.

### General Availability Decision

Use objective evidence to determine whether ART is ready for broader
public adoption.

### Definition of Done

Epic 68 shall be considered complete when:

- A formal community beta program exists.
- Beta participation requirements are documented.
- An accessible beta enrollment process exists.
- Beta participants can obtain ART easily.
- Web beta access is available.
- Desktop beta distribution is available where applicable.
- Beta versions are clearly identified.
- Release notes are available.
- Diverse participants have been recruited.
- Accessibility testers have participated.
- Assistive technology users have participated.
- Real-world workflows have been tested.
- File-based collaboration has been tested.
- Server-based collaboration has been tested where available.
- Shared tasks have been tested.
- Shared progress logs have been tested.
- @mentions have been tested.
- Merge conflict workflows have been tested.
- Organization functionality has been tested.
- Organization Metrics have been tested.
- Authentication has been tested.
- Device linking has been tested.
- Integrations have been tested.
- Web/desktop workflows have been tested.
- Desktop installation has been tested.
- Desktop updating has been tested.
- A centralized feedback mechanism exists.
- Accessibility feedback can be submitted.
- Security vulnerabilities have a separate reporting mechanism.
- Feedback is categorized.
- Beta issues are triaged.
- Critical issues receive appropriate priority.
- Validated defects are converted into actionable development issues.
- Feature requests are evaluated.
- Community feedback can influence roadmap decisions.
- Beta metrics are collected appropriately.
- Privacy is preserved.
- Usability testing has been conducted.
- Accessibility usability testing has been conducted.
- Beta documentation exists.
- Known issues are documented.
- Beta support is available.
- Contributors can transition from beta participants into contributors.
- Community resources are accessible.
- A feedback-to-development loop is established.
- Regression tests are created for appropriate beta defects.
- Release cadence is established.
- Version compatibility is documented.
- Data migration procedures exist where needed.
- Backup guidance is available.
- Safe beta-testing guidance is available.
- Beta exit criteria are established.
- Community readiness has been evaluated.
- Adoption requirements have been identified.
- Enterprise feedback has been evaluated where available.
- Government feedback has been evaluated where available.
- Accessibility conformance feedback has been incorporated.
- Documentation feedback has been incorporated.
- The ART roadmap has been updated based on validated community
  feedback.
- A community beta summary report has been completed.
- An accessibility beta summary has been completed.
- Major beta milestones have been communicated.
- A documented decision has been made regarding readiness for broader
  adoption.

### Final Requirement

The community beta shall not simply be a period in which ART is made
available to the public.

It shall be a structured opportunity to learn whether ART actually works
for the people it is intended to serve.

The beta program shall provide a bridge between:

- Development and real-world use.
- Technical testing and practical workflows.
- Accessibility conformance and actual accessibility.
- Individual users and collaborative teams.
- Local-first usage and server-based collaboration.
- Small organizations and enterprise environments.

ART shall use the beta program to listen to its users, identify problems
that internal development cannot reveal, correct those problems, and
continuously improve the product.

The ultimate goal is to emerge from beta with an ART that is not merely
technically functional, but **trusted, accessible, usable, reliable,
secure, privacy-conscious, and genuinely valuable to the accessibility
community.**

## Epic 69 — Production Release, Public Launch & Adoption

### Epic Overview

Transition the Accessibility Reporting Tool (ART) from community beta
into a stable production release suitable for broad public use and
adoption.

This epic shall consolidate the results of the community beta program,
address release-blocking issues, establish production-release criteria,
prepare ART for public launch, and create the infrastructure and
processes necessary to support widespread adoption.

ART shall be positioned as a mature, accessible, privacy-conscious,
open-source accessibility reporting platform that can be used by:

- Individual accessibility professionals.
- Independent consultants.
- Accessibility testing teams.
- Startups.
- Small businesses.
- Large enterprises.
- Government agencies and offices.
- Educational institutions.
- Nonprofit organizations.
- For-profit organizations.
- Accessibility service providers.
- Software development teams.
- Quality assurance teams.

### General Requirements

The production release shall not occur simply because development is
complete.

ART shall be released for general use only after:

- Critical beta defects have been resolved.
- Critical accessibility barriers have been resolved.
- Major security issues have been addressed.
- Privacy requirements have been reviewed.
- Documentation is complete.
- Core workflows have been validated.
- Web and desktop versions have been validated.
- Collaboration workflows have been tested.
- Import/export functionality has been tested.
- Report outputs have been validated.
- Known limitations have been documented.

### Beta Exit Review

Review the results of Epic 68.

Evaluate:

- Beta feedback.
- Bug reports.
- Accessibility findings.
- Usability findings.
- Performance findings.
- Security findings.
- Privacy findings.
- Integration issues.
- Collaboration issues.
- Documentation issues.
- Feature requests.

### Release Blocking Issues

Identify issues that must be resolved before production release.

Release blockers shall include issues affecting:

- Data loss.
- Data corruption.
- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Fundamental accessibility.
- Core report functionality.
- File integrity.
- Collaboration integrity.
- Exported report integrity.

### Known Issues

Create a production known-issues list.

Each known issue shall identify:

- Description.
- Affected platform.
- Affected feature.
- Severity.
- Workaround where available.
- Planned resolution where appropriate.

### Production Readiness Review

Conduct a formal production-readiness review.

Review:

- Functionality.
- Accessibility.
- Security.
- Privacy.
- Performance.
- Reliability.
- Documentation.
- Deployment.
- Desktop distribution.
- Web deployment.
- Collaboration.
- Integrations.
- Support processes.

### Release Candidate

Create a production release candidate.

The release candidate shall represent the version intended for public
release.

### Release Candidate Testing

Perform final testing against the release candidate.

Test:

- Web application.
- Desktop application.
- Authentication.
- Device linking.
- File-based collaboration.
- Server-based collaboration.
- Reports.
- Tasks.
- Projects.
- Progress Logs.
- Organization Metrics.
- Integrations.
- Import/export.
- Settings.
- Accessibility.
- Performance.

### Accessibility Release Validation

Perform a final accessibility validation before production release.

Verify:

- Keyboard accessibility.
- Screen-reader support.
- Low-vision support.
- Visual settings.
- Focus management.
- Accessible names.
- Forms.
- Dialogs.
- Menus.
- Tables.
- Live regions.
- Dynamic content.
- Error handling.

### Assistive Technology Validation

- JAWS.
- NVDA.
- Narrator.
- VoiceOver.
- TalkBack.
- ChromeVox.
- Braille displays.
- Magnification.
- Other assistive technologies.

### Security Release Validation

Perform final security review.

Verify:

- Authentication.
- Authorization.
- Session handling.
- OAuth.
- Passwordless authentication.
- Device linking.
- Data storage.
- File handling.
- Integrations.
- Server communication.
- Access controls.

### Privacy Release Validation

Verify that the production release complies with ART's privacy
requirements.

Confirm:

- Data collection is minimized.
- Local data remains under user control.
- Server data is appropriately protected.
- Authentication information is protected.
- Diagnostic information is appropriately handled.
- Privacy documentation is current.

### Performance Validation

Verify that ART performs acceptably under realistic workloads.

Test:

- Large reports.
- Large projects.
- Large numbers of tasks.
- Large numbers of findings.
- Large organizations.
- Large metrics datasets.
- Large exports.
- Large shared reports.

### Reliability Testing

Verify that ART behaves predictably during:

- Interrupted saves.
- Interrupted exports.
- Interrupted imports.
- Network failures.
- Synchronization failures.
- Merge conflicts.
- Application crashes.
- Browser refreshes.
- Desktop application restarts.

### Data Integrity

operations.

### Backup and Recovery

Validate documented backup and recovery procedures.

### Web Release

- Deployment.
- HTTPS.

- Version identification.

2.  Activate the download link.
